docs.title: 2.8 Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM): Proposals and Why They Are Hard
docs.text:
QRAM would be a memory that, given an address register in superposition, returns a superposition of the stored data in time logarithmic in memory size. Many fault-tolerant QML speed-ups assume it. Designs such as the bucket-brigade exist on paper, but building one that is large, fast and error-tolerant remains an unsolved engineering and physics challenge, and some analyses question whether it can ever pay off.

Bucket-brigade QRAM for 8 memory cells. Address bits route one level at a time; only routers on queried paths activate.

Think of it like…

QRAM is like a librarian who could fetch every book you ask for at once by walking a single corridor — the plan looks elegant, but the corridor needs a switch at every junction, and any one faulty switch spoils every book.

Real-world example

Theo's resource estimate for a quantum regression assumes a QRAM holding 2^30 numbers. The bucket-brigade design needs about 10^9 routing elements, each needing high fidelity, and if queries must be error-corrected the routing hardware could instead run a fast classical parallel algorithm. He reports the speed-up as 'conditional on passive, scalable QRAM'.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Store N classical values in a memory indexed by log₂N address bits.
  2. Load a superposition of addresses Σ α_i|i⟩ into the address register.
  3. Route each address through a binary tree of quantum switches (bucket-brigade) to the data cell.
  4. Copy data into an output register: Σ α_i|i⟩|x_i⟩; then un-route to disentangle the tree.
  5. Repeat for every query — algorithms often need many queries per run.

Who uses it

Fault-tolerant algorithm designers, quantum-architecture researchers and anyone evaluating linear-algebra speed-up claims must understand QRAM.

Key takeaway

Know the distinction: QRAM queries in O(log N) depth but need O(N) physical components; QROM circuits on standard qubits cost about O(N) gates per query.

Going deeper

  • A bucket-brigade QRAM for N cells needs about N routers arranged in a log₂N-level tree; a query activates O(log N) routers per branch of the superposition.
  • Hann et al. (2021) showed bucket-brigade query infidelity scales polylogarithmically with N under generic local noise, much better than fan-out designs.
  • Jaques and Rattew argue that if the memory must be actively controlled and error-corrected, the O(N) control hardware could perform comparably fast classical parallel computation, erasing most asymptotic advantage.
  • In fault-tolerant chemistry algorithms, data loading is done with QROM circuits whose T-count scales with the number of entries, a cost explicitly included in modern resource estimates.
  • No large-scale QRAM has been demonstrated as of 2026; small proof-of-principle routing experiments and proposals (superconducting-phononic, photonic, atomic) remain at the research stage.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating QRAM as existing hardware when quoting speed-ups; it is a hypothetical component.
  • Confusing O(log N) query depth with O(log N) hardware: the memory still needs about N physical elements.
  • Ignoring that dequantisation results assume classical analogues of the same data structure, often removing the speed-up.

docs.title: 2.9 Quantum Data vs Classical Data
docs.text:
Classical data is numbers in files, which must be encoded into qubits at a cost. Quantum data is already a quantum state — produced by a quantum simulation, a chemistry experiment, a quantum sensor or a quantum network — so there is no loading step, but also no way to copy it or read it fully. Many of the clearest QML advantages are about quantum data.

Classical vs quantum data for QML

Classical data Quantum data Form Numbers in files States from a quantum process Loading cost Encoding circuit, often Ω(d) None (already quantum) Copying Free Impossible (no-cloning) Key resource Training points, gates Copies / experiments Proven advantage Contrived tasks only Exponential in some tasks Example Fraud transactions Spin-chain ground states

Quantum data skips loading but turns every training example into an experiment.

Think of it like…

Classical data is like a printed photograph you must scan into a computer; quantum data is like a live scene in front of the camera — nothing to scan, but you only get to take a limited number of snapshots and the scene changes when you look.

Real-world example

Physicist Aiko's quantum simulator produces ground states of a spin chain at different magnetic fields. Rather than measuring each state fully (which would need exponentially many measurements), she feeds the states directly into a small quantum convolutional circuit that outputs 'ordered' or 'disordered' after a few hundred shots per state.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the data source: a file (classical), a quantum process producing states (quantum), or measurements of states (classical data about quantum systems).
  2. For classical data, budget encoding cost; for quantum data, budget the number of copies (experiments) available.
  3. Decide whether to measure first (convert to classical shadows or features) or process coherently with a quantum model.
  4. Use quantum memory and joint measurements of several copies when available — this is where exponential separations appear.
  5. Evaluate with the right metric: accuracy per copy or per experiment, not only per training point.

Who uses it

Quantum physicists, quantum-sensing engineers, quantum chemists and learning theorists work with quantum data.

Key takeaway

State it clearly in interviews: quantum data avoids the input problem, and provable exponential advantages exist for learning from it — but every copy costs an experiment and cannot be cloned.

Going deeper

  • Huang, Kueng and Preskill (PRL 2021) proved that for predicting many observables, quantum-memory learners can need exponentially fewer copies than conventional learners, a pure QQ advantage.
  • Classical shadows need about O(log M / ε²) snapshots to estimate M local observables to precision ε, making them the standard bridge from quantum data to classical ML.
  • When quantum data must be measured anyway, the problem becomes classical ML on measurement records; Huang et al. (Science 2022, 'Provably efficient machine learning for quantum many-body problems') showed classical ML can predict ground-state properties efficiently from such data.
  • Benchmark quantum datasets such as NTangled (Schatzki et al. 2021) provide states with controlled entanglement for testing QQ models; the tools chapter lists available datasets.
  • Because each copy is consumed by measurement, training on quantum data is limited by experiment repetition rates, typically thousands of shots per second on superconducting hardware.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Applying CQ intuitions to quantum data: there is no encoding step, but there is a copy budget.
  • Assuming quantum data can be stored and reused like a file; it decoheres and cannot be cloned.
  • Measuring everything with full tomography when classical shadows or coherent processing would need far fewer copies.

docs.title: 2.10 Encoding and Expressivity: The Fourier-Series View
docs.text:
A key insight (Schuld, Sweke & Meyer 2021) is that a quantum model with rotation encodings computes a sum of sines and cosines of the input — a truncated Fourier series. The encoding decides which frequencies are available; the trainable gates decide how much of each frequency appears. So the encoding, not just the trainable circuit, sets what a model can possibly learn.

Max frequency vs number of RY uploads of x. Each Pauli-rotation upload adds one integer frequency; scaled encodings grow faster.

Think of it like…

The encoding is like choosing which keys exist on a piano; the trainable part decides how hard each key is pressed. If the piano lacks high notes, no amount of practice will play a high melody.

Real-world example

Ben fits the target f(x) = sin(3x) with a model using one RY(x) encoding. The best fit is a flat line, because only frequency 1 is available and sin 3x is orthogonal to it. Re-uploading x three times adds frequencies 2 and 3, and the model fits the target almost perfectly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write each encoding gate as e^{−i x G} with generator G (for Pauli rotations, G = σ/2 with eigenvalues ±1/2).
  2. The accessible frequencies are all differences of sums of generator eigenvalues across the encoding gates.
  3. With L Pauli-rotation encodings of x, the spectrum is the integers −L…L.
  4. Trainable blocks determine the Fourier coefficients c_ω; flexible blocks can realise many coefficient sets.
  5. Match the spectrum to the target's smoothness by scaling inputs and choosing the number of uploads.

Who uses it

QML theorists, model designers choosing encodings, and reviewers assessing expressivity claims use this view.

Key takeaway

One-line summary for interviews: 'quantum models with angle encodings are partial Fourier series — the encoding fixes the frequencies, the trainable circuit fixes the coefficients'.

Going deeper

  • For an encoding gate e^{−ixG}, frequencies are differences λ_j − λ_k of sums of generator eigenvalues; Pauli generators σ/2 have eigenvalues ±1/2, so each upload contributes differences in {−1, 0, 1}.
  • Schuld, Sweke and Meyer showed that serial and parallel repetitions give the same spectrum, and that with sufficiently flexible trainable blocks a model can approach any square-integrable function as uploads grow.
  • The number of independent Fourier coefficients grows with the spectrum, but the trainable circuit has finitely many parameters, so not every coefficient combination is reachable in practice.
  • Because models are trigonometric polynomials, their outputs are periodic in x; inputs should be scaled into less than one period to avoid wrap-around artefacts in predictions.
  • Fourier analysis also enables dequantisation: if a model's spectrum is small and coefficients can be estimated, a classical surrogate can replace it (Schreiber et al. 2023; Landman et al. 2022).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Adding trainable layers to fix underfitting when the real limit is the encoding's frequency spectrum.
  • Confusing expressivity (functions representable) with expressibility (coverage of Hilbert space).
  • Assuming larger spectra are always better: they can cause overfitting and harder training.

docs.title: Try it: Compute a model's Fourier coefficients numerically
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml, numpy as np
dev = qml.device('default.qubit', wires=1)

@qml.qnode(dev)
def f(x):
    for _ in range(3):                 # 3 uploads → frequencies up to 3
        qml.RY(x, wires=0); qml.RX(0.7, wires=0)
    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(0))

xs = np.linspace(0, 2*np.pi, 64, endpoint=False)
coeffs = np.fft.rfft([f(x) for x in xs]) / 64
print(np.round(np.abs(coeffs[:6]), 4))   # zero above frequency 3

A trained 4-feature model's 81 coefficients are fitted from data, then deployed without a QPU. Exponentially large spectraEncoding design research · Concept · Research · Advanced Encodings with scaled generators can give exponentially many frequencies, but coefficients then become hard to control or estimate. Scale factors 1, 2, 4, …, 2^9 give frequencies up to 1,023 on 10 encodings.

docs.title: 2.11 Dimensionality Reduction Before Encoding
docs.text:
Real data is wide — an image has hundreds of pixels, a genome thousands of features — but today's circuits handle only a handful of inputs. So almost every QML pipeline first shrinks data with classical tools: principal component analysis, autoencoders, feature selection, downsampling or features from a pre-trained network. This step is necessary but can quietly do most of the learning.

Squeezing wide data into a few qubits. Fit every transform on training data only; then encode.

Think of it like…

It is like summarising a 300-page novel into an 8-sentence blurb before translating it: the translation is now feasible, but the quality of the blurb largely decides what the reader understands.

Real-world example

Ola compresses 784-pixel MNIST digits '3' versus '8' to 8 principal components that keep under half of the pixel variance. An 8-qubit classifier reaches 96% test accuracy — but logistic regression on the same 8 components reaches 98%, showing the PCA step carries most of the information.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Standardise features (zero mean, unit variance) so no feature dominates.
  2. Choose a reducer: PCA, feature selection, autoencoder, downsampling or pre-trained embeddings.
  3. Pick the output dimension to match the qubit budget and encoding (e.g. 8 features → 8 qubits).
  4. Fit the reducer on training data only, then apply it to validation and test data.
  5. Rescale reduced features to angle ranges and always evaluate a classical model on the same reduced features.

Who uses it

Every applied QML practitioner and data scientist trying quantum models on realistic datasets does this step.

Key takeaway

Best practice to state in interviews: fit PCA/scalers on training data only, and report a classical baseline on the same reduced features.

Going deeper

  • PCA via singular value decomposition costs about O(min(m·d², m²·d)) for m samples and d features — seconds for typical QML datasets — so it is never the bottleneck.
  • In MNIST-style QML demos, 8-16 principal components or 4×4 to 8×8 downsampled images are standard; amplitude encoding of 16×16 images needs 8 qubits but deep circuits.
  • Transfer learning with 'dressed quantum circuits' (Mari et al. 2020) wraps a quantum layer between classical layers, so the classical network does most of the feature engineering.
  • When a reducer is strong, the quantum model's job becomes easy and gains are hard to attribute; ablation studies remove the quantum layer to measure its contribution.
  • Fitting scalers and PCA inside each cross-validation fold (e.g. scikit-learn Pipeline) avoids leakage and gives honest estimates.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Fitting PCA or scalers on all data before splitting, which leaks test information.
  • Crediting the quantum model for accuracy that the classical reducer already delivered.
  • Reducing to too few components and blaming the quantum model for poor accuracy.

docs.title: Try it: A leak-free PCA → angle pipeline (scikit-learn)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=1)
prep = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), PCA(n_components=8), MinMaxScaler((0, np.pi)))
Atr = prep.fit_transform(Xtr)   # fit on train only
Ate = prep.transform(Xte)
print(Atr.shape, Atr.min().round(2), Atr.max().round(2))

docs.title: 2.12 Qubit Count and Depth Budgets
docs.text:
Every encoding spends two scarce resources: qubits (width) and gates (depth). Today's devices offer tens to a few hundred qubits, but noise means only a limited number of two-qubit gates can run before results become unreliable. Planning an encoding means checking it fits both budgets — plus a shot budget and, for simulation, a memory budget.

Qubits needed for 16 features. Amplitude encoding saves qubits but pays in gates; basis encoding pays in qubits.

Think of it like…

It is like packing for a budget flight: there is a limit on the number of bags (qubits) and on total weight (gate depth). A clever packing (encoding) gets everything important on board without excess-baggage fees (noise).

Real-world example

Rosa has 16 features and a device with 99.5% two-qubit fidelity. Basis encoding at 8 bits needs 128 qubits (too many). A full ZZ map needs 240 CNOTs per repetition, giving only about 30% clean runs before routing. Angle encoding on 16 qubits plus a linear entangling layer needs 15 CNOTs per layer — she chooses that with 3 re-uploads.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List budgets: available qubits, two-qubit fidelity, connectivity, shots per circuit, simulator memory.
  2. Compute each candidate encoding's qubits and two-qubit gate count for your feature count.
  3. Add routing overhead after transpiling to the target topology.
  4. Estimate circuit success ≈ (two-qubit fidelity)^(number of two-qubit gates).
  5. Keep total two-qubit gates where estimated success stays comfortably high (e.g. above 50%), or plan error mitigation.

Who uses it

QML engineers preparing hardware runs, researchers sizing simulations and reviewers checking feasibility use these budgets.

Key takeaway

Handy rule: with two-qubit fidelity F, about ln 2 / (1 − F) gates halve your signal — roughly 140 gates at 99.5% and 700 at 99.9%.

Going deeper

  • With two-qubit fidelity F, the number of gates that halves expected signal is about ln 2 / (1 − F): 69 at 99%, 139 at 99.5% and 693 at 99.9%.
  • Coherence budgets: superconducting two-qubit gates take tens to hundreds of nanoseconds and T2 is typically 50-300 µs, allowing on the order of 10^3 sequential layers at best; ion gates take tens to hundreds of microseconds but coherence lasts seconds.
  • IBM's Nighthawk was announced as supporting circuits with up to 5,000 two-qubit gates in 2025, with stated targets of 7,500 by end of 2026; treat such figures as upper bounds requiring mitigation.
  • Simulation memory: complex128 needs 16 GiB at 30 qubits and 256 GiB at 34; adjoint differentiation needs a few extra state copies, so budget 2-3× the state size.
  • A full training run's shot cost is roughly steps × batch size × circuits per gradient × shots, which is why most QML training happens in simulation and hardware is reserved for evaluation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Budgeting on the logical circuit rather than the transpiled one, which can have several times more CNOTs.
  • Assuming all device qubits are equally good; pick the best-calibrated subset for your circuit.
  • Forgetting that every shot of every training step pays the full encoding cost.

docs.title: Try it: Count gates for candidate encodings (PennyLane specs)
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml, numpy as np
x = np.random.rand(8)
dev = qml.device('default.qubit', wires=8)

for name, enc in {'angle': lambda: qml.AngleEmbedding(x, wires=range(8)),
                  'iqp':   lambda: qml.IQPEmbedding(x, wires=range(8))}.items():
    @qml.qnode(dev)
    def c():
        enc(); return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(0))
    print(name, qml.specs(c, level='device')())   # MultiRZ = one ZZ term (2 CNOTs on hardware)

docs.title: 2.13 Choosing an Encoding for Images, Tabular Data and Graphs
docs.text:
There is no single best encoding. Tabular data usually suits scaled angle encoding with re-uploading; images need heavy reduction or special image encodings; graphs map naturally onto qubit couplings and Hamiltonians; categorical data suits basis or one-hot encoding. Good choices respect the data's structure and symmetries and fit the hardware budget.

Starting-point encodings by data type

Tabular Images Graphs Pre-processing Standardise, PCA/selection CNN features, PCA, downsample Node/edge features, weights Default encoding Angle + re-uploading Angle on features Edges → ZZ couplings Alternative Dense angle, IQP Amplitude, FRQI/NEQR Rydberg evolution kernel Structure to keep Feature scales Locality Permutation symmetry Classical rival Gradient boosting CNN Graph neural network

Defaults to try first; always compare with the best classical model for that data type.

Think of it like…

Choosing an encoding is like choosing a container for moving house: books go in small sturdy boxes, clothes in bags, a sofa needs its own wrapping. Forcing everything into one container type wastes space or breaks things.

Real-world example

Kemi's team has three tasks. Customer churn (12 numeric columns) gets standard scaling and a 12-qubit angle encoding with 2 re-uploads. X-ray thumbnails are reduced with a pre-trained CNN to 8 features. A molecule toxicity set is encoded graph-wise, edges becoming ZZ couplings. Each is compared with XGBoost, a CNN and a graph neural network.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the data type and size: tabular, image, graph, sequence, text, categorical, or quantum.
  2. Identify structure to preserve: locality (images), permutation symmetry (graphs, sets), periodicity, order.
  3. Shortlist encodings that respect the structure and fit the qubit/gate budget.
  4. Prototype two or three in simulation with the same trainable model and tuned input scaling.
  5. Pick by validation performance, robustness to noise and cost — then test once.

Who uses it

Applied QML scientists, consultants scoping pilots and students designing projects make these choices.

Key takeaway

A strong answer names a default per data type — tabular: angle + re-uploading; images: classical features then angle, or amplitude for compression; graphs: Hamiltonian/coupling encodings respecting permutation symmetry.

Going deeper

  • Bowles, Ahmed and Schuld (2024) observed that model rankings varied by dataset family, supporting the practice of trying more than one encoding with tuned input scaling.
  • Image-specific encodings such as FRQI (2011) and NEQR (2013) need 2n position qubits for a 2^n × 2^n image plus colour qubits, and their preparation circuits are deep, so they remain mostly theoretical for ML.
  • Geometric QML (Larocca et al. 2022; Meyer et al. 2023) builds invariances into circuits, shrinking the hypothesis space and often improving trainability and sample efficiency.
  • For graphs, Pasqal's quantum evolution kernel (2021) and permutation-equivariant QAOA-style circuits are the main proposals; graph neural networks remain the classical benchmark to beat.
  • Quantinuum's lambeq toolkit (released 2021) converts sentences into string diagrams and then circuits, a structure-based alternative to compressing word embeddings into angles.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using one encoding for every dataset: performance depends strongly on matching encoding to data structure.
  • Encoding raw pixels of large images directly instead of compressing them first.
  • Ignoring symmetries such as node relabelling, which forces the model to learn them from data.

docs.title: 2.14 Worked Examples with Circuits
docs.text:
This section walks through small encodings you can check by hand or run in seconds: basis-encoding a number, amplitude-encoding a 4-vector with a single rotation, computing an angle-encoding kernel value, counting gates in a ZZ map, and sizing image encodings. Working the numbers yourself builds intuition faster than reading formulas.

A complete 2-qubit worked circuit. Read from bottom to top: encode, entangle, train, measure.

Think of it like…

Like learning to cook by making three simple dishes start to finish rather than reading the whole cookbook: each example teaches a technique you will reuse.

Real-world example

In a study group, Yusuf and Chloe split the examples: Yusuf verifies that RY(1.855) on qubit 0 prepares (0.6, 0, 0.8, 0) in PennyLane's ordering; Chloe computes the angle-encoding kernel between (0.2, 1.0) and (1.2, 1.0) as cos²(0.5) ≈ 0.770 and confirms it with a simulator.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write the input and the target state or quantity on paper.
  2. Choose the encoding and draw the circuit (gates per qubit, in order).
  3. Compute the expected amplitudes, probabilities or kernel values by hand.
  4. Run the circuit in a simulator and compare.
  5. Count qubits and two-qubit gates to check the hardware budget.

Who uses it

Students, interview candidates and engineers validating library behaviour use small worked examples like these.

Key takeaway

In interviews, being able to compute a kernel value or a single-qubit amplitude by hand is a strong signal of real understanding.

Going deeper

  • For amplitudes (a, 0, b, 0) with a, b ≥ 0 the state factorises as (a|0⟩ + b|1⟩)⊗|0⟩, so a single RY(2·arccos a) suffices; generic 4-vectors need two RY layers plus CNOTs.
  • The compute-uncompute kernel uses 2× the encoding depth; the swap test instead uses 2n + 1 qubits and controlled-SWAPs but works for mixed states.
  • Bit-ordering check: PennyLane lists qubit 0 as the leftmost bit while Qiskit lists it as the rightmost, so the same state prints as '1101' or '1011' — always confirm with a known basis state.
  • Kernel matrices are symmetric with ones on the diagonal in the noise-free case; on hardware, diagonal entries below 1 directly measure noise and can guide mitigation.
  • Shot-noise intuition: a kernel entry near 0.01 estimated with 1,000 shots has a standard error of about 0.003 — relative error 30%, illustrating why concentrated kernels need many shots.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing Qiskit and PennyLane bit orders when checking worked answers.
  • Forgetting RY(θ) uses θ/2 in its amplitudes: cos(θ/2), not cos θ.
  • Estimating tiny kernel values with few shots and trusting the noisy result.

docs.title: Try it: Compute-uncompute kernel for the worked example (PennyLane)
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml, numpy as np
dev = qml.device('default.qubit', wires=2)   # exact; add shots to see sampling noise

@qml.qnode(dev)
def kernel_circuit(x1, x2):
    qml.AngleEmbedding(x1, wires=[0, 1], rotation='Y')
    qml.adjoint(qml.AngleEmbedding)(x2, wires=[0, 1], rotation='Y')
    return qml.probs(wires=[0, 1])

k = kernel_circuit(np.array([0.2, 1.0]), np.array([1.2, 1.0]))[0]
print(round(float(k), 3), 'exact:', round(np.cos(0.5)**2, 3))

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
A
docs.text: Adjoint differentiation Simulator-only method that computes all parameter gradients of a circuit by running it backwards, costing about one extra pass. Amplitude encoding Storing 2^n normalised numbers in the amplitudes of n qubits; compact, but preparing the state usually needs deep circuits. Amplitude estimation Fault-tolerant algorithm estimating probabilities or averages with quadratically fewer samples than classical Monte Carlo. Angle encoding Encoding each feature as a rotation angle on a qubit; simple and shallow but uses one qubit per feature. Ansatz The chosen structure of a parameterised circuit, such as hardware-efficient layers or a problem-inspired design.

docs.title: B
docs.text: Barren plateau A training landscape where gradients shrink exponentially with qubit count, making optimisation practically impossible. Basis encoding Writing a bit-string directly into qubit states |0> and |1>, one bit per qubit. BQP Bounded-error quantum polynomial time: the class of problems a quantum computer can solve efficiently with small error.

docs.title: C
docs.text: Circuit Born machine (QCBM) A generative model that samples bit-strings from the measurement distribution of a trained quantum circuit. Classical shadows Compact classical descriptions of a quantum state from randomised measurements, used to predict many properties efficiently. Classical surrogate A classical model that reproduces a trained quantum model's predictions, testing whether the quantum part is needed. CUDA-Q NVIDIA's open-source programming model for hybrid quantum-classical programs, optimised for GPU simulation.

docs.title: D
docs.text: Data re-uploading Encoding the same input several times between trainable layers to increase a quantum model's expressivity. Density matrix A matrix description of a quantum state that can represent noise and mixtures, needing 4^n entries for n qubits. Dequantisation Finding a classical algorithm that matches a claimed quantum speed-up, as Ewin Tang did for recommendation systems.

docs.title: E
docs.text: Entanglement Correlation between qubits that cannot be described by treating each qubit separately. Error mitigation Techniques such as ZNE, PEC and readout correction that reduce noise bias in expectation values at a cost in shots. Expectation value The average outcome of measuring an observable, estimated on hardware from many shots. Exponential concentration The tendency of quantum kernel values or cost functions to cluster around a fixed value as qubits grow. Expressibility How well a parameterised circuit's states cover the space of all possible states.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Fault-tolerant quantum computing Computing with error-corrected logical qubits so long algorithms can run reliably; not yet available at useful scale. Feature map A circuit that maps classical data into a quantum state; the quantum analogue of a kernel feature map. Fidelity kernel A quantum kernel defined as the squared overlap between the states encoding two data points.

docs.title: G
docs.text: Generalisation How well a model trained on some data performs on new, unseen data.

docs.title: H
docs.text: Hamiltonian The operator describing a quantum system's energy; used as observables, encodings and learning targets. Hardware-efficient ansatz A circuit built from gates and connections native to a device, minimising depth but prone to barren plateaus. HHL algorithm Harrow-Hassidim-Lloyd quantum algorithm for linear systems; exponential speed-up only under strict assumptions. Hilbert space The mathematical space of quantum states; its dimension doubles with every added qubit. Hybrid quantum-classical model A model where a classical computer optimises or post-processes the outputs of quantum circuits.

docs.title: I
docs.text: Inductive bias The assumptions a model family builds in, which decide which patterns it learns easily. ISA circuit A circuit already transpiled to a specific device's native gates and qubit layout, as required by IBM's V2 primitives.

docs.title: K
docs.text: Kernel method A learning approach, such as the support vector machine, that compares data points through a similarity function.

docs.title: L
docs.text: Logical qubit An error-corrected qubit encoded across many physical qubits.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Measurement Reading out qubits, which collapses the state and returns random outcomes with probabilities set by the state.

docs.title: N
docs.text: NISQ Noisy intermediate-scale quantum: today's era of tens to hundreds of imperfect qubits without full error correction. Noise model A description of gate, readout and decoherence errors used to simulate realistic hardware.

docs.title: O
docs.text: Observable A measurable quantity represented by a Hermitian operator, such as Pauli-Z on one qubit.

docs.title: P
docs.text: Parameterised quantum circuit (PQC) A circuit with adjustable gate angles that are trained like the weights of a neural network. Parameter-shift rule Exact gradient method evaluating a circuit at shifted parameter values, usually two runs per parameter. PennyLane Xanadu's open-source framework for differentiable quantum programming, integrated with PyTorch and JAX. Primitive (Qiskit) Standard Qiskit interface for running circuits: the Estimator returns expectation values, the Sampler returns counts. Projected quantum kernel A kernel built from reduced (local) properties of encoded states, designed to avoid exponential concentration.

docs.title: Q
docs.text: QAOA Quantum approximate optimisation algorithm: alternating problem and mixer layers trained to find good solutions. QRAM Quantum random access memory: a proposed device for loading classical data in superposition; not yet practical. QSVT Quantum singular value transformation, a framework unifying many fault-tolerant quantum algorithms. Quantum advantage A demonstrated benefit over the best classical methods: in speed, data needed, or practical outcome. Quantum annealing Analog quantum optimisation that slowly evolves a system towards low-energy solutions of an Ising problem. Quantum convolutional neural network (QCNN) A layered quantum model with convolution and pooling steps, used for phase recognition. Quantum GAN (QGAN) A generative adversarial network where the generator, discriminator or both are quantum circuits. Quantum-inspired algorithm A classical algorithm that borrows ideas from quantum computing, such as tensor networks or sampling tricks. Quantum kernel A similarity measure between data points computed from their encoded quantum states. Quantum natural gradient An optimiser that rescales gradients by the geometry of quantum states (the Fubini-Study metric). Quantum neural network (QNN) A parameterised quantum circuit used as a trainable model, often inside a hybrid network. Quantum reservoir computing Using a fixed quantum system as a feature generator and training only a classical readout layer. Qubit The basic unit of quantum information, able to be in a superposition of 0 and 1. QUBO Quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation, the problem format used by quantum annealers and QAOA.

docs.title: S
docs.text: Sample complexity The number of training examples or experiments needed to learn a task to a given accuracy. Shot One run of a circuit followed by measurement; many shots are averaged, with error shrinking as 1/sqrt(shots). Simulability Whether a quantum computation can be reproduced efficiently on a classical computer. SPSA Simultaneous perturbation stochastic approximation: a gradient estimate from two evaluations, popular on noisy hardware. Superposition A quantum state that is a weighted combination of basis states, such as |0> and |1> together.

docs.title: T
docs.text: Tensor network A way of representing large states or matrices as connected small tensors, used for simulation and classical ML. Transpilation Rewriting a circuit into a device's native gates and connectivity, adding SWAPs where needed.

docs.title: U
docs.text: Unitary A reversible, norm-preserving matrix describing an ideal quantum gate or circuit.

docs.title: V
docs.text: Variational quantum classifier (VQC) A classifier made of a feature map, a trainable ansatz and a measurement, trained in a hybrid loop. VQE Variational quantum eigensolver: a hybrid algorithm that minimises a Hamiltonian's energy with a parameterised circuit.

docs.title: Z
docs.text: Zero-noise extrapolation (ZNE) Error mitigation that runs circuits at amplified noise and extrapolates results back to zero noise.

docs.title: Chapter 1: QML Foundations
docs.text: Quantum machine learning sits where quantum computing meets machine learning. This chapter gives you the shared language: the four quadrants of classical and quantum data and algorithms, a quantum refresher for ML people and an ML refresher for physicists, the maths toolkit, NISQ versus fault-tolerant hardware, complexity and classical simulation as yardsticks, a history from HHL to today's honest benchmarks, the map of model families, the end-to-end workflow, and a checklist for separating hype from evidence.

docs.title: 1.1 What Quantum Machine Learning Is (and Is Not)
docs.text:
Quantum machine learning (QML) is the study of how quantum computers and machine learning can help each other. Mostly it means using a small quantum circuit as part of a learning model — the circuit turns data into a quantum state, gets nudged by trainable knobs, and is measured to produce a prediction. It also covers using ordinary machine learning to understand quantum systems.

Anatomy of a typical QML model. Only the middle three boxes are quantum; everything else is ordinary ML.

Think of it like…

Think of a quantum circuit as an unusual new kind of lens in a camera. Machine learning is still the photographer; QML asks whether swapping in this strange lens ever gives a sharper picture — and for which scenes.

Real-world example

Amara, a data-science student at the fictional Lakeside University, takes 200 labelled sensor readings, squeezes each into 4 numbers, feeds them into rotation angles on 4 simulated qubits, adds 24 trainable rotations, and measures one qubit to output 'faulty' or 'healthy'. A classical optimiser tunes the 24 angles until the training loss stops falling.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from a learning task: classify, regress, cluster, generate, or learn about a physical system.
  2. Encode the input data into a quantum state with a feature map (rotation angles, amplitudes, or a Hamiltonian).
  3. Process the state with a circuit — fixed (kernel methods) or with trainable parameters (variational models).
  4. Measure many times ('shots') to estimate expectation values that become predictions or kernel entries.
  5. Train with a classical optimiser and compare honestly against strong classical baselines.

Who uses it

Researchers in universities and quantum companies, quantum software engineers, and data scientists in finance, pharma and energy who evaluate quantum methods meet QML.

Key takeaway

In interviews define QML as 'machine learning where some part of the model or data is quantum' and immediately add that no practical advantage on classical data has yet been demonstrated.

Going deeper

  • Most current QML research uses circuits of 2-30 qubits simulated on laptops or GPUs; hardware experiments typically use tens of qubits with shallow depth because noise accumulates with every gate.
  • Two broad families dominate: variational models with trainable gates, and kernel methods with fixed circuits; Schuld (2021) showed many variational models can be rewritten as kernel methods.
  • A model's output is an expectation value ⟨ψ(x,θ)|O|ψ(x,θ)⟩, a number between the smallest and largest eigenvalue of the observable O, for example between -1 and +1 for Pauli-Z.
  • Estimating an expectation to precision ε needs roughly 1/ε² shots: about 10,000 shots for ±0.01, which makes each training step slow and costly on real hardware.
  • The field also includes learning about quantum data — states made by experiments or sensors — where provable exponential advantages exist (Huang et al., Science 2022).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking QML means 'running a neural network on a quantum computer': most models are small hybrid circuits trained by classical optimisers.
  • Assuming quantum means faster: on classical data no practical speed-up or accuracy gain has been convincingly shown as of 2026.
  • Treating a simulator result as a quantum result: simulations of 20 qubits prove the idea works mathematically, not that hardware will match it.

docs.title: Try it: A minimal quantum model in PennyLane (pip install pennylane)
docs.text:
import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import numpy as np

dev = qml.device('default.qubit', wires=2)

@qml.qnode(dev)
def model(x, theta):
    qml.RY(x[0], wires=0); qml.RY(x[1], wires=1)   # encode
    qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 1])
    qml.RY(theta[0], wires=0); qml.RY(theta[1], wires=1)  # trainable
    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(0))

print(model(np.array([0.3, 1.2]), np.array([0.1, -0.4])))

docs.title: 1.2 The Four Quadrants: CC, CQ, QC and QQ
docs.text:
QML is often drawn as a 2×2 grid. One axis asks whether the data is classical (C) or quantum (Q); the other asks whether the algorithm runs on a classical (C) or quantum (Q) computer. The four boxes — CC, CQ, QC and QQ — help you say precisely which kind of 'quantum machine learning' someone means.

The four QML quadrants

Classical algorithm Quantum algorithm Classical data CC: ordinary & quantum-inspired ML CQ: circuits on images, tables Quantum data QC: ML for decoding, calibration QQ: learning directly from states Proven advantage? n/a (baseline) CQ: contrived only; QQ: yes Typical demo AlphaQubit-style decoder (QC) Kernel SVM on 8 features (CQ)

First letter = data, second letter = algorithm; evidence for advantage is strongest in QQ.

Think of it like…

Picture a kitchen: the ingredients are either ordinary (classical data) or exotic (quantum data), and the cook either uses a normal oven (classical algorithm) or an experimental one (quantum algorithm). Each pairing is a different recipe category.

Real-world example

At the fictional Northfield Quantum Lab, Dev classifies handwritten digits with a quantum circuit (CQ), his colleague Lin trains a neural network to calibrate qubits (QC), and their professor studies learning directly from states produced by a quantum sensor (QQ). The CC corner is ordinary ML — including quantum-inspired algorithms.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Ask: where does the data come from — a database or file (classical), or a quantum system's state (quantum)?
  2. Ask: what processes it — CPUs/GPUs (classical) or a quantum processor (quantum)?
  3. Place the work in a box: first letter = data, second letter = algorithm (the common convention).
  4. Use the box to judge claims: CQ advantages are the hardest to prove; QQ advantages are the best established.

Who uses it

Lecturers, review authors and interviewers use this grid to frame QML discussions and research proposals.

Key takeaway

Memorise the convention: first letter is the data type, second is the device — 'CQ' means classical data, quantum algorithm (some authors reverse it, so always say it out loud).

Going deeper

  • The grid appears in Schuld & Petruccione's textbooks and in many surveys; some authors write the algorithm first, so 'QC' can mean either direction — always define the convention.
  • CQ faces the input problem: n classical numbers need at least about n gate parameters to load, so loading time can cancel any quantum speed-up on the processing step.
  • QQ advantages are rigorous: Huang, Kueng and Preskill (2021) and Huang et al. (2022) proved exponential separations in the number of experiments needed when quantum memory is available.
  • QC is commercially the most mature quadrant in 2026: neural decoders, automated calibration and ML-based state tomography are used on real quantum hardware.
  • Provable CQ speed-ups exist only for constructed problems, such as the discrete-logarithm-based task of Liu, Arunachalam and Temme (Nature Physics 2021).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using 'QML' to mean only CQ: half the field (QC and QQ) is about quantum data, where the strongest results live.
  • Assuming CQ results transfer to QQ or vice versa: proven advantages for quantum data say nothing about classifying photos.
  • Forgetting CC baselines: every CQ claim must be compared with classical and quantum-inspired classical methods.

A tensor-network model trained on MNIST using PyTorch on a GPU sits in CC. CQ — classical data, quantum algorithmQuadrant taxonomy · Concept · Emerging · Beginner The best-known QML: loading classical data such as images or tables into circuits; advantage here is unproven in practice. Huang et al. (Science 2022) showed learning properties of quantum states with exponentially fewer experiments when states are stored and processed quantumly. A literature review cites this paper when introducing the CC/CQ/QC/QQ grid. A spreadsheet of house prices is classical; the output state of a molecule simulation circuit is quantum. Training a kernel SVM is classical, but computing its kernel entries on a QPU puts the work in CQ. An RL agent finds pulse shapes that raise a two-qubit gate's fidelity from 99.2% to 99.5% overnight. A future pipeline routes a sensor's entangled probe state straight into a quantum classifier instead of measuring it first.

docs.title: 1.3 Why People Hope QML Helps — and What Is Genuinely Unknown
docs.text:
Researchers hope quantum computers could make learning faster, need less data, or find patterns classical models miss, because quantum states live in enormous mathematical spaces and can represent correlations that are hard to simulate. But hope is not evidence: for typical classical datasets nobody has shown a clear, practical quantum advantage, and some proposed speed-ups were later matched classically.

Claims and evidence

Hoped-for benefit Status in 2026 Faster linear algebra Exponential speed-ups (HHL) Caveats; many dequantised Less training data Sample-complexity gains Proven for quantum data Better models New inductive biases No fair benchmark win yet Contrived tasks Discrete-log learning Proven, not practical Optimisation Better training/annealing Mixed, mostly heuristic

Rigorous advantages exist mainly for quantum data or contrived problems.

Think of it like…

It is like hearing a new sports shoe 'could' make you run faster: the material is genuinely new, but until athletes beat their own records in fair races, the claim is a hypothesis.

Real-world example

Priya, an analyst at fictional Helix Pharma, is asked whether QML will speed up toxicity prediction. She lists the arguments for (quantum-native chemistry data, possible new inductive biases) and against (loading costs, noise, no benchmark wins yet) and recommends a small, time-boxed study with a strong classical baseline.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the claimed benefit: speed (runtime), sample efficiency (less data), or model quality (better generalisation).
  2. Check the assumptions: error-corrected hardware, fast data loading, special data structure.
  3. Check whether a classical algorithm (including quantum-inspired) achieves the same result.
  4. Look for evidence: theorems, numerical benchmarks with fair baselines, or hardware experiments.
  5. Classify the claim as proven, plausible-but-unproven, or refuted (dequantised or beaten).

Who uses it

Technology strategists, research managers and investors need this balanced view before funding QML projects.

Key takeaway

A strong interview answer separates three kinds of advantage — computational speed, sample complexity and model expressivity — and says which are proven for which data.

Going deeper

  • Classical models are strong: on small tabular tasks used in QML papers, gradient-boosted trees, SVMs and small MLPs typically reach near-ceiling accuracy, leaving little room for any quantum gain.
  • Hilbert-space dimension 2^n gives quantum models a huge feature space, but kernel-concentration and barren-plateau results show that very large spaces often make learning harder, not easier.
  • Dequantisation results (Tang 2018; Chia, Gilyén, Li, Lin, Tang and Wang, STOC 2020) show that low-rank linear-algebra speed-ups need either high-rank data or very precise answers to survive.
  • Advantages in learning from quantum experiments were demonstrated on hardware with up to about 40 superconducting qubits (Huang et al., Science 2022), so the QQ hope is concrete.
  • Most experts in 2026 regard practical CQ advantage as an open question that likely requires fault-tolerant hardware and carefully chosen, structured data.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating 'exponentially large Hilbert space' as evidence of speed-up: measurement reveals only a few bits per shot.
  • Citing old speed-up claims without checking whether they were dequantised or qualified later.
  • Concluding QML is 'useless': rigorous advantages exist for quantum data, and the classical-data question is open, not settled negative.

docs.title: 1.4 Quantum Refresher for ML People: Qubits, Gates, Measurement, Shots, Entanglement
docs.text:
A qubit is the quantum version of a bit: before you look, it is described by two complex numbers (amplitudes) whose squared sizes give the chances of reading 0 or 1. Gates are reversible operations that rotate these amplitudes; measurement gives a single random bit and destroys the superposition. Because each run gives only one random outcome, you repeat the circuit many times ('shots') and average.

From qubits to an estimated number. Each shot yields one bitstring; only averages over many shots become model outputs.

Think of it like…

A qubit is like a spinning coin whose tilt you can steer precisely with gates; looking at it makes it land heads or tails. To learn the tilt you must spin and catch many identical coins and count the results.

Real-world example

Ken prepares one qubit with an RY(π/3) rotation, so P(1) = sin²(π/6) = 0.25. He runs 1,000 shots and gets 262 ones, estimating ⟨Z⟩ = (738 − 262)/1000 = 0.476, close to the true 0.5. With 100 shots his estimate would wobble by about ±0.09.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Qubits start in |0⟩; the state of n qubits is a vector of 2^n complex amplitudes.
  2. Single-qubit gates (RX, RY, RZ, H) rotate one qubit; two-qubit gates (CNOT, CZ) create entanglement.
  3. A circuit is a sequence of gates, mathematically one big unitary matrix applied to the state vector.
  4. Measurement in the computational basis returns a bitstring with probability |amplitude|².
  5. Repeat for N shots; average to estimate expectation values such as ⟨Z⟩, with error about 1/√N.

Who uses it

Every QML practitioner, quantum software developer and algorithm engineer uses these concepts daily.

Key takeaway

Remember: n qubits ↔ 2^n amplitudes, but one measurement yields only n bits — and shot noise shrinks only as 1/√shots.

Going deeper

  • One-qubit rotation RY(θ) = exp(−iθY/2); a common QML convention is that a feature x enters as an angle, so the model depends on x through sines and cosines of x/2 multiples.
  • Standard error of ⟨Z⟩ from N shots is √((1 − ⟨Z⟩²)/N), at most 1/√N: 0.032 for 1,000 shots and 0.01 for 10,000 shots.
  • Typical 2025-2026 two-qubit gate fidelities: around 99.9% on leading trapped-ion machines such as Quantinuum Helios (reported 99.921%) and roughly 99.5-99.9% on the best superconducting chips.
  • Gates are not free to place: superconducting chips have fixed nearest-neighbour connectivity, so long-range interactions need SWAP gates (3 CNOTs each), inflating depth.
  • Holevo's bound (1973) limits what measurement can extract: n qubits can deliver at most n classical bits of information, regardless of the 2^n amplitudes.
  • Measurements in other bases are done by rotating first: measuring X means applying H and then measuring Z.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing a qubit 'is 0 and 1 at the same time' and computes all answers in parallel: interference, not parallel readout, is what algorithms exploit.
  • Reading one shot as the model's answer: a single shot is a random sample; the output is an average over many shots.
  • Ignoring that measurement disturbs the state: you cannot peek mid-circuit and continue unchanged.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate ⟨Z⟩ from shots with Qiskit (pip install qiskit)
docs.text:
from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.primitives import StatevectorSampler
import numpy as np

qc = QuantumCircuit(1)
qc.ry(np.pi/3, 0)
qc.measure_all()
counts = StatevectorSampler().run([qc], shots=1000).result()[0].data.meas.get_counts()
print(counts, 'Z estimate:', (counts.get('0',0)-counts.get('1',0))/1000)  # exact: 0.5

docs.text: Name What it does Example QubitBasic unit of quantum information · Concept · Current · Beginner A two-level quantum system with state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, where |α|² + |β|² = 1. A superconducting transmon or a trapped ytterbium ion each serves as a physical qubit. Bloch sphereGeometric picture of one qubit · Math · Current · Beginner Any pure one-qubit state is a point on a unit sphere; rotations RX, RY, RZ turn it about the three axes. RY(π/2) moves |0⟩ from the north pole to the equator, giving 50/50 measurement odds. SuperpositionQuantum mechanics principle · Concept · Current · Beginner A state with non-zero amplitude on several basis states at once; amplitudes can interfere, adding or cancelling. H|0⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2; applying H again returns |0⟩ by destructive interference on |1⟩. Rotation gates RX, RY, RZStandard gate set · Concept · Current · Beginner Single-qubit gates rotating the state by a chosen angle; the main way data and trainable parameters enter QML circuits. RY(x) with x = 0.8 rad encodes a scaled feature; RZ(θ) holds a trainable weight. CNOT and CZStandard two-qubit gates · Concept · Current · Beginner Entangling gates: CNOT flips the target if the control is 1; CZ adds a minus sign when both are 1. H on qubit 0 then CNOT(0,1) makes the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2. EntanglementQuantum correlation · Concept · Current · Beginner Correlation between qubits that cannot be described by giving each qubit its own state; necessary but not sufficient for quantum advantage. Measuring one half of a Bell pair as 0 guarantees the other reads 0, even though each alone looks random. Measurement and the Born ruleBorn rule (1926) · Concept · Current · Beginner Measuring gives outcome k with probability |amplitude_k|²; afterwards the state collapses to the observed outcome. A 3-qubit state with amplitude 0.6 on |101⟩ returns '101' in 36% of shots. ShotsRepetitions of a circuit · Concept · Current · Beginner Independent runs of the same circuit used to estimate probabilities; statistical error falls as one over the square root of shots. Quadrupling shots from 1,000 to 4,000 only halves the error bar on ⟨Z⟩. Observable and expectation valueHermitian operator · Math · Current · Beginner A measurable quantity represented by a Hermitian matrix; its expectation ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ is the average result over many shots. ⟨Z₀Z₁⟩ on a Bell state equals +1 because both qubits always agree. Hilbert-space dimension 2^nTensor-product structure · Math · Current · Beginner The state of n qubits needs 2^n complex amplitudes; 50 qubits already need about 10^15 numbers. Storing a 30-qubit state vector in double precision takes 16 GiB of RAM. Unitary evolutionPostulate of quantum mechanics · Math · Current · Intermediate Every gate is a unitary matrix (U†U = I), so circuits are reversible and preserve total probability. Running a circuit followed by its inverse returns any input state exactly, absent noise. Decoherence and gate errorHardware noise · Concept · Current · Beginner Unwanted interaction with the environment that degrades states; each gate has an error rate, typically 0.1-1% for two-qubit gates. A circuit with 300 two-qubit gates at 99.5% fidelity succeeds cleanly only about 22% of the time. Mixed state / density matrixQuantum statistics · Math · Current · Intermediate A matrix ρ describing probabilistic mixtures of states, needed to model noise and subsystems of entangled states. One qubit of a Bell pair alone is maximally mixed: ρ = I/2, a 50/50 coin with no phase. Pauli matrices X, Y, ZPauli group · Math · Current · Beginner Three 2×2 Hermitian, unitary matrices that act as basic gates and basic observables; Pauli strings span all n-qubit observables. The observable Z⊗I⊗Z measures whether qubits 0 and 2 agree, ignoring qubit 1.

docs.title: 1.5 ML Refresher for Physics People: Loss, Gradients, Generalisation, Kernels, Networks
docs.text:
Machine learning builds a function from examples. In supervised learning you have inputs with known labels, choose a model with adjustable parameters, measure its mistakes with a loss function, and adjust parameters along the gradient to reduce the loss. The real goal is generalisation — doing well on data the model has never seen — which you check on a held-out test set.

The supervised training loop. QML keeps this loop and replaces only the 'predict' step with a quantum circuit.

Think of it like…

Learning is like tuning a guitar by ear: you pluck (predict), hear how far off the note is (loss), turn the peg in the direction that helps (gradient step), and finally check the tuning on a song you haven't practised (test set).

Real-world example

Sofia has 1,000 labelled images of wind-turbine blades. She trains a model on 800, tunes settings on 100 and tests on the last 100. Training accuracy reaches 99% but test accuracy is 82% — the model has overfitted, so she adds regularisation and data augmentation and gets 91% on test data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Split data into training, validation and test sets (e.g. 80/10/10) before looking at results.
  2. Pick a model class and a loss function such as cross-entropy or mean squared error.
  3. Compute gradients of the loss with respect to parameters and update them with an optimiser (SGD, Adam).
  4. Tune hyperparameters on the validation set, never on the test set.
  5. Report test performance once, compared against simple and strong baselines.

Who uses it

Physicists moving into QML, quantum hardware engineers and anyone reviewing QML papers need this vocabulary.

Key takeaway

Know the bias-variance trade-off, why a test set must stay untouched, and that kernels compute inner products in feature space — the bridge to quantum kernels.

Going deeper

  • Classical deep learning relies on backpropagation, whose cost is a small constant times one forward pass; quantum circuits need about 2 extra circuit evaluations per parameter with the parameter-shift rule, so 100 parameters mean ~200 circuits per gradient.
  • Kernel methods scale with the number of training points m: building the Gram matrix needs m(m−1)/2 kernel evaluations and solving the SVM costs between m² and m³ operations.
  • Generalisation bounds relate test error to training error plus a complexity term; for quantum models Caro et al. (2022) bounded this term by the number of trainable gates.
  • Standard toy datasets in QML papers include Iris (150 samples, 4 features), two moons, breast cancer Wisconsin (569 samples, 30 features) and downsampled MNIST.
  • Hyperparameters — learning rate, layer count, regularisation — matter as much as model choice; fair QML comparisons give classical baselines the same tuning budget.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reporting training accuracy as the result: only test accuracy on untouched data measures learning.
  • Tuning on the test set: repeated peeking leaks information and inflates the reported score.
  • Comparing a heavily tuned quantum model with an untuned classical baseline, which makes any quantum result look better than it is.

docs.title: Try it: A classical baseline you should always run first (scikit-learn)
docs.text:
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.svm import SVC

X, y = make_moons(n_samples=300, noise=0.2, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=0)
clf = SVC(kernel='rbf', C=1.0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
print('test accuracy:', clf.score(Xte, yte))

Predicting whether an email is spam from 5,000 labelled emails. Unsupervised and generative learningCore ML paradigm · Concept · Current · Beginner Finding structure without labels (clustering, dimensionality reduction) or learning to sample new data like the training data. k-means groups customers into 4 segments; a generative model produces new realistic molecules. Loss functionOptimisation objective · Math · Current · Beginner A number measuring how wrong predictions are; training minimises it. Common choices are cross-entropy and mean squared error. Predicting 0.7 for a true label 1 gives a squared error of 0.09. Gradient descentCauchy 1847; SGD variants · Optimiser · Current · Beginner Repeatedly move parameters a small step opposite to the gradient of the loss; stochastic versions use mini-batches. With learning rate 0.1 and gradient 2.0, a weight of 1.5 updates to 1.3. Adam optimiserKingma & Ba 2014 (ICLR 2015) · Optimiser · Current · Beginner Gradient method with per-parameter adaptive step sizes from running averages of gradients; the default in many QML codes. A variational classifier is trained with Adam at learning rate 0.01 for 200 steps. BackpropagationRumelhart, Hinton & Williams 1986 · Algorithm · Current · Beginner Efficient computation of all gradients in a network by the chain rule; quantum hardware cannot do this directly, so QML uses parameter-shift rules. PyTorch computes a million gradients in one backward pass; a QPU needs about two circuit runs per parameter. Generalisation and overfittingStatistical learning theory · Concept · Current · Beginner Generalisation is performance on unseen data; overfitting is memorising training data so test performance drops. A model scoring 100% on training data but 60% on test data has overfitted. Train / validation / test splitStandard ML practice · Technique · Current · Beginner Separate data for fitting, for choosing hyperparameters, and for a final unbiased estimate of performance. With 1,000 samples: 700 train, 150 validation, 150 test, fixed by a random seed. Cross-validationStandard ML practice · Technique · Current · Beginner Rotating which part of the data is held out to get a more reliable estimate of performance on small datasets. Five-fold cross-validation on 200 samples trains five models, each tested on a different 40. Bias-variance trade-offStatistical learning theory · Concept · Current · Intermediate Too simple a model underfits (high bias); too flexible a model overfits (high variance); good models balance both. A straight line underfits a sine wave; a degree-20 polynomial through 15 points overfits it. Kernel trickAizerman et al. 1964; Boser, Guyon & Vapnik 1992 · Math · Current · Intermediate Computing inner products in a high-dimensional feature space directly via a kernel function, without building the features. An RBF kernel compares two points as exp(−γ‖x−x'‖²), implicitly using infinitely many features. Support vector machine (SVM)Cortes & Vapnik 1995 · Model · Current · Beginner Classifier finding the widest-margin boundary between classes; with kernels it draws curved boundaries. QSVMs swap in quantum kernels. scikit-learn's SVC(kernel='precomputed') accepts a kernel matrix computed on a quantum device. Neural network (MLP)Multilayer perceptron · Model · Current · Beginner Layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinear activations; the classical baseline most QNNs are compared with. A 2-layer MLP with 32 hidden units reaches 97% on a toy 'two moons' dataset in seconds. RegularisationStandard ML practice · Technique · Current · Beginner Penalties or tricks such as weight decay, dropout or early stopping that discourage overfitting. Adding L2 penalty 0.001 × Σθ² keeps a classifier's weights small and improves test accuracy.

docs.title: 1.6 The Maths Toolkit: Vectors, Dirac Notation, Tensor Products and Unitaries
docs.text:
QML papers are written in linear algebra. Quantum states are vectors, gates are matrices, measurements are averages computed with matrices, and combining qubits uses the tensor (Kronecker) product, which is why sizes double with every qubit. Learning a handful of notations — kets, bras, inner products — unlocks most papers.

From notation to model output. Each layer of maths maps to one part of a QML model.

Think of it like…

Dirac notation is like musical notation: it looks strange at first, but once you can read |ψ⟩ and ⟨ϕ|ψ⟩ you can 'hear' what a paper's circuit is doing without running it.

Real-world example

Lena checks a two-qubit encoding by hand. |0⟩ = (1, 0) and RY(π/2)|0⟩ = (0.707, 0.707). The tensor product with another |0⟩ gives the 4-vector (0.707, 0, 0.707, 0). Its inner product with |00⟩ is 0.707, so P(00) = 0.5 — matching her simulator.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write states as column vectors (kets |ψ⟩) and their conjugate transposes as row vectors (bras ⟨ψ|).
  2. Combine qubits with the Kronecker product: two 2-vectors give a 4-vector, n qubits give a 2^n-vector.
  3. Apply gates as matrix-vector products; whole circuits are products of matrices.
  4. Compute overlaps ⟨ϕ|ψ⟩ (similarity) and expectation values ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩ (predictions).
  5. Use traces and density matrices when noise or subsystems are involved.

Who uses it

Anyone reading QML papers, implementing simulators or interviewing for quantum algorithm roles needs this toolkit.

Key takeaway

Memorise: fidelity between pure states = |⟨ϕ|ψ⟩|², and the quantum kernel k(x, x') is exactly this quantity for two encoded data points.

Going deeper

  • Simulators store n-qubit states as arrays of 2^n complex numbers (16 bytes each in complex128), and apply a one-qubit gate by touching all 2^n entries in pairs.
  • Physics papers write |ψ(x)⟩ = U(x)|0⟩^⊗n for an encoded state; ML papers often write φ(x) for the same feature vector, so the quantum kernel is k(x,x') = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x')⟩|².
  • The trace inner product Tr(A†B) turns observables into vectors, so a quantum model ⟨O⟩ = Tr(ρ(x)O) is a linear model in the space of density matrices — the root of the 'quantum models are kernel methods' view.
  • Qubit ordering differs between frameworks: Qiskit uses little-endian (qubit 0 is the rightmost bit) while PennyLane and Cirq print qubit 0 first, a common source of bugs.
  • Global phase e^{iα}|ψ⟩ is unobservable, so two circuits whose matrices differ by a global phase are physically identical.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up probability and amplitude: amplitudes can be negative or complex; probabilities are their squared magnitudes.
  • Forgetting the complex conjugate in ⟨ϕ|: overlaps computed without conjugation are wrong for complex states.
  • Confusing qubit-ordering conventions between Qiskit and PennyLane, which silently flips bitstrings.

docs.title: Try it: Check a two-qubit state by hand with NumPy
docs.text:
import numpy as np
RY = lambda t: np.array([[np.cos(t/2), -np.sin(t/2)], [np.sin(t/2), np.cos(t/2)]])
zero = np.array([1, 0])
psi = np.kron(RY(np.pi/2) @ zero, zero)   # 4 amplitudes
print(psi)                     # [0.707 0 0.707 0]
print(abs(psi)**2)             # probabilities of 00,01,10,11

docs.title: Key algorithms, circuits, techniques, tools & papers
docs.text: Name What it does Example Ket and bra (Dirac notation)Paul Dirac, 1939 · Math · Current · Beginner |ψ⟩ is a column vector for a state; ⟨ψ| is its conjugate-transpose row vector. |+⟩ = (|0⟩ + |1⟩)/√2 is the vector (0.707, 0.707). Inner product ⟨ϕ|ψ⟩Linear algebra · Math · Current · Beginner A complex number measuring overlap between two states; its squared magnitude is the probability of finding one in the other. ⟨0|+⟩ = 0.707, so measuring |+⟩ gives 0 with probability 0.5. Tensor (Kronecker) productLinear algebra · Math · Current · Beginner The operation combining subsystems: an m-vector and an n-vector give an mn-vector; it is why qubit state size doubles per qubit. numpy.kron([1,0],[0,1]) gives [0,1,0,0], the two-qubit state |01⟩. Unitary matrixLinear algebra · Math · Current · Beginner A complex matrix U with U†U = I; it preserves vector length, so all gates and noiseless circuits are unitary. The Hadamard H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]] is unitary and is its own inverse. Hermitian matrixLinear algebra · Math · Current · Beginner A matrix equal to its conjugate transpose; it has real eigenvalues and represents observables and Hamiltonians. Pauli-Z = diag(1, −1) is Hermitian; its eigenvalues ±1 are the possible measurement results. Expectation value ⟨ψ|O|ψ⟩Quantum mechanics · Math · Current · Beginner Average measurement result of observable O on state ψ; the standard output of a QML model. For RY(θ)|0⟩, ⟨Z⟩ = cos θ, so θ = π/3 gives 0.5. FidelityQuantum information · Metric · Current · Beginner Similarity of two quantum states; for pure states |⟨ϕ|ψ⟩|², from 0 (orthogonal) to 1 (identical). A fidelity kernel compares two encoded images by the fidelity of their quantum states. Density matrix and traceQuantum statistics · Math · Current · Intermediate ρ = |ψ⟩⟨ψ| or a mixture; expectations become Tr(ρO), which also works for noisy states. A depolarised qubit has ρ = 0.9|0⟩⟨0| + 0.1·I/2, giving ⟨Z⟩ = 0.9. Partial traceQuantum statistics · Math · Current · Intermediate Operation that discards some qubits and returns the state of the rest; used in projected quantum kernels. Tracing out qubit 1 of a Bell state leaves qubit 0 in the mixed state I/2. Matrix exponential e^{−iHt}Schrödinger equation · Math · Current · Intermediate Turns a Hermitian Hamiltonian into a unitary evolution; rotation gates and Hamiltonian encodings are matrix exponentials. RZ(θ) = exp(−iθZ/2) is a time evolution under the Hamiltonian Z/2. Eigenvalues and eigenvectorsLinear algebra · Math · Current · Beginner Directions a matrix only stretches, and the stretch factors; observable eigenvalues are the possible measurement outcomes. Z⊗Z has eigenvalues +1 (for |00⟩, |11⟩) and −1 (for |01⟩, |10⟩). Fourier seriesClassical analysis · Math · Current · Intermediate Writing a function as a sum of sines and cosines; QML models with angle encoding are truncated Fourier series in the data. A model with one RY(x) encoding can only represent a + b·cos x + c·sin x. Big-O notationComplexity theory · Math · Current · Beginner Describes how cost grows with problem size, ignoring constant factors; essential for reading speed-up claims. Grover search takes O(√N) queries versus O(N) classically: 1,000 versus 1,000,000 for N = 10^6.

docs.title: 1.7 NISQ vs Fault-Tolerant Eras: What Each Allows for QML
docs.text:
Today's quantum computers are 'noisy intermediate-scale quantum' (NISQ) devices: tens to a few hundred physical qubits whose errors build up after a few thousand gates at most. Fault-tolerant (FT) machines will use quantum error correction to combine many physical qubits into reliable 'logical' qubits, allowing millions of operations. QML ideas split along this line: short variational circuits for NISQ, deep linear-algebra algorithms for FT.

NISQ vs fault-tolerant QML

NISQ (now) Fault-tolerant (future) Qubits ~50-1,000 physical, noisy Thousands of logical qubits Usable depth ~10^2-10^4 two-qubit gates 10^9+ logical operations Error handling Mitigation, post-processing Full error correction QML methods Variational circuits, kernels HHL, QSVT, amplitude estimation Data loading Angle encodings, small inputs Assumes QRAM or oracles Evidence Heuristic, small benchmarks Proven speed-ups, big overheads

Variational and kernel QML target NISQ; HHL-style linear algebra needs fault tolerance.

Think of it like…

NISQ machines are like writing in wet sand — you can sketch quickly, but the tide (noise) washes it away before you finish a long essay. Fault tolerance is like carving in stone with a proof-reader checking every letter: slower per letter but permanent.

Real-world example

Omar's team at fictional Orion Bank wants quantum Monte Carlo for risk. Resource estimates show they need thousands of logical qubits and around 10^9 error-corrected gates, so they shelve that plan for FT hardware and meanwhile benchmark a 12-qubit variational classifier on a NISQ device to build skills.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. NISQ (Preskill 2018): 50-1,000 noisy qubits, no full error correction, depth limited by gate errors.
  2. Error mitigation (zero-noise extrapolation, readout correction) stretches NISQ results at extra shot cost.
  3. Early fault tolerance: first logical qubits and below-threshold error correction (Google Willow, 2024).
  4. Full FT: thousands of logical qubits, deep circuits; roadmaps such as IBM's target a large FT machine by 2029.
  5. QML algorithms needing QRAM, phase estimation or HHL-style linear algebra wait for this era.

Who uses it

Strategy teams, quantum algorithm researchers and anyone planning a QML roadmap must know which era an idea needs.

Key takeaway

Rule of thumb: if an algorithm uses quantum phase estimation, amplitude estimation at high precision, or QRAM, it is a fault-tolerant algorithm, not a NISQ one.

Going deeper

  • A surface-code logical qubit of distance d uses about 2d² physical qubits; distance 25 means roughly 1,250 physical qubits per logical qubit at 0.1% physical error rates.
  • Google's Willow results (Nature, published 2025) reported logical error per cycle falling by a factor of about 2.14 with each step of code distance from 3 to 5 to 7.
  • IBM said in November 2025 that it expects community-verified quantum advantage by the end of 2026 and aims for a large-scale fault-tolerant computer by 2029; treat roadmaps as targets, not facts.
  • Error-mitigation cost grows exponentially with circuit size: probabilistic error cancellation can need sampling overheads of 10-1,000× even for modest circuits.
  • Babbush et al. (PRX Quantum 2021) argued quadratic speed-ups are unlikely to pay off on early FT machines because error-corrected logical operations are many orders of magnitude slower than classical operations.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing eras: claiming a NISQ demo of HHL proves exponential speed-up, when it only solved a 2×2 or 4×4 toy system.
  • Assuming physical qubit counts equal usable qubits: 1,000 noisy qubits may support only shallow circuits on a subset.
  • Treating vendor roadmaps as delivered hardware; plan with what is available today and check announcements.

docs.title: 1.8 Quantum Hardware Platforms and What They Mean for QML
docs.text:
Quantum computers are built from very different physical systems: superconducting circuits, trapped ions, neutral atoms, photons, and special-purpose annealers. Each has different qubit counts, speeds, connectivity and noise, which change which QML circuits are practical. Choosing a platform is like choosing a GPU: the same model can be fast on one and impractical on another.

Platforms through a QML lens

Superconducting Trapped ion Neutral atom Typical size (2025-26) ~100-160 qubits ~30-100 qubits Hundreds-thousands of atoms Connectivity Nearest-neighbour All-to-all Reconfigurable Gate speed Tens of ns Microseconds+ Microseconds Two-qubit fidelity ~99.5-99.9% ~99.9% ~99.5% (best reports) QML sweet spot Many shots, local circuits Dense feature maps Graph/Hamiltonian encodings

Connectivity and fidelity, not raw qubit count, decide which feature maps run well.

Think of it like…

Hardware platforms are like vehicles: a sports car (superconducting) is fast but has a fixed road map, a train (trapped ions) connects every station but runs slower, and a fleet of drones (neutral atoms) scales up quickly but is still learning to fly in formation.

Real-world example

Jun is choosing hardware for an 8-qubit IQP-style feature map that entangles every pair of qubits. On a heavy-hex superconducting chip, routing adds dozens of SWAP gates; on a fully connected trapped-ion system it runs as written. Because his circuit is short but dense, he picks the ion machine despite slower gates.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Note your circuit's needs: qubit count, two-qubit gate count, connectivity pattern, shots required.
  2. Compare platforms on two-qubit fidelity, connectivity, gate speed and queue/cost.
  3. Transpile the circuit to each device's native gates and topology and compare the resulting depth.
  4. Pick the platform whose compiled circuit has the best estimated fidelity for the shot budget you can afford.

Who uses it

Quantum software engineers, QML researchers planning hardware runs and procurement teams at research labs use this comparison.

Key takeaway

Know the trade-off in one line each: superconducting = fast but local; trapped ions = high fidelity, all-to-all, slow; neutral atoms = many qubits, analog modes; photonics = room-temperature, continuous variables; annealers = optimisation only.

Going deeper

  • Shot throughput matters for QML training: superconducting devices execute thousands of circuits per second, while trapped-ion systems run far fewer, so a 1,000-step training loop can take hours versus days.
  • IBM's heavy-hex lattice gives each qubit at most three neighbours to reduce crosstalk; its newer square-lattice Nighthawk raises connectivity with 218 couplers for 120 qubits.
  • Neutral-atom platforms such as QuEra's Aquila (256 atoms, on Amazon Braket) run analog Rydberg Hamiltonians, suited to Hamiltonian encodings and graph problems rather than generic gate circuits.
  • Continuous-variable photonic QML uses modes instead of qubits, with displacement and squeezing gates; it underlies early PennyLane demos and Xanadu's quantum neural network work.
  • Vendor fidelity figures are usually best-pair or median values; check the calibration data for the specific qubits your transpiled circuit uses.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing by qubit count alone: a 1,000-qubit device with poor fidelity may run less useful QML than a 30-qubit high-fidelity one.
  • Forgetting SWAP overhead: an all-to-all feature map on a nearest-neighbour chip can triple in depth after transpilation.
  • Using an annealer for gate-model circuits: annealers solve Ising/QUBO problems and cannot run feature maps or variational circuits.
