docs.text: Name What it does Example Superconducting qubits (transmons)IBM, Google, Rigetti, IQM and others · Hardware · Current · Beginner Tiny circuits cooled near absolute zero; gate times tens of nanoseconds, fixed nearest-neighbour connectivity. IBM's Heron r2 processors offer 156 qubits on a heavy-hex lattice through IBM Quantum Platform. Trapped-ion qubitsQuantinuum, IonQ and others · Hardware · Current · Beginner Charged atoms held by electromagnetic fields; very high fidelities and all-to-all connectivity, but gates are microseconds or slower. Quantinuum's 98-qubit Helios lets any qubit interact with any other in a feature map. Neutral-atom arraysQuEra, Pasqal, Atom Computing, Infleqtion and others · Hardware · Emerging · Beginner Atoms held in laser tweezers and entangled via Rydberg states; scale to thousands of atoms and support analog Hamiltonian evolution. A Caltech team reported a tweezer array of 6,100 atomic qubits (Nature, 2025), though not a full processor. Photonic quantum computersXanadu, PsiQuantum, Quandela and others · Hardware · Emerging · Intermediate Use light pulses as qubits or continuous-variable modes; networking-friendly, with fault-tolerant designs under development. Xanadu's photonic work inspired continuous-variable QML templates such as displacement and squeezing embeddings in PennyLane. Quantum annealersD-Wave (Advantage, Advantage2) · Hardware · Current · Beginner Special-purpose machines that find low-energy states of Ising problems; used for optimisation and sampling, not gate circuits. D-Wave's Advantage2 (generally available 2025) offers over 4,400 qubits for QUBO-based feature selection experiments. Qubit connectivityHardware topology · Concept · Current · Beginner Which qubit pairs can interact directly; limited connectivity forces SWAP gates that lengthen circuits. Entangling qubits 0 and 9 on a line of 10 qubits needs about 8 SWAPs, each 3 CNOTs. Native gate setHardware compilation · Concept · Current · Intermediate The gates a device performs physically; all other gates are compiled into them by the transpiler. IBM Heron devices natively use CZ plus single-qubit rotations; a CNOT compiles into CZ with Hadamards. TranspilationQiskit transpiler, tket and others · Technique · Current · Beginner Rewriting a circuit to a device's gate set and connectivity while minimising depth and gate count. Qiskit's transpile(circuit, backend, optimization_level=3) usually yields fewer two-qubit gates than level 0 for the same feature map. Coherence times T1 and T2Hardware characterisation · Metric · Current · Beginner How long qubits keep their state (T1) and phase (T2); circuits must finish well within these times. Transmons with T1 around 100-300 microseconds and 50-nanosecond gates allow roughly a few thousand sequential gates. Two-qubit gate fidelityRandomized benchmarking · Metric · Current · Beginner Probability a two-qubit gate does the right thing; the single most important number for QML circuit depth. At 99.9% fidelity, 700 two-qubit gates still leave roughly 50% overall success. Analog quantum processingNeutral atoms and simulators · Concept · Emerging · Intermediate Running a programmable Hamiltonian continuously rather than discrete gates; natural for Hamiltonian-based encodings and graph kernels. Pasqal's quantum evolution kernel maps a molecule's graph onto atom positions and lets the system evolve. Qubit modality trade-offPlatform comparison · Concept · Current · Intermediate No platform wins on every axis; speed, fidelity, scale and connectivity trade against each other. A 1,000-atom array has the most qubits but slower cycle times than a 156-qubit superconducting chip.

docs.title: 1.9 Complexity Basics for QML: BQP, Query and Sample Complexity
docs.text:
Complexity theory asks how resources — time, queries, data samples — grow as problems get bigger. BQP is the class of problems quantum computers solve efficiently; query complexity counts calls to a data 'oracle'; sample complexity counts how many training examples a learner needs. These tools tell you whether a quantum speed-up is real, and they explain why an exponentially large Hilbert space does not automatically mean exponential speed-up.

How costs grow with N = 10^12 items. Quadratic speed-ups are large on paper; FT overheads per query decide whether they pay off.

Think of it like…

Complexity is like comparing travel times by how they scale with distance: a bicycle and a car might tie across town, but over 1,000 km the difference in growth rate decides everything.

Real-world example

Ravi reads a claim that a quantum classifier 'uses 2^50 dimensions with 50 qubits'. Using complexity basics he asks: how many shots to estimate the output to ±0.01? (~10,000.) How many gates to load the data? (Proportional to the data size.) Is there a classical algorithm with the same scaling? (A random-features method.) The claim shrinks to 'no proven speed-up'.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fix the resource being measured: runtime, oracle queries, training samples, or qubits.
  2. Express the growth in Big-O as a function of input size n, precision ε and other parameters.
  3. Compare the best known quantum algorithm with the best known (not just naive) classical algorithm.
  4. Check end-to-end costs: loading, processing, and reading out the answer.
  5. Distinguish proven lower bounds from conjectures such as BQP ≠ BPP.

Who uses it

Quantum algorithm researchers, theory-minded QML scientists and technical due-diligence teams use these ideas to evaluate claims.

Key takeaway

Memorise: Grover gives at most a quadratic query speed-up for unstructured search, and quantum examples give at most constant-factor improvements in PAC sample complexity (Arunachalam & de Wolf).

Going deeper

  • BQP contains BPP and is contained in PSPACE; whether BQP is strictly larger than BPP is unproven, so most 'exponential speed-ups' are relative to the best known classical algorithm.
  • Statistical query lower bounds and shot noise interact: estimating any expectation to precision ε costs O(1/ε²) shots, while amplitude estimation reduces this to O(1/ε) but needs deep, fault-tolerant circuits.
  • Sample complexity and runtime differ: a learner may need few samples but exponential computation, or vice versa; QML advantage claims must say which resource improves.
  • Exponential separations in learning from quantum experiments (Huang, Kueng & Preskill, PRL 2021; Chen, Cotler, Huang & Li, FOCS 2021) concern the number of experiments, not runtime on classical data.
  • Kernel methods show the capacity paradox: a 2^n-dimensional feature space with random features makes kernel values concentrate near a constant, so exponentially many shots are needed to distinguish them.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing quantum algorithms to naive classical ones instead of the best known classical algorithm.
  • Ignoring precision: an O(log N) algorithm needing O(1/ε²) shots and ε = 10^-6 is not fast.
  • Treating BQP ≠ BPP as proven; it is a widely believed conjecture.

docs.title: Key algorithms, circuits, techniques, tools & papers
docs.text: Name What it does Example BQPBernstein & Vazirani 1993 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Bounded-error quantum polynomial time: problems a quantum computer solves in polynomial time with error probability at most 1/3. Factoring integers is in BQP thanks to Shor's algorithm but is not known to be in BPP. BPP and PClassical complexity classes · Concept · Current · Intermediate P: problems solvable in polynomial time; BPP: with randomness and bounded error. Widely believed BPP = P but strictly inside BQP. Training a linear SVM is in P; simulating general quantum circuits is believed not to be in BPP. Query complexityOracle model · Concept · Current · Intermediate Counting calls to a black-box function or data oracle; allows provable separations, unlike runtime. Finding one marked item in N needs about N/2 classical queries on average versus about (π/4)√N with Grover. Sample complexityLearning theory · Concept · Current · Intermediate Number of training examples a learner needs to reach error ε with confidence 1 − δ. Learning a class with VC dimension d needs on the order of d/ε examples, classical or quantum. PAC learningValiant 1984 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Probably Approximately Correct framework: a learner must, with high probability, output a hypothesis with low error. Quantum PAC learning gives the learner superposition examples Σ√D(x)|x, f(x)⟩ instead of samples. Arunachalam & de Wolf quantum sample boundArunachalam & de Wolf (2017-2018) · Theorem · Current · Advanced Showed quantum examples reduce PAC sample complexity by at most a constant factor compared with classical examples. A quantum learner cannot use superposition examples to learn a general concept class from exponentially fewer samples. Grover's algorithmGrover 1996 · Algorithm · Current · Beginner Unstructured search in O(√N) queries, a provably optimal quadratic speed-up used in many QML proposals. Searching 10^12 items needs about 10^6 Grover iterations, each a costly error-corrected oracle call. Holevo boundHolevo 1973 · Theorem · Current · Intermediate n qubits can transmit at most n bits of classical information, despite needing 2^n amplitudes to describe them. Amplitude-encoding a 1,024-number vector in 10 qubits does not let you read back 1,024 numbers from one copy. Exponential space ≠ exponential speed-upRecurring QML lesson · Concept · Current · Beginner A big Hilbert space only helps if interference concentrates answers into few measurable bits faster than classical methods can. A random 50-qubit circuit explores 2^50 amplitudes but yields nothing useful for classification. Classical shadowsHuang, Kueng & Preskill, Nature Physics 2020 · Technique · Current · Advanced Random-measurement protocol that predicts many properties of a state from few copies; a key tool in quantum learning theory. From about 1,000 randomised snapshots, a lab estimates hundreds of two-qubit correlators at once. Oracle / input model assumptionQuantum algorithms · Concept · Current · Intermediate Speed-ups often assume data available through a fast quantum oracle (e.g. QRAM); the end-to-end cost may differ. A recommendation speed-up assumed QRAM-style access; with only classical sampling access, Tang matched it classically. Exponential separation (learning)Learning theory · Concept · Research · Advanced Proven exponential gap between quantum and classical learners for specific tasks, usually under oracle or cryptographic assumptions. Learning from quantum experiments with quantum memory shows an exponential gap in required experiments.

docs.title: 1.10 Classical Simulation: The Yardstick Every QML Claim Must Beat
docs.text:
Before trusting a quantum result, ask: could a normal computer just simulate it? Exact state-vector simulation needs memory that doubles with every qubit, so it stops near 45-50 qubits, but cleverer methods — tensor networks, Clifford tricks, Pauli propagation — can simulate many larger circuits if they are shallow or lightly entangled. If a QML model is easy to simulate, it cannot offer quantum advantage.

Memory for an exact state vector. Each extra qubit doubles memory — exact simulation stops near 45-50 qubits.

Think of it like…

It is like a magic trick: if a skilled conjuror can reproduce it with ordinary props, it isn't magic. Classical simulation is the conjuror who tries to reproduce every quantum 'trick'.

Real-world example

Elena's team reports a 60-qubit QML model on hardware. A reviewer notes the circuit has only nearest-neighbour gates and depth 6, so a matrix-product-state simulator reproduces it on a laptop in minutes. The paper is revised to say 'scalable demonstration' rather than 'beyond classical'.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Count qubits, depth and entanglement structure of the circuit.
  2. Up to ~30 qubits: exact state-vector simulation on a laptop or GPU.
  3. Shallow or 1D-local circuits: try matrix product states or other tensor networks.
  4. Mostly Clifford circuits or low-weight observables: try stabiliser or Pauli-propagation methods.
  5. Only if every method fails at practical cost can the experiment claim to be beyond classical simulation.

Who uses it

QML researchers, reviewers, quantum-advantage teams and simulator developers (NVIDIA cuQuantum, Qiskit Aer, PennyLane Lightning) work on this boundary.

Key takeaway

Memorise: state-vector memory = 16 bytes × 2^n — 30 qubits ≈ 16 GiB, 40 qubits ≈ 16 TiB, 50 qubits ≈ 16 PiB.

Going deeper

  • Complex128 amplitudes take 16 bytes and complex64 take 8; record exact simulations of around 45 qubits have used large supercomputers with distributed memory.
  • Tensor networks attack shallow or low-entanglement circuits: cost grows exponentially in entanglement or in depth × width of the light cone, not in qubit count.
  • Google's 2019 'supremacy' sampling task was later simulated far faster than first estimated using tensor-network contraction, a cautionary tale for advantage claims.
  • For QML, simulability results (Cerezo et al. 2025; Schreiber et al. 2023 on classical surrogates) suggest many trainable models can be dequantised once a modest amount of quantum data is collected.
  • Reviewers increasingly ask authors to state which classical simulation methods were tried and their cost, alongside classical ML baselines.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Equating 'more than 50 qubits' with 'impossible to simulate': structure, not width alone, decides simulability.
  • Using a classical simulator result as evidence of quantum advantage — if it was simulated, it was classical.
  • Assuming noise makes circuits harder to simulate; it usually makes them easier.

docs.title: Try it: Watch memory double with each qubit (Python)
docs.text:
for n in (20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 50):
    gib = 16 * 2**n / 2**30
    print(f'{n} qubits: {gib:,.3f} GiB for a complex128 state vector')

docs.title: Key algorithms, circuits, techniques, tools & papers
docs.text: Name What it does Example State-vector simulationStandard simulator method · Technique · Current · Beginner Stores all 2^n amplitudes and applies gates exactly; memory and time double with each added qubit. PennyLane's lightning.qubit simulates a 25-qubit variational classifier on a laptop. Tensor-network simulation (MPS)Matrix product states; Vidal 2003 · Technique · Current · Intermediate Represents states as networks of small tensors; efficient when entanglement is limited, e.g. shallow 1D circuits. An MPS with bond dimension 64 simulates a 100-qubit, depth-5 nearest-neighbour circuit in seconds. Stabiliser (Clifford) simulationGottesman-Knill theorem; Aaronson & Gottesman 2004 · Technique · Current · Intermediate Circuits of only Clifford gates (H, S, CNOT) are simulable in polynomial time, so they cannot give quantum advantage. Stim simulates Clifford error-correction circuits with thousands of qubits in seconds to benchmark decoders. Pauli propagationRecent simulation family (2023-2025) · Technique · Emerging · Advanced Tracks how a measured observable spreads backward through the circuit as Pauli strings, truncating small terms. Researchers used it to classically reproduce expectation values from some large noisy hardware experiments. A single 80 GB GPU holds a 32-qubit complex64 state vector (32 GiB) with room to spare. Gottesman-Knill theoremGottesman 1998 · Theorem · Current · Intermediate Circuits made only of Clifford gates with computational-basis inputs and measurements can be simulated efficiently classically. A feature map using only H and CNOT gates cannot be a source of quantum advantage. Entanglement entropy and bond dimensionTensor-network theory · Metric · Current · Advanced Entanglement across a cut sets the bond dimension an MPS needs; low entanglement means cheap simulation. A state with 10 bits of entanglement across the middle needs bond dimension at least 2^10 = 1,024. Classical surrogateSchreiber et al. 2023 and others · Technique · Research · Advanced A classical model, such as a Fourier-series fit, trained to imitate a quantum model's outputs. After querying a trained 6-qubit model on random inputs, a classical Fourier model reproduces its predictions. Simulability-trainability linkCerezo et al., Nature Communications 16, 7907 (2025) · Concept · Research · Advanced Argues many quantum models provably free of barren plateaus are classically simulable after collecting some quantum data. A trainable model with a local cost is shown to act inside a polynomial-size subspace that a laptop can handle. Noise helps simulationSimulation theory · Concept · Current · Advanced Noise damps high-weight correlations, so noisy deep circuits often become easier to simulate classically. At 1% gate noise, contributions from long Pauli strings shrink exponentially and can be truncated. Quantum-advantage trackersIBM and partners' community tracker (2025) · Resource · Emerging · Intermediate Open trackers where advantage claims are posted and classical simulation teams try to refute them. IBM and partners added three candidate experiments to an open tracker in November 2025.

docs.title: 1.11 A Short History of QML: From HHL to Honest Benchmarks
docs.text:
QML grew in waves. First came bold fault-tolerant algorithms promising exponential speed-ups for linear algebra (2009-2014). Then classical computer scientists showed several of those speed-ups could be matched classically (from 2018), while near-term variational and kernel models rose — along with their problems, such as barren plateaus. Since 2021 the field has focused on where advantage is provable and on careful benchmarking.

Milestones in QML. Bold speed-up claims (left) gave way to careful theory and benchmarking (right).

Think of it like…

The history reads like a gold rush: early prospectors announced huge finds, surveyors later checked which claims held real gold, and today's miners dig more carefully with better maps.

Real-world example

Grace prepares a journal-club talk. She lines up five papers: HHL (2009) for the big promise, Tang (2018) for the dequantisation shock, McClean et al. (2018) for barren plateaus, Huang et al. (2021) for 'power of data', and Bowles, Ahmed & Schuld (2024) for today's sober benchmarking.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. 2009-2014: fault-tolerant linear-algebra era — HHL, quantum PCA, quantum SVM, recommendation systems.
  2. 2014-2019: near-term turn — VQE, QAOA, quantum circuit learning, quantum kernels on hardware.
  3. 2018-2020: reality checks — dequantisation and barren plateaus.
  4. 2021-2022: theory of advantage — power of data, projected kernels, learning from experiments.
  5. 2023-2026: simulability debate and large-scale fair benchmarks.

Who uses it

Researchers, students preparing literature reviews and interviewers testing context knowledge all use this timeline.

Key takeaway

Be able to name one paper per wave with year: HHL 2009, Rebentrost 2014, Tang 2018, McClean 2018, Havlíček 2019, Huang 2021/2022, Bowles 2024.

Going deeper

  • Early fault-tolerant proposals assumed QRAM-style quantum access to data, so their exponential speed-ups were about the quantum part only; Aaronson's 2015 commentary made these assumptions widely known.
  • Dequantisation spread fast: after Tang's 2018 result, classical analogues followed for quantum PCA, low-rank regression and SVMs, unified by Chia, Gilyén, Li, Lin, Tang and Wang (STOC 2020).
  • The NISQ turn produced software: PennyLane (2018), Qiskit Machine Learning, and TensorFlow Quantum (2020) made trainable circuits accessible to ML researchers.
  • Barren-plateau research expanded from random circuits (2018) to cost-function locality (Cerezo et al. 2021), noise-induced plateaus (Wang et al. 2021) and expressibility (Holmes et al. 2022).
  • Since 2024 the emphasis has been on reproducible benchmarks, simulability analysis and finding structured problems where quantum models are provably or empirically useful.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting 2009-2014 speed-ups without the later caveats; many were qualified by dequantisation or loading costs.
  • Confusing Rebentrost's 2014 fault-tolerant QSVM with the 2019 NISQ quantum-kernel 'QSVM'.
  • Thinking the field has 'failed': the lessons redirected research towards provable and well-benchmarked questions.

docs.text: Name What it does Example HHL algorithmHarrow, Hassidim & Lloyd, PRL 103, 150502 (2009) · Paper · Research · Intermediate Quantum algorithm for solving sparse, well-conditioned linear systems with exponential speed-up under strict assumptions; the spark of QML. Covered in depth in the fault-tolerant chapter; here it marks the start of the speed-up era. Different from the 2019 kernel-style 'QSVM' run on NISQ hardware. Later partly dequantised for low-rank classical data. A historian of the field cites it as the first book-length QML treatment. The same 'circuit plus classical optimiser' loop became the template for quantum neural networks. Tang found it as an undergraduate while trying to prove the quantum speed-up was genuine. Read alongside Havlíček et al. to understand quantum kernels from both theory and experiment. Quantum advantage in learning from experimentsHuang et al., Science 376, 1182 (2022) · Paper · Current · Advanced Demonstrated on Google hardware that quantum-memory learners need exponentially fewer experiments for certain tasks. A landmark for the QQ quadrant: advantage proven and shown experimentally. 'Better than classical?' benchmarksBowles, Ahmed & Schuld 2024 · Paper · Current · Beginner Systematic benchmark of 12 QML models on 160 datasets that found classical baselines generally win. Its open-source code is used by students to rerun models fairly. Debated widely in 2024-2025 and covered in the variational-circuits chapter.

docs.title: 1.12 The Map of QML Model Families
docs.text:
QML is not one algorithm but a family tree. Variational circuits act like small neural networks; quantum kernels supply similarity scores to classical SVMs; generative models learn to sample data; fault-tolerant algorithms speed up linear algebra; annealers and QAOA tackle optimisation; and quantum-inspired methods bring the ideas back to classical hardware. Knowing the map tells you which chapter to open for which problem.

QML model families.

Think of it like…

Like a hardware store's aisle signs — fasteners, power tools, paint — the model map tells you which aisle has the tool for your job before you start browsing shelves.

Real-world example

Hannah, a new hire at fictional Quanta Analytics, gets three requests: classify sensor faults, generate synthetic financial scenarios, and choose a portfolio. She maps them to a variational classifier or quantum kernel, a quantum circuit Born machine, and a QUBO solved by annealing or QAOA — each with a classical baseline.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the ML task: classification/regression, generation, optimisation, or linear algebra.
  2. Match the hardware era: NISQ-friendly (variational, kernels, annealing) or fault-tolerant (HHL, QSVT).
  3. Pick a family and its strongest classical competitor.
  4. Consult the relevant chapter for design details, then prototype in simulation.

Who uses it

Solution architects, QML researchers and consultants use this map to scope projects.

Key takeaway

Interviewers often ask 'variational model or kernel?' — answer: kernels give convex training but scale with dataset size squared; variational models scale with parameters but risk barren plateaus.

Going deeper

  • Schuld (2021) showed that variational models with data-encoding followed by trainable gates and measurement are linear models in a feature space, so their optimum lies in the span of training-point kernels — the 'quantum models are kernel methods' result.
  • Kernel methods need m(m−1)/2 circuit evaluations for m training points: 10,000 points mean about 50 million overlap circuits, each needing many shots.
  • Variational models scale with parameter count p: one parameter-shift gradient costs 2p circuit evaluations, independent of dataset size apart from mini-batching.
  • Jerbi et al. (Nature Communications 2023) showed that some data re-uploading models can be more efficient than kernel versions in certain learning tasks, so the two families are not interchangeable.
  • This guide covers variational models in depth in chapter 20, kernels and generative models in chapter 30, fault-tolerant algorithms in chapter 40 and optimisation in chapter 50.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Picking a quantum model before checking the task type: optimisation problems need QUBO/QAOA thinking, not a classifier.
  • Assuming kernels avoid all trainability issues: kernel values can concentrate exponentially, needing huge shot counts.
  • Forgetting the quantum-inspired option, which often delivers the useful idea on classical hardware.

docs.text: Name What it does Example Variational quantum classifier / QNNMitarai 2018; Farhi & Neven 2018; Schuld et al. 2020 · Model · Current · Beginner Trainable parameterised circuit used like a neural network for classification or regression. A quantum circuit Born machine learns the 'bars and stripes' pattern distribution on 9 qubits. A variational policy plays CartPole in simulation as a proof of concept. A kernel study compares the quantum kernel with an RBF kernel tuned over the same budget.

docs.title: 1.13 The QML Workflow End to End
docs.text:
A real QML project follows the ML lifecycle with extra quantum steps: frame the problem, build a classical baseline, shrink and scale the data, pick an encoding and model, train in a simulator, add realistic noise, optionally run on hardware with error mitigation, and evaluate honestly with statistics. Most of the time goes into data preparation and fair comparison, not the circuit itself.

QML project workflow. The quantum-specific steps sit inside a normal ML lifecycle bracketed by baselines and statistics.

Think of it like…

It is like testing a new recipe in a restaurant: first cook the house favourite (baseline), then prepare ingredients (data), try the new recipe in a test kitchen (simulator), then on a busy night (hardware) — and only keep it if diners prefer it in a blind taste test.

Real-world example

Tomás at fictional GreenGrid Energy predicts transformer faults from 30 sensor features. He gets 94% with gradient-boosted trees, reduces features to 8 with PCA, trains an 8-qubit re-uploading classifier in simulation (91%), adds a device noise model (88%), runs 5 seeds on hardware (86 ± 2%), and reports no advantage — saving his company an expensive pilot.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Frame the task and success metric; build and tune strong classical baselines first.
  2. Pre-process: clean, scale features to angle ranges, reduce dimensions to fit the qubit budget.
  3. Design: choose encoding, model family (variational or kernel), observable and loss.
  4. Simulate: train noise-free, then with a noise model and finite shots; tune hyperparameters on validation data.
  5. Execute: transpile for hardware, budget shots and cost, apply error mitigation.
  6. Evaluate and report: multiple seeds, confidence intervals, same tuning budget as baselines, open code.

Who uses it

QML researchers, quantum software developers and applied scientists in industry labs run this workflow.

Key takeaway

In interviews, mention the classical baseline first and the quantum circuit last — it signals scientific maturity.

Going deeper

  • Shot budgets dominate hardware costs: gradient estimation needs about 2 circuits per parameter per data point per step, so training is usually done in simulation and only inference runs on hardware.
  • Noise models built from calibration data (T1, T2, gate and readout errors) predict hardware performance only roughly; drift between calibrations can change results day to day.
  • Fair comparisons give classical and quantum models equal hyperparameter-search budgets and identical data splits; Bowles et al. (2024) used grid searches for every model.
  • Report effect sizes with uncertainty — for example accuracy mean ± standard deviation over at least 5 seeds — and test whether differences are statistically meaningful.
  • Record versions: QML libraries change APIs often, and transpiler versions change compiled circuits, so pin package versions in requirements files.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Starting with the quantum circuit and adding a weak baseline at the end, which biases the comparison.
  • Training directly on hardware with huge shot budgets when simulation would answer the question cheaply.
  • Reporting the best seed only; show variation across seeds and data splits.

docs.title: 1.14 Hype vs Reality: Reading QML Claims Critically
docs.text:
QML attracts big headlines — 'quantum AI', 'exponential speed-up', 'quantum-enhanced' products. Some claims are solid science with narrow scope; many are marketing or overgeneralised from toy experiments. A short checklist — baseline, scale, assumptions, simulability, statistics — lets you sort them quickly and speak credibly to employers and clients.

Five-question claim check. A claim must pass every gate before you accept 'quantum advantage'.

Think of it like…

Treat QML headlines like nutrition labels on snack packets: 'contains real fruit!' may be true, but you check the ingredients list and the serving size before believing it is healthy.

Real-world example

A start-up pitch to fictional Riverside Insurance claims '1,000× faster fraud detection with quantum AI'. Analyst Bea asks for the classical baseline (untuned logistic regression), dataset size (400 rows, 4 features), hardware (a simulator) and repeatability (one seed). She concludes the claim is unsupported and recommends against the contract.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Check the baseline: is it a tuned, modern classical model on identical data?
  2. Check scale: qubits, data size and features — toy or realistic?
  3. Check assumptions: QRAM, fault tolerance, special data structure?
  4. Check simulability and dequantisation: could a classical method do the same?
  5. Check statistics and openness: seeds, error bars, code, peer review.

Who uses it

Analysts, investors, product managers, journalists and students choosing research topics all need this skill.

Key takeaway

A crisp interview line: 'As of 2026 there is no demonstrated practical QML advantage on classical data; provable advantages exist for quantum data and contrived problems.'

Going deeper

  • Bowles, Ahmed and Schuld (2024) found that removing entanglement often did not hurt QML models on their 160 datasets, undermining claims that 'quantumness' drove performance.
  • Many QML demos use datasets such as Iris, breast cancer, two moons or 4×4 downsampled MNIST that classical models solve near perfectly in milliseconds.
  • Company roadmaps, such as targets for fault tolerance by 2029, are plans; separate them from peer-reviewed demonstrations when writing reports.
  • Healthy scepticism is not cynicism: provable advantages for quantum data (Huang et al. 2022) and for contrived problems (Liu et al. 2021) are real results with clear scope.
  • Funders and employers value people who can explain both the promise and the limits; the field moved toward honest benchmarking partly after the 2018-2024 reality checks.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Dismissing all QML as hype: provable results exist and research directions remain open.
  • Accepting 'quantum-enhanced' claims without asking which part, if any, ran on a quantum computer.
  • Confusing 'beyond brute-force simulation' with 'better than the best classical method'.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Quantum Kernels, Generative Models & Quantum RL
docs.text: Not every quantum model is trained by nudging circuit angles. This chapter covers the kernel route — where a quantum computer only measures similarities and a classical support vector machine does the learning — from fidelity and projected kernels to kernel alignment, exponential concentration and the few provable advantage results. It then turns to quantum generative models (Born machines, QGANs, Boltzmann machines, diffusion), generalisation theory, quantum reinforcement learning and transformer proposals, and closes with the classical tools that keep QML honest: tensor networks, quantum-inspired methods and classical shadows for learning from quantum data.

docs.title: 4.1 Kernel Methods Refresher: Similarity Instead of Weights
docs.text:
Kernel methods classify data by comparing every pair of points with a similarity function called a kernel. A kernel secretly measures similarity in a huge 'feature space' without ever writing the features down — the kernel trick. Support vector machines (SVMs), kernel ridge regression and Gaussian processes all work this way, and quantum kernels plug straight into them.

How a kernel method learns. Swap the kernel box for a quantum circuit and you have a quantum kernel method.

Think of it like…

Instead of describing every song with hundreds of measurements, you ask a DJ 'how similar are these two songs?' for every pair — and that table of similarities is all the learning algorithm needs.

Real-world example

Mei at the fictional SafeBank detects fraudulent transfers using 2,000 labelled examples. She computes a 2,000 × 2,000 Gram matrix with a Gaussian (RBF) kernel — about 2 million unique pairwise similarities — and trains an SVM that ends up relying on only 140 'support vectors'. Predicting a new transfer needs just 140 kernel evaluations against those points.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a kernel k(x, x′) = ⟨φ(x), φ(x′)⟩ — an inner product of (possibly huge) feature vectors.
  2. Build the Gram matrix Kᵢⱼ = k(xᵢ, xⱼ) on the training data; it must be symmetric and positive semi-definite (PSD).
  3. Solve a convex optimisation problem: an SVM (hinge loss) or kernel ridge regression (squared loss).
  4. By the representer theorem, the optimal model is f(x) = Σᵢ αᵢ k(xᵢ, x), a weighted sum over training points.
  5. Predict new points by computing their kernel values against the training (support) points.

Who uses it

Data scientists, ML engineers in finance and bioinformatics, and every QML researcher working on quantum kernels rely on this toolbox.

Key takeaway

Memorise why kernels matter for QML: training is convex (a global optimum, no barren plateaus in the training step), but costs O(N²) kernel evaluations for N training points.

Going deeper

  • Mercer's theorem: every symmetric positive semi-definite kernel equals an inner product in some feature space; the RBF kernel exp(−γ‖x − x′‖²) corresponds to an infinite-dimensional one.
  • Training needs O(N²) kernel evaluations and about O(N³) time for a direct solve, so classical kernel methods need approximations such as Nyström or random Fourier features (Rahimi & Recht 2007) beyond roughly 10⁵ points.
  • SVMs (Cortes & Vapnik 1995) maximise the margin between classes; the hyperparameter C trades margin width against training errors, and only points with αᵢ > 0 (support vectors) affect predictions.
  • Because the training problem is convex, kernel methods reach the global optimum for a given kernel — the main attraction of quantum kernels compared with variational circuits.
  • The kernel's bandwidth (γ for RBF) sets the inductive bias: too large and the Gram matrix approaches the identity (memorisation); too small and every point looks alike.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Forgetting to scale features before an RBF kernel: one feature with a large range dominates every distance.
  • Treating any similarity score as a valid kernel: non-PSD matrices can break SVM solvers, so check the smallest eigenvalue.
  • Forgetting test-time cost: every prediction needs kernel values against all support vectors.

docs.title: Try it: A classical kernel SVM with a precomputed Gram matrix (scikit-learn)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_circles
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import rbf_kernel

X, y = make_circles(200, noise=0.1, factor=0.4, random_state=0)
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = X[:150], X[150:], y[:150], y[150:]

K_train = rbf_kernel(Xtr, Xtr, gamma=2.0)     # 150 x 150 Gram matrix
K_test = rbf_kernel(Xte, Xtr, gamma=2.0)      # test-vs-train similarities
svm = SVC(kernel="precomputed").fit(K_train, ytr)

print("accuracy:", svm.score(K_test, yte), "support vectors per class:", svm.n_support_)
print("smallest eigenvalue (PSD check):", np.linalg.eigvalsh(K_train).min())

docs.title: 4.2 Quantum Kernels & Fidelity Kernels
docs.text:
A quantum kernel uses a quantum circuit as the feature map: each data point x is encoded into a quantum state |φ(x)⟩, and the similarity of two points is the overlap of their states, k(x, x′) = |⟨φ(x)|φ(x′)⟩|² — the fidelity kernel. The quantum computer only estimates these overlaps; a classical SVM does the learning. The idea was introduced in 2019 by Schuld & Killoran and by Havlíček and colleagues.

Training and using a quantum kernel. The QPU only estimates overlaps; learning happens in a classical convex solver.

Think of it like…

Two fingerprints are pressed onto the same piece of glass and you measure how much they overlap: the more the ridges line up, the more similar the two people are.

Real-world example

Omar at the fictional PharmaQ encodes 6 molecular descriptors on 6 qubits. For each pair of molecules he runs the encoding circuit for molecule A followed by the inverse circuit for molecule B and counts how often all six qubits read 0: 412 out of 1,000 shots gives k ≈ 0.41. Filling a 300-molecule Gram matrix takes 44,850 such circuits.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick an encoding circuit U(x), so that |φ(x)⟩ = U(x)|0…0⟩.
  2. Compute-uncompute: run U(x), then the inverse U(x′)†, then measure all qubits.
  3. The probability of the all-zero outcome equals |⟨φ(x′)|φ(x)⟩|², the fidelity kernel value.
  4. Alternatively, use a swap test on two registers (twice the qubits plus one ancilla) when states cannot be uncomputed.
  5. Repeat for every pair to fill the Gram matrix, then train a classical SVM or kernel ridge model.

Who uses it

QML researchers, quantum software teams at IBM, Xanadu and start-ups, and applied scientists running pilots in finance, chemistry and high-energy physics use quantum kernels.

Key takeaway

Know both estimators: compute-uncompute needs n qubits and double depth; the swap test needs 2n + 1 qubits and gives P(0) = (1 + F)/2.

Going deeper

  • Schuld & Killoran ('Quantum machine learning in feature Hilbert spaces', PRL 2019) framed data encodings as feature maps into Hilbert space, making quantum kernels a natural kernel method.
  • The fidelity kernel equals Tr[ρ(x)ρ(x′)] for pure states and is PSD when computed exactly; shot noise and hardware noise can make an estimated Gram matrix slightly non-PSD, requiring repair.
  • Product encodings are classically easy: with RX(xⱼ) on each qubit the kernel is Πⱼ cos²((xⱼ − x′ⱼ)/2), so 'quantum kernel' does not automatically mean 'hard to compute classically'.
  • Schuld ('Supervised quantum machine learning models are kernel methods', arXiv 2021) showed variational models with fixed encodings are linear models in the same feature space, so the kernel optimum bounds them.
  • Cost: N training points need N(N − 1)/2 off-diagonal circuits; 1,000 points at 1,000 shots each is about 5 × 10⁸ shots before a single test prediction.
  • Kübler, Buchholz & Schölkopf ('The inductive bias of quantum kernels', NeurIPS 2021) argued that quantum kernels need a well-matched inductive bias, otherwise they generalise poorly despite their huge feature spaces.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming 'quantum kernel' means classically hard: many simple encodings give closed-form kernels a laptop computes instantly.
  • Forgetting test-time cost: each new prediction needs one circuit per support vector, each with many shots.
  • Skipping PSD repair on hardware Gram matrices: negative eigenvalues from noise can destabilise the SVM solver.

docs.title: Try it: Fidelity kernel + scikit-learn SVM, checked against its closed form
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons

n = 2
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def overlap(x1, x2):
    qp.AngleEmbedding(x1, wires=range(n))             # U(x1)
    qp.adjoint(qp.AngleEmbedding)(x2, wires=range(n)) # U(x2)^dagger
    return qp.probs(wires=range(n))

def kernel(x1, x2):
    return overlap(x1, x2)[0]                         # probability of |00>

X, y = make_moons(80, noise=0.1, random_state=0)
K = qp.kernels.square_kernel_matrix(X, kernel, assume_normalized_kernel=True)
svm = SVC(kernel="precomputed").fit(K, y)
print("train accuracy:", svm.score(K, y))
# this simple product encoding has a classical closed form:
print(kernel(X[0], X[1]), np.prod(np.cos((X[0] - X[1]) / 2) ** 2))

docs.title: 4.3 QSVM: The Havlíček et al. 2019 Experiment and Its Legacy
docs.text:
'QSVM' usually means a classical support vector machine fed with a quantum kernel. In 2019 an IBM team led by Vojtěch Havlíček ran it on a superconducting chip using 2 qubits, with an encoding they conjectured to be hard to simulate at larger sizes. It became the template for hundreds of later quantum-kernel papers — and for later critiques.

From SVMs to quantum kernels on hardware. The 2019 experiment sits between early theory and the 2021-2024 critical results.

Think of it like…

A QSVM is a classic car with a new engine swapped in: the chassis (the SVM) is decades old and well understood; only the engine (the kernel) is quantum.

Real-world example

Students at the fictional Danube Tech reproduce the experiment in simulation: 2 qubits, an IQP-style encoding of Hadamards plus Z and ZZ phase rotations repeated twice, and a synthetic dataset whose labels were generated from the feature map itself. Their exact simulation separates the classes perfectly; adding readout noise lowers kernel values and accuracy, and they explain why this dataset says nothing about real-world advantage.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Generate an 'engineered' dataset whose labels come from the quantum feature map, with a gap between classes.
  2. Encode each 2-D point using two repetitions of Hadamard gates followed by Z and ZZ phase rotations.
  3. Estimate every kernel entry on hardware with a compute-uncompute circuit and many shots, mitigating errors.
  4. Train a classical SVM on the measured Gram matrix.
  5. Compare with a variational quantum classifier trained on the same encoding.

Who uses it

Anyone reading QML literature meets this experiment; QML engineers reproduce it when learning Qiskit or PennyLane kernel tools.

Key takeaway

Do not confuse the two QSVMs: Rebentrost, Mohseni & Lloyd (2014) is a fault-tolerant HHL-style algorithm; Havlíček et al. (2019) is a NISQ quantum-kernel SVM.

Going deeper

  • Havlíček, Córcoles, Temme, Harrow, Kandala, Chow & Gambetta ('Supervised learning with quantum-enhanced feature spaces', Nature 2019) presented a variational classifier and quantum kernel estimation on 2 qubits of a 5-qubit IBM processor.
  • Their feature map applies phases φ(x) = xᵢ on single qubits and (π − x₁)(π − x₂) on the pair, after Hadamard layers; they conjectured that such kernels are hard to estimate classically at scale.
  • The data were artificially constructed from the feature map with a separation gap, so high accuracy demonstrated feasibility on hardware, not advantage on real data.
  • Peters et al. (2021, a Fermilab-Google collaboration) ran a quantum kernel on 17 qubits of Google's Sycamore processor to classify supernova data with 67 features, reaching accuracy comparable to noiseless simulation.
  • Qiskit Machine Learning provides QSVC and QSVR classes wrapping scikit-learn's SVC and SVR around a quantum kernel; since version 0.7 the library has been co-maintained by IBM and the Hartree Centre.
  • Later analyses (power of data 2021, exponential concentration 2022-2024, benchmarking 2024) reframed the question from 'can it run?' to 'can it beat a well-tuned classical kernel on this data?'

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing the 2014 HHL-based QSVM with the 2019 kernel QSVM — their hardware needs and assumptions are completely different.
  • Citing the 2019 accuracy as evidence of advantage: the dataset was engineered to suit the kernel.

docs.title: Try it: A QSVM with an IQP-style (H + Z + ZZ) feature map in PennyLane
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC

n = 2
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def k_circ(x1, x2):
    qp.IQPEmbedding(x1, wires=range(n), n_repeats=2)          # H, Z and ZZ phases, twice
    qp.adjoint(qp.IQPEmbedding)(x2, wires=range(n), n_repeats=2)
    return qp.probs(wires=range(n))

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
X = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (60, 2))
y = np.where(np.sin(X[:, 0]) * np.sin(X[:, 1]) > 0, 1, -1)    # toy labels
K = qp.kernels.square_kernel_matrix(X, lambda a, b: k_circ(a, b)[0])
print("train accuracy:", SVC(kernel="precomputed").fit(K, y).score(K, y))

A 2-qubit kernel matrix from IBM hardware is passed to a standard SVM solver. Havlíček et al. 2019IBM, Nature 567, 2019 · Paper · Current · Beginner Landmark experiment demonstrating a quantum kernel classifier and a variational classifier on superconducting hardware. It is one of the most cited QML papers and the source of the ZZ feature-map design. Points whose label-function value lies within ±0.3 of zero are removed from the dataset. Two qubits are trivially simulable; the conjecture concerns kernels on many qubits. With 150 support vectors at 1,000 shots, one prediction costs 150,000 shots. Normal card transactions train the model; unusual ones fall outside the learned boundary.

docs.title: 4.4 Kernel Alignment & Trainable Quantum Kernels
docs.text:
A fixed quantum kernel may not suit your data. Trainable quantum kernels add adjustable angles to the encoding circuit and tune them so that the kernel's similarity pattern matches the labels: points of the same class look similar, points of different classes look different. The score being maximised is called kernel-target alignment.

Training a quantum kernel. Only the kernel's angles θ are trained; the SVM is fitted once at the end.

Think of it like…

It is like adjusting a microscope's focus until cells of the same type look alike and different types look clearly different — before you start sorting them.

Real-world example

Hana at the fictional VinoQ classifies two grape varieties from 4 chemical measurements. Her initial embedding kernel has alignment 0.18 and SVM test accuracy 71%. After 300 gradient steps maximising alignment on random 8-point batches, alignment rises to 0.46 and test accuracy to 89% — and she confirms on a separate validation set that the gain is real.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Build an embedding circuit U(x, θ) mixing data-encoding gates with trainable gates.
  2. Define the kernel k_θ(x, x′) = |⟨0|U(x′, θ)†U(x, θ)|0⟩|².
  3. Compute kernel-target alignment A = ⟨K, yyᵀ⟩_F / (‖K‖_F · ‖yyᵀ‖_F) on a mini-batch of labelled points.
  4. Take gradient steps on θ to maximise A (parameter-shift gradients pass through the kernel circuits).
  5. Freeze θ, build the full Gram matrix and train the SVM as usual.

Who uses it

QML researchers and engineers tuning kernels for real datasets; the same idea appears in classical multiple-kernel learning.

Key takeaway

With ±1 labels the ideal Gram matrix is yyᵀ (+1 for same class, −1 otherwise); alignment measures the cosine similarity between your K and that ideal.

Going deeper

  • Kernel-target alignment comes from classical kernel learning (Cristianini, Shawe-Taylor, Elisseeff & Kandola, NeurIPS 2001); centered alignment (Cortes, Mohri & Rostamizadeh, JMLR 2012) subtracts means first and copes better with class imbalance.
  • Hubregtsen, Wierichs, Gil-Fuster, Derks, Faehrmann & Meyer ('Training quantum embedding kernels on near-term quantum computers', PRA 2022) introduced the approach behind PennyLane's kernel tutorial, including noise mitigation for kernel matrices.
  • Glick et al. (Nature Physics 2024) used alignment to tune the fiducial state of covariant quantum kernels for data with group structure and ran the method on 27 superconducting qubits.
  • Each alignment step costs about B²/2 kernel circuits for batch size B plus their gradients, so batches of 4-16 points keep training affordable on hardware.
  • Thanasilp, Wang, Cerezo & Holmes (Nature Communications 2024) showed that alignment training of expressive embeddings can itself suffer exponential concentration, so trainable kernels inherit barren-plateau-like problems.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Computing alignment on the whole training set every step: that costs N² circuits; use small random mini-batches.
  • Optimising alignment on test data: tune θ only on training folds and confirm gains on held-out data.
  • Ignoring class imbalance: plain alignment rewards majority-class structure; use centered alignment or rescaled labels.

docs.title: Try it: Train a quantum embedding kernel by maximising target alignment
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
from pennylane import numpy as pnp
import numpy as np

n = 2
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

def embed(x, theta):
    for l in range(2):
        qp.AngleEmbedding(x, wires=range(n))
        qp.BasicEntanglerLayers(theta[l:l + 1], wires=range(n), rotation=qp.RY)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def k_circ(x1, x2, theta):
    embed(x1, theta)
    qp.adjoint(embed)(x2, theta)
    return qp.probs(wires=range(n))

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(-1, 1, (12, 2))
y = np.sign(X[:, 0] * X[:, 1])                    # XOR-like labels
theta = pnp.array(rng.normal(0, 0.5, (2, n)), requires_grad=True)

def align(t):
    return qp.kernels.target_alignment(
        X, y, lambda a, b: k_circ(a, b, t)[0], assume_normalized_kernel=True)

opt = qp.AdamOptimizer(0.1)
print("alignment before:", align(theta))
for _ in range(25):
    theta = opt.step(lambda t: -align(t), theta)
print("alignment after: ", align(theta))

docs.title: 4.5 Projected Quantum Kernels & the Power of Data
docs.text:
Huang and colleagues (Nature Communications 2021) showed that data make classical learners surprisingly strong: a classical model trained on examples can often predict the output of a quantum process that is hard to compute directly. They gave a test — the geometric difference — for whether a quantum kernel could beat classical kernels on a dataset, and introduced projected quantum kernels, which compare small (few-qubit) pieces of states instead of whole states.

Fidelity vs projected quantum kernels

Fidelity kernel Projected kernel Compares Whole n-qubit states 1-qubit reduced states Formula |⟨φ(x)|φ(x′)⟩|² exp(−γ Σₖ ‖ρₖ − ρ′ₖ‖²) Many qubits Tends toward identity matrix Keeps useful distances Measured with Overlap circuit Local tomography / shadows Bandwidth knob Only via encoding scale γ, like an RBF kernel

Projecting onto local pieces keeps distances meaningful as qubits grow.

Think of it like…

Comparing two cities by their entire maps makes every pair look completely different; comparing them neighbourhood by neighbourhood (a projected kernel) reveals meaningful similarities.

Real-world example

Yusuf at the fictional Halcyon Quantum computes the geometric difference between his fidelity kernel and a tuned RBF kernel on 500 points and finds it small, meaning a classical kernel should do at least as well whatever the labels. Only after relabelling the data with a function engineered from the quantum kernel does the geometric difference become large — and the projected quantum kernel then wins.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Encode each data point x into an n-qubit state ρ(x).
  2. Estimate the reduced density matrices ρₖ(x) of each qubit (or small group), e.g. with classical shadows.
  3. Projected kernel: k(x, x′) = exp(−γ Σₖ ‖ρₖ(x) − ρₖ(x′)‖²_F).
  4. Compute the geometric difference g between classical and quantum Gram matrices on your data.
  5. If g is small, a classical kernel is provably competitive for any labels; if g approaches √N, labels can exist where the quantum kernel wins.

Who uses it

QML theorists, Google Quantum AI-style research groups and careful practitioners use this framework before investing in hardware experiments.

Key takeaway

Key formula: g(K_C‖K_Q) = √‖√K_Q K_C⁻¹ √K_Q‖∞ — small g means no possible quantum prediction advantage on that dataset with that classical kernel.

Going deeper

  • Huang, Broughton, Mohseni, Babbush, Boixo, Neven & McClean ('Power of data in quantum machine learning', Nature Communications 2021) based their analysis on prediction-error bounds rather than on whether a circuit is hard to simulate.
  • The model complexity s_K = yᵀK⁻¹y controls the error bound: when a Gram matrix is close to the identity, s_K approaches N and the model cannot generalise.
  • Fidelity kernels on many qubits tend to make distinct inputs nearly orthogonal, so the Gram matrix approaches the identity and the model memorises; projecting onto local reduced states restores a usable notion of distance.
  • Their abstract reports a prediction advantage over some classical models on engineered datasets using up to 30 qubits, and a rigorous speed-up for a projected quantum model in the fault-tolerant regime.
  • Single-qubit reduced density matrices can be estimated efficiently with classical shadows, so projected kernels need far fewer measurement settings than full tomography.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling a near-identity fidelity Gram matrix 'expressive': it means memorisation, and test accuracy will collapse.
  • Concluding advantage from engineered labels: real-world labels rarely have the structure that makes g large.
  • Skipping the geometric-difference check before booking expensive hardware time, only to find a classical kernel matches the result.

docs.title: Try it: A projected quantum kernel from single-qubit reduced density matrices
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
import numpy as np

n = 4
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def rdms(x):
    qp.IQPEmbedding(x, wires=range(n))
    return [qp.density_matrix(wires=[k]) for k in range(n)]   # one 2x2 matrix per qubit

def projected_kernel(x1, x2, gamma=1.0):
    d = sum(np.linalg.norm(np.array(a) - np.array(b)) ** 2      # Frobenius distances
            for a, b in zip(rdms(x1), rdms(x2)))
    return np.exp(-gamma * d)

x1, x2 = np.random.rand(n), np.random.rand(n)
print("projected kernel:", projected_kernel(x1, x2))
print("self-similarity :", projected_kernel(x1, x1))            # always 1

docs.title: 4.6 Exponential Concentration of Quantum Kernels & Bandwidth Fixes
docs.text:
As qubits are added, many quantum kernels give almost the same value — typically close to 0 — for every pair of different points, so the Gram matrix looks like the identity. Telling values apart then needs exponentially many shots, and the trained model effectively ignores its input. Thanasilp, Wang, Cerezo & Holmes traced this to expressive embeddings, global measurements, entanglement and noise. A popular fix is to shrink the encoding angles with a 'bandwidth' factor so states stay closer together.

Average fidelity of Haar-random states, 1/2ⁿ. Unstructured kernels drift toward these tiny values as qubits are added.

Think of it like…

It is like zooming a camera so far in that every portrait becomes a blur of skin: all photos look equally (dis)similar. Zooming back out — a smaller bandwidth — restores recognisable differences.

Real-world example

Tariq at the fictional Orbital AI uses a 20-qubit IQP kernel. Off-diagonal values average around 10⁻⁶, well below what 10,000 shots can resolve (about 10⁻⁴), so his SVM predicts a single class. Multiplying every input by a bandwidth factor c = 0.1 lifts typical kernel values into the 0.1-0.5 range, and test accuracy recovers to match a tuned RBF kernel.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Diagnose: histogram the off-diagonal kernel values at increasing qubit counts and watch mean and variance shrink.
  2. Estimate the shot cost: values or differences of size δ need at least about 1/δ shots, often 1/δ².
  3. Fix the encoding: scale inputs by a bandwidth c < 1 (x → c·x) and choose c by cross-validation.
  4. Prefer projected (local) kernels over global fidelity kernels.
  5. Reduce depth, entanglement and noise, then re-check concentration at the target size.

Who uses it

Anyone scaling quantum kernels beyond a handful of qubits — QML researchers, hardware benchmarking teams and reviewers of kernel papers.

Key takeaway

Haar-random states on n qubits have average fidelity 1/2ⁿ — a quick sanity number for how fast unstructured kernels concentrate.

Going deeper

  • Thanasilp, Wang, Cerezo & Holmes ('Exponential concentration in quantum kernel methods', arXiv 2022; Nature Communications 2024) proved concentration from four sources: expressive embeddings, global measurements, entanglement and noise.
  • With concentrated kernels and polynomially many shots, the estimated Gram matrix is dominated by statistical noise, so the trained model's predictions become essentially independent of the test input.
  • Shaydulin & Wild ('Importance of kernel bandwidth in quantum machine learning', PRA 2022) showed that tuning a bandwidth factor rescues fidelity kernels at larger qubit counts; Canatar et al. (TMLR 2023) linked bandwidth to generalisation through kernel spectral bias.
  • A small bandwidth keeps all states close to the starting state, so the kernel behaves like a low-order function of x; critics note this can also make the kernel easier to approximate classically.
  • Hardware noise compounds the problem: strong depolarising noise drives every state toward the maximally mixed state, pushing kernel values toward 1/2ⁿ for all pairs.
  • Projected and covariant kernels resist concentration better because they compare local or structured information, but they also concentrate once reduced states become nearly maximally mixed.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Celebrating perfect training accuracy from a near-identity Gram matrix: it is memorisation, and test accuracy will collapse.
  • Choosing the bandwidth on the test set: tune it with cross-validation on training data only.
  • Checking concentration only at 4-6 qubits: the effect is exponential and becomes obvious only as n grows.

docs.title: Try it: Watch kernel values concentrate — and recover with bandwidth scaling
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
import numpy as np

def offdiag_stats(n, c=1.0, pairs=30):
    dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

    @qp.qnode(dev)
    def k(x1, x2):
        qp.IQPEmbedding(c * x1, wires=range(n), n_repeats=2)
        qp.adjoint(qp.IQPEmbedding)(c * x2, wires=range(n), n_repeats=2)
        return qp.probs(wires=range(n))

    vals = [k(*np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, (2, n)))[0] for _ in range(pairs)]
    return round(np.mean(vals), 5), round(np.var(vals), 7)

for n in [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]:
    print(n, "qubits  c=1:", offdiag_stats(n), "  c=0.1:", offdiag_stats(n, c=0.1))

docs.title: 4.7 Provable Advantage Constructions: The Discrete-Log Learning Problem
docs.text:
To prove that a quantum learner can beat every classical one, researchers construct special learning problems from tasks believed hard for classical computers. Liu, Arunachalam & Temme (Nature Physics 2021) built one from the discrete logarithm problem — the maths behind some public-key cryptography — and showed a quantum kernel learns it efficiently, while no efficient classical learner can do noticeably better than random guessing (assuming discrete log is classically hard). It is a genuine proof, but the problem is artificial and needs a fault-tolerant computer.

The discrete-log learning separation

Any efficient classical learner Quantum kernel learner Sees Samples (x, f_s(x)) The same samples Key step Would need to compute log_g x Period finding exposes log_g x Accuracy ≤ ½ + 1/poly (if DLP is hard) High, with a large margin Hardware Ordinary computer Fault-tolerant QPU Data realism Artificial Artificial

Same data, same task — the difference is whether discrete log can be computed.

Think of it like…

It is like proving a master key-cutter beats every lock-picker on one specially designed lock: impressive and rigorous, but it tells you nothing about the locks on ordinary houses.

Real-world example

Student Elena at the fictional Uppsala Quantum Club explains it in a seminar. The data are numbers x modulo a huge prime p; each label says whether the hidden exponent k with gᵏ = x mod p falls inside a secret interval. A classical learner that beat chance would effectively compute discrete logarithms; the quantum feature map uses Shor-style period finding to expose k, after which an SVM separates the classes easily.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a function believed hard classically: the discrete logarithm modulo a large prime p with generator g.
  2. Define labels: f_s(x) = +1 if log_g(x) lies in the interval [s, s + (p − 3)/2], otherwise −1, for a secret s.
  3. Classical hardness: an efficient classical learner beating random guessing by an inverse-polynomial margin would yield an efficient discrete-log algorithm.
  4. Quantum learner: a feature map built on Shor-style circuits maps x to states encoding log_g(x); a kernel SVM separates the classes with a large margin.
  5. Robustness: the quantum kernel keeps high accuracy even with finite-shot estimation errors.

Who uses it

Quantum learning theorists, complexity researchers and anyone evaluating 'provable quantum advantage' claims in QML need to understand this construction.

Key takeaway

Interview line: the separation is conditional on the classical hardness of discrete log, uses artificial data, and needs fault-tolerant Shor-type circuits — it proves possibility, not practicality.

Going deeper

  • The result is a separation under a standard cryptographic assumption (classical hardness of discrete logarithms), not an unconditional proof; it inherits its power from Shor's 1994 algorithm.
  • For cryptographically sized primes, the feature map needs fault-tolerant Shor-type circuits, far beyond today's noisy processors.
  • Earlier separations include Servedio & Gortler (SIAM Journal on Computing 2004) on quantum versus classical learnability, and Sweke, Seifert, Hangleiter & Eisert (Quantum 2021) on learning certain discrete distributions.
  • Jerbi et al. ('Quantum machine learning beyond kernel methods', Nature Communications 2023) showed some re-uploading models need exponentially more data when recast as kernels — a separation between quantum model families, not against classical ML.
  • Further proposals derive learning problems from quantum simulation or other classically hard computations; their labels are hard to compute classically, but realistic datasets rarely look like these constructions.
  • Practical takeaway: provable advantages exist for cryptographic or physics-derived structure; for everyday tabular or image data there is no proof and little empirical evidence of quantum advantage.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Citing Liu et al. as proof that QSVMs beat classical ML on real data: it covers one artificial, cryptography-based problem.
  • Forgetting the assumption: the separation holds only if discrete logarithms are classically hard.

docs.title: Try it: Toy version of the discrete-log dataset (tiny prime — NOT hard!)
docs.text:
p, g = 23, 5                 # 5 generates the multiplicative group mod 23
s = 7                        # secret start of the 'positive' interval
half = (p - 3) // 2          # interval length from the construction

# Brute force works only because p is tiny; for a 2048-bit prime it is believed infeasible.
dlog = {pow(g, k, p): k for k in range(p - 1)}
data = [(x, 1 if (dlog[x] - s) % (p - 1) <= half else -1) for x in range(1, p)]
print(data)
# A quantum feature map recovers dlog[x] with Shor-style period finding,
# after which the two classes are separated by a wide margin.

For p = 23 and g = 5, x = 10 gives k = 3, but 2048-bit primes are infeasible classically. Concept class f_sLiu, Arunachalam & Temme 2021 · Concept · Research · Advanced Labels +1 when log_g(x) falls in an interval starting at secret s; the family is indexed by s. Learning f_s from samples amounts to locating the secret interval of exponents. Cryptographic hardness assumptionComplexity theory · Concept · Current · Intermediate Separations rely on problems believed — but not proven — classically intractable. If someone found a fast classical discrete-log algorithm, the separation would vanish. Shor's algorithmShor 1994 · Algorithm · Current · Beginner Quantum period finding that factors integers and computes discrete logarithms in polynomial time. The quantum feature map borrows Shor's circuit to compute log_g(x) for each data point. Learning separationQuantum learning theory · Concept · Current · Intermediate A task where quantum learners provably succeed with resources that would make all classical learners fail. A separation is stated with explicit assumptions, resources and accuracy guarantees. Distribution-learning separationSweke, Seifert, Hangleiter & Eisert, Quantum 2021 · Paper · Research · Advanced Showed certain discrete distributions are efficiently learnable by quantum but not classical generative learners, under assumptions. It is the generative-modelling counterpart of the discrete-log classification result. Quantum vs classical learnabilityServedio & Gortler, SIAM Journal on Computing 2004 · Paper · Current · Advanced Early study of when quantum examples or queries make concept classes easier to learn, with separations based on hardness. Learning-theory courses use it to introduce quantum PAC and exact learning. QML beyond kernel methodsJerbi et al., Nature Communications 2023 · Paper · Current · Advanced Some re-uploading quantum models need exponentially more training data when expressed as kernels. A model learnable from 100 samples as a re-uploading circuit could need far more as a kernel. Margin robustness to shot noiseLiu, Arunachalam & Temme 2021 · Concept · Research · Advanced Large-margin separation keeps accuracy high even when kernel entries are estimated with finite shots. Kernel errors of a few percent leave the SVM's decisions unchanged on this problem. Random-guessing barrier (½ + 1/poly)Classical hardness statement · Metric · Research · Advanced Classical learners cannot exceed chance accuracy by more than an inverse-polynomial margin on the task. At best, a classical model might reach 50.001% on large instances. Physics-derived learning tasksProposals from several groups since 2021 · Concept · Research · Advanced Learning problems whose labels come from classically hard quantum simulations rather than cryptography. Labels from long-time dynamics of a 100-qubit spin system define a candidate advantage task.

docs.title: 4.8 Quantum Circuit Born Machines (QCBMs)
docs.text:
A generative model learns to produce new samples that look like its training data. A quantum circuit Born machine uses the fact that measuring a quantum state gives random bitstrings with probabilities equal to the squared amplitudes (the Born rule). Train the circuit so its measurement statistics match the data distribution, and then every shot is a new sample.

Training a quantum circuit Born machine. Sampling is free on hardware; the loss compares samples, not probabilities.

Think of it like…

It is like tuning a set of loaded dice until rolling them reproduces the pattern of results in your notebook — after that, every roll is a fresh, realistic sample.

Real-world example

Analyst Grace at the fictional HarbourRe models joint defaults of 8 insurers as 8-bit strings (1 = default). She trains an 8-qubit QCBM with a maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) loss on 5,000 historical scenarios. After training, 1,000 shots produce 1,000 new stress scenarios whose pairwise default correlations closely match the history — and she checks that most generated strings are new rather than copies of training data.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Represent each data sample as a bitstring, discretising continuous values onto a grid of 2ⁿ points if needed.
  2. Prepare |ψ(θ)⟩ with a PQC; the model distribution is p_θ(x) = |⟨x|ψ(θ)⟩|².
  3. Compare model samples with data using a loss: MMD (sample-based) or KL divergence (needs probabilities).
  4. Update θ using parameter-shift gradients of the MMD loss or a gradient-free optimiser.
  5. Generate: measure the trained circuit; each shot is a new sample.

Who uses it

QML researchers in finance (scenario generation), high-energy physics (event generation) and hardware benchmarking use Born machines.

Key takeaway

Remember why MMD is preferred: Born machines are implicit models — sampling is easy on hardware, but exact probabilities of individual bitstrings are not available.

Going deeper

  • Benedetti, Garcia-Pintos, Perdomo, Leyton-Ortega, Nam & Perdomo-Ortiz (npj Quantum Information 2019) proposed QCBMs for benchmarking shallow circuits; Liu & Wang (PRA 2018) introduced gradient training with an MMD loss.
  • Coyle, Mills, Danos & Kashefi ('The Born supremacy', npj Quantum Information 2020) argued certain Born machines, e.g. IQP-based ones, sample from distributions believed hard to sample classically.
  • Rudolph, Lerch, Thanasilp, Kiss, Shaya, Vallecorsa, Grossi & Holmes (npj Quantum Information 2024) showed explicit losses such as KL divergence suffer a new kind of barren plateau, while MMD trainability depends on its kernel bandwidth.
  • Tensor-network Born machines (Han, Wang, Fan, Wang & Zhang, PRX 2018) are classical models with exact sampling — the natural baseline for any QCBM claim.
  • Generalisation matters more than fit: Gili et al. ('Do quantum circuit Born machines generalize?', 2023) proposed metrics for producing valid, novel samples rather than memorised training bitstrings.
  • Applications studied include financial scenario generation, loading probability distributions for quantum Monte Carlo, and benchmarking hardware by how well it reproduces target distributions.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Training with KL divergence from exact probabilities on many qubits: these are unavailable on hardware and prone to barren plateaus.
  • Judging success by reproducing training bitstrings: that is memorisation; measure validity and novelty of samples.
  • Ignoring discretisation: n qubits give only 2ⁿ grid points for a continuous variable.

docs.title: Try it: Train a 3-qubit Born machine to reproduce a target distribution
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
from pennylane import numpy as pnp
import numpy as np

n = 3
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)
target = np.array([0.4, 0.05, 0.05, 0.0, 0.05, 0.0, 0.05, 0.4])   # mostly 000 and 111

@qp.qnode(dev)
def born(w):
    qp.StronglyEntanglingLayers(w, wires=range(n))
    return qp.probs(wires=range(n))           # Born rule: p(x) = |<x|psi>|^2

def kl(w):
    p = born(w)
    mask = target > 0
    return pnp.sum(target[mask] * pnp.log(target[mask] / (p[mask] + 1e-10)))

w = pnp.array(np.random.default_rng(0).normal(0, 0.5, (3, n, 3)), requires_grad=True)
opt = qp.AdamOptimizer(0.1)
for _ in range(200):
    w = opt.step(kl, w)
print(np.round(born(w), 3))   # close to target; on hardware you would sample with shots

docs.title: 4.9 QGANs, Quantum Boltzmann Machines & Quantum Diffusion
docs.text:
Beyond Born machines, three classical generative ideas have quantum versions. Quantum GANs pit a quantum generator against a quantum or classical discriminator. Quantum Boltzmann machines model data with the thermal state of a quantum Hamiltonian. Quantum diffusion proposals learn to reverse a step-by-step noising process — sometimes to generate quantum data such as ensembles of states.

Quantum GAN training loop. The generator is quantum; the discriminator is often classical.

Think of it like…

A GAN is a forger and an art detective making each other better; a Boltzmann machine is a landscape where likely data sit in valleys; a diffusion model learns to un-blur a photo step by step.

Real-world example

A team at the fictional LuxQuant builds a patch QGAN: four small quantum sub-generators, each producing one strip of an 8 × 8 handwritten-digit image, trained against a small classical discriminator. After a few hundred steps the generated digits are recognisable — the same capability classical GANs reached years ago without any constraints on image size, which the team states clearly in its report.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. QGAN: a PQC generator G(θ) produces samples; a discriminator D(φ), classical or quantum, scores real versus fake; θ and φ are updated in turns.
  2. Patch QGAN: several small quantum generators each produce part of an image, so the model fits on few qubits.
  3. QBM: define a Hamiltonian H(θ) including transverse-field terms; the model distribution comes from the Gibbs state e^(−H)/Z; train to match data statistics.
  4. Quantum diffusion: a forward process adds noise (random unitaries or depolarising steps); a learned backward circuit removes it step by step.
  5. Evaluate sample quality and compare with classical generators of similar size and training budget.

Who uses it

Generative-modelling researchers, finance teams exploring distribution loading, and physicists generating quantum data explore these models.

Key takeaway

Name the key papers: QGANs (Lloyd & Weedbrook; Dallaire-Demers & Killoran, 2018), QBMs (Amin et al., PRX 2018), quantum diffusion QuDDPM (Zhang et al., PRL 2024).

Going deeper

  • Lloyd & Weedbrook (PRL 2018) and Dallaire-Demers & Killoran (PRA 2018) proposed quantum GANs; Zoufal, Lucchi & Woerner (npj Quantum Information 2019) used a qGAN to load a log-normal distribution for option pricing with amplitude estimation.
  • Huang et al. (Physical Review Applied 2021) demonstrated a patch-style QGAN generating handwritten digits on a superconducting processor; PennyLane's QGAN tutorial follows this patch design.
  • Amin, Andriyash, Rolfe, Kulchytskyy & Melko ('Quantum Boltzmann machine', PRX 2018) added a transverse field to Boltzmann machines and trained with bounds on the log-likelihood; quantum annealers have been studied as Boltzmann samplers.
  • Kieferová & Wiebe (PRA 2017) studied generative training of QBMs, including for quantum state tomography; preparing low-temperature Gibbs states is itself hard, which limits near-term use.
  • Zhang, Xu, Chen & Zhuang (PRL 2024) proposed QuDDPM, a quantum denoising diffusion model that generates ensembles of quantum states, such as correlated noise and many-body phases.
  • GAN training is notoriously unstable (mode collapse, oscillation); quantum versions add shot noise and barren plateaus, so published demonstrations remain small.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming QGANs beat classical GANs: published demos use tiny images that classical GANs handle easily.
  • Forgetting that low-temperature Gibbs-state preparation is hard: QBMs do not sidestep this cost.
  • Treating quantum diffusion models as ready-to-use tools: they are early research proposals tested on small systems.

docs.title: 4.10 Generalisation Bounds for Quantum Models
docs.text:
Generalisation asks whether a model that fits its training data will also work on new data. Caro and colleagues (Nature Communications 2022) proved that for a quantum model with T trainable gates, the generalisation error grows roughly like √(T log T / N) for N training examples — so circuits with few parameters need little data. Later work showed such uniform bounds can be loose: quantum models can also memorise random labels.

Bound scaling √(T log T / N) for T = 20. Constants omitted: the shape shows how quickly more data tightens the guarantee.

Think of it like…

It is like a student who learned only a few tricks from 10 practice questions: the fewer tricks, the more likely their exam score matches their practice score — though it says nothing about whether either score is high.

Real-world example

Zara at the fictional Q-Health trains a QCNN with 20 trainable gates on 2,000 labelled quantum states. The scaling √(T log T / N) suggests a train-test gap on the order of 0.17 (ignoring constants); her measured gap is 0.04, consistent with the bound being valid but loose. She then runs a random-label test and finds the model can fit 30% of shuffled labels, a sign of extra capacity the bound does not capture.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define the generalisation error: expected loss on new data minus training loss.
  2. Caro et al. bound: the error grows as O(√(T log T / N)) for T parameterised local gates and N examples.
  3. If gates are reused, as in QCNN filters, the effective T is smaller and fewer examples suffice.
  4. If only K of T gates change significantly in training, the error scales roughly as √(K log T / N).
  5. Check empirically: held-out data, cross-validation and randomised-label tests.

Who uses it

QML theorists, researchers planning dataset sizes for quantum-data experiments, and reviewers judging overfitting claims use these results.

Key takeaway

A generalisation bound limits the gap between training and test error — it is not an accuracy guarantee and not evidence of quantum advantage.

Going deeper

  • Caro, Huang, Cerezo, Sharma, Sornborger, Cincio & Coles ('Generalization in quantum machine learning from few training data', Nature Communications 2022) applied their bound to QCNN phase classification and to learning unitaries such as the quantum Fourier transform.
  • Gil-Fuster, Eisert & Bravo-Prieto (Nature Communications 2024) showed QNNs can fit randomly labelled data, so uniform complexity-based bounds cannot explain why they generalise — echoing Zhang et al.'s 2017 deep-learning finding.
  • Caro et al. (Nature Communications 2023) studied out-of-distribution generalisation for learning quantum dynamics, showing training on simple product states can suffice for predictions on entangled states.
  • Other tools include Rademacher complexity and covering numbers of circuit families, effective dimension (Abbas et al. 2021) and information-theoretic bounds (Banchi, Pereira & Pirandola, PRX Quantum 2021).
  • For kernel models, the data-dependent quantity yᵀK⁻¹y from Huang et al. (2021) plays the role of model complexity in the error bound.
  • Good bounds tell you roughly how much data you need; they do not prove advantage, since a classical model may generalise equally well on the same task.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading the bound as a guarantee of accuracy: it bounds the train-test gap, not the training error itself.
  • Assuming few parameters always generalise well: encoding and data distribution matter, and random-label tests can reveal large memorisation capacity.

docs.title: Try it: How the bound's scaling shrinks with more data (constants omitted)
docs.text:
import numpy as np

T = 20                                          # trainable local gates
for N in [50, 200, 1_000, 5_000, 20_000]:
    print(f"N = {N:>6}:  sqrt(T log T / N) = {np.sqrt(T * np.log(T) / N):.3f}")
# Shared gates (e.g. QCNN filters) reduce the effective T and tighten the bound.
