docs.title: 4.11 Quantum Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
In reinforcement learning (RL) an agent learns by trial and error, collecting rewards from an environment. Quantum RL replaces the agent's policy or value network with a PQC, uses quantum search to speed up exploration, or lets agents interact with quantum environments. Results so far are small-scale, with a few rigorous separations on artificial tasks.

One step of a variational quantum RL agent. Every decision costs many shots, and every update costs 2P gradient circuits.

Think of it like…

A quantum RL agent is like a chess learner whose 'intuition' is a quantum circuit — the board, the rules, the rewards and the practice games all remain classical.

Real-world example

Student Luca at the fictional Turin Robotics trains a 4-qubit policy on the CartPole task (4 observations, 2 actions) with the REINFORCE algorithm. Each step encodes the cart's state into rotations, measures two observables, turns them into action probabilities with a softmax and samples an action. After about 500 episodes the agent balances the pole for the maximum 500 steps — exactly what a small classical network with around 100 weights achieves.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The environment returns a state s; encode it into the circuit, often with data re-uploading.
  2. Policy PQC: measure observables and apply a softmax to get action probabilities π_θ(a|s).
  3. Value-based alternative: the circuit outputs Q-values for each action (variational deep Q-learning).
  4. Collect rewards; compute policy gradients (REINFORCE) or temporal-difference targets.
  5. Update θ with parameter-shift gradients and a classical optimiser; repeat over many episodes.

Who uses it

QML researchers, robotics and control groups exploring quantum agents, and quantum-control teams using RL for experiments work in this area.

Key takeaway

Separate the three flavours: PQC policies or value functions (variational QRL), Grover-style exploration speed-ups, and agents learning about quantum environments.

Going deeper

  • Early proposals include Dong, Chen, Li & Tarn (IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics B, 2008), using superposition for action selection, and Dunjko, Taylor & Briegel (PRL 2016) on quantum-enhanced agent-environment interaction.
  • Chen et al. (IEEE Access 2020) and Lockwood & Si (2020) used variational circuits as deep Q-networks; Skolik, Jerbi & Dunjko ('Quantum agents in the Gym', Quantum 2022) showed trainable output scaling matters on CartPole and FrozenLake.
  • Jerbi, Gyurik, Marshall, Briegel & Dunjko (NeurIPS 2021) introduced raw-PQC and softmax-PQC policies and proved a learning separation on RL environments built from the discrete-log problem.
  • Saggio et al. (Nature 2021) showed a photonic agent learning faster through a quantum communication channel with its environment — a Grover-like speed-up in learning time, not a PQC policy.
  • Projective simulation (Briegel & De las Cuevas, Scientific Reports 2012) is a physics-inspired agent model with quantum variants developed by the same Innsbruck community.
  • RL needs very many policy evaluations, each needing many shots, so hardware runs are tiny; most published results are classical simulations of small circuits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing up Grover-type learning speed-ups with PQC policies: they are different mechanisms with different requirements.
  • Benchmarking only on CartPole: tiny classical networks solve it, so it cannot show quantum advantage.
  • Ignoring the shot cost per action: every single decision requires repeated circuit measurements.

docs.title: Try it: A softmax-PQC policy choosing an action for one CartPole state
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
from pennylane import numpy as pnp
import numpy as np

n, n_actions = 4, 2
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def policy_circuit(state, w):
    for layer in w:
        qp.AngleEmbedding(state, wires=range(n))        # re-upload the observation
        qp.BasicEntanglerLayers(layer[None], wires=range(n))
    return [qp.expval(qp.Z(0) @ qp.Z(1)), qp.expval(qp.Z(2) @ qp.Z(3))]

def policy(state, w, beta=2.0):
    logits = beta * pnp.stack(policy_circuit(state, w))
    return pnp.exp(logits) / pnp.sum(pnp.exp(logits))   # softmax-PQC

w = pnp.array(np.random.uniform(0, np.pi, (3, n)), requires_grad=True)
cart_state = np.array([0.02, -0.1, 0.03, 0.2])   # position, velocity, angle, angular velocity
probs = policy(cart_state, w)
action = np.random.choice(n_actions, p=np.array(probs))
print(probs, "-> action", action)

Shows quadratic speed-ups in some exploration settings via Grover-like amplitude amplification. The agent found rewarded actions in fewer interaction rounds than its classical counterpart. An agent learns pulse settings that prepare a target state with 99% fidelity.

docs.title: 4.12 Quantum Transformers & Attention Proposals
docs.text:
Transformers — the models behind modern chatbots — rely on 'attention', in which every token (a word or image patch) compares itself with every other token. Researchers have proposed quantum versions: circuits computing attention scores from state overlaps, quantum vision transformers built from orthogonal-layer circuits, and transformer blocks built with quantum linear-algebra tools. All are early research tested on small datasets.

A hybrid quantum self-attention layer. Most proposals keep normalisation and the output head classical.

Think of it like…

Attention is a classroom where every student glances around to see whose notes are most relevant; quantum proposals try to let that glancing happen through interference between quantum states.

Real-world example

Nadia at the fictional TextQ tests a quantum self-attention layer on a 50-sentence sentiment dataset. Each word embedding becomes a 4-qubit state, attention weights come from measured overlaps, and a classical head classifies the sentence. Accuracy matches a tiny classical attention model, and she notes that the experiment says nothing about scaling to the millions of tokens real language models process.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Encode each token (word or image patch) as a quantum state or as rotation angles.
  2. Compute query and key representations with PQCs and estimate their similarities (overlaps or expectation values).
  3. Normalise the scores, usually classically with a softmax, and mix the value vectors.
  4. Stack with classical feed-forward layers and train end to end.
  5. Fault-tolerant alternative: implement whole blocks with block-encodings, linear combinations of unitaries and QSVT.

Who uses it

QML researchers at universities and companies such as QC Ware and Quantinuum, and NLP researchers curious about quantum models, work on these proposals.

Key takeaway

When you read 'quantum transformer', ask three questions: how many parameters and tokens, how the data are loaded, and which classical baseline it was compared with.

Going deeper

  • Quantum self-attention neural networks (QSANN; Li, Zhao & Wang, 2022) used Gaussian-projected PQC outputs as attention scores for text classification on small public datasets.
  • Cherrat, Kerenidis, Mathur, Landman, Strahm & Li ('Quantum Vision Transformers', Quantum 2024) proposed three architectures from orthogonal layers, simulated them on medical-image benchmarks and ran small experiments on up to 6 superconducting qubits.
  • Khatri, Matos, Coopmans & Clark ('Quixer', arXiv 2024) built a quantum transformer from linear combinations of unitaries and QSVT, reporting results competitive with a classical baseline on a practical language-modelling task.
  • Other 2024 work examined whether quantum linear algebra (block-encodings of attention matrices) could implement transformer blocks; input loading and readout costs decide whether any speed-up survives.
  • Classical attention costs about O(L²d) for L tokens of dimension d; quantum proposals often claim polynomial savings that disappear if data loading requires QRAM.
  • No quantum transformer has been shown to beat classical transformers at practical scale; models with billions of parameters lie far beyond any foreseeable quantum simulation or hardware.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading 'quantum transformer' as 'quantum large language model': tested models have tens to thousands of parameters and toy data.
  • Quoting asymptotic speed-ups while ignoring the cost of loading token data into quantum states.

docs.title: Try it: Toy attention weights from quantum state overlaps
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
import numpy as np

n = 3
dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=n)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def overlap(q, k):
    qp.AngleEmbedding(q, wires=range(n), rotation="Y")
    qp.adjoint(qp.AngleEmbedding)(k, wires=range(n), rotation="Y")
    return qp.probs(wires=range(n))

tokens = np.random.default_rng(3).uniform(0, np.pi, (4, n))    # 4 tokens, 3 features each
scores = np.array([[overlap(a, b)[0] for b in tokens] for a in tokens])
weights = np.exp(4 * scores) / np.exp(4 * scores).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)  # softmax
print(np.round(weights, 2))      # row i: how much token i attends to each token

docs.title: 4.13 Tensor Networks & Quantum-Inspired Classical ML
docs.text:
Tensor networks are classical data structures, invented to simulate quantum many-body systems, that store huge arrays of numbers as chains or trees of small ones. They double as machine-learning models (matrix product states as classifiers or generators), as simulators of quantum circuits, and as the backbone of 'quantum-inspired' methods that bring quantum ideas to ordinary computers. They are often the toughest classical baselines for QML claims.

Where tensor networks meet QML. The same data structure is a model, a simulator and a baseline.

Think of it like…

It is like compressing a gigantic spreadsheet into a chain of small linked tables: you can still look up any cell, and when the data have limited 'connectedness', storage shrinks from astronomical to manageable.

Real-world example

Data scientist Jonas at the fictional NordStats classifies 28 × 28 handwritten digits with a matrix product state, mapping every pixel to a 2-component vector. With a modest bond dimension the model runs on a laptop and reaches accuracy in the high 90s, following Stoudenmire & Schwab (2016). He uses it as the classical baseline in a QCNN study — and it wins.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map each input feature to a small local vector, e.g. a pixel value x ↦ [cos(πx/2), sin(πx/2)].
  2. The model's weights form one huge tensor W; approximate it by a matrix product state (MPS) with bond dimension χ.
  3. Train by sweeping along the chain (DMRG-style) or by gradient descent with automatic differentiation.
  4. Bond dimension χ controls capacity: memory grows like n·d·χ² instead of dⁿ.
  5. Reuse: the same MPS can simulate circuits, generate samples, or be compiled into gates to initialise a quantum circuit.

Who uses it

Computational physicists, ML researchers, GPU-simulation engineers and companies offering quantum-inspired software use tensor networks.

Key takeaway

Remember: tensor networks are efficient when entanglement is limited (area law); a QML model whose circuits stay low-entanglement is likely tensor-network simulable.

Going deeper

  • Stoudenmire & Schwab ('Supervised learning with tensor networks', NeurIPS 2016) trained an MPS classifier on MNIST with DMRG-style sweeps and reported under 1% test error at large bond dimension.
  • An MPS with bond dimension χ represents states whose entanglement across any cut is at most log₂χ bits; volume-law entangled states need χ exponential in n.
  • Tensor-network circuit simulation (libraries such as quimb, ITensor and NVIDIA's cuTensorNet) underlies much of the evidence that many QML models are classically simulable.
  • Quantum-inspired linear-algebra algorithms (from Tang's 2018 recommendation-system result onward) use length-squared sampling to 'dequantise' some QML speed-ups; the fault-tolerant chapter covers them in depth.
  • Industry uses include tensor-network compression of neural networks, including large language models (for example Multiverse Computing's CompactifAI), and tensor-train factorisation of large embedding tables.
  • Rudolph et al. (Nature Communications 2023) used MPS solutions to pretrain quantum circuits, mapping tensor-network parameters onto gates to start training away from barren plateaus.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling quantum-inspired methods 'quantum': they run entirely on classical hardware, whatever the marketing says.
  • Assuming tensor networks can simulate any circuit: highly entangled (volume-law) states need exponentially large bond dimensions.
  • Skipping a tensor-network baseline when claiming a QML model is hard to simulate.

docs.title: Try it: Compress a 10-qubit state into a matrix product state with SVDs (NumPy only)
docs.text:
import numpy as np

n, chi = 10, 4                                   # qubits, maximum bond dimension
psi = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=2 ** n)
psi /= np.linalg.norm(psi)

cores, rest = [], psi.reshape(1, -1)
for k in range(n - 1):
    rest = rest.reshape(rest.shape[0] * 2, -1)
    U, S, Vh = np.linalg.svd(rest, full_matrices=False)
    keep = min(chi, len(S))                      # truncate to bond dimension chi
    cores.append(U[:, :keep].reshape(-1, 2, keep))
    rest = np.diag(S[:keep]) @ Vh[:keep]
cores.append(rest.reshape(-1, 2, 1))

print("MPS numbers:", sum(c.size for c in cores), "vs full state:", 2 ** n)
# Random states are highly entangled and compress badly; low-entanglement states compress well.

docs.title: 4.14 Classical Shadows & Learning from Quantum Data
docs.text:
Sometimes the data are already quantum: states produced by a sensor, a chemistry experiment or another quantum computer. Full tomography of an n-qubit state needs exponentially many measurements, but classical shadows (Huang, Kueng & Preskill 2020) measure each copy in a random basis and keep a compact classical record that predicts many properties at once. Shadows then feed classical or quantum ML models.

From quantum state to classical shadow to prediction. One set of random measurements answers many different questions later.

Think of it like…

Instead of making a full 3-D scan of a sculpture, you snap quick photos from random angles; from enough snapshots you can answer many specific questions — its height, its symmetry — without ever rebuilding the whole model.

Real-world example

Physicist Aiko at the fictional Kyoto Quantum Devices collects 2,000 random-Pauli snapshots from each of 300 prepared 20-qubit states. From the shadows she estimates all 190 two-point correlators ⟨ZᵢZⱼ⟩ per state and trains a classical kernel model that predicts each state's phase, reaching 96% test accuracy — no quantum circuit is involved in the learning itself.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Prepare one copy of the unknown state ρ.
  2. Apply a random unitary from a fixed ensemble — e.g. a random Pauli basis on each qubit — and measure all qubits.
  3. Store the basis choice and outcome bits: one 'snapshot'.
  4. Invert the measurement channel to turn each snapshot into an unbiased estimate of ρ, then average many.
  5. Predict many observables with median-of-means estimation, or feed the shadow features into ML models.

Who uses it

Experimental physicists, quantum hardware characterisation teams and QML researchers working with quantum data rely on classical shadows.

Key takeaway

Memorise the scaling: predicting M observables to accuracy ε needs about log(M) × (shadow norm)² / ε² snapshots; k-local Pauli observables with random Pauli shadows cost a factor 3ᵏ.

Going deeper

  • Huang, Kueng & Preskill ('Predicting many properties of a quantum system from very few measurements', Nature Physics 2020) proved the log(M) scaling in the number of observables and introduced the shadow norm.
  • Random Pauli shadows suit local observables (cost 3ᵏ for k-local Paulis), while random Clifford shadows suit global, low-rank observables such as fidelity with a target state.
  • Huang, Kueng, Torlai, Albert & Preskill ('Provably efficient machine learning for quantum many-body problems', Science 2022) showed classical ML trained on shadows can predict ground-state properties and classify phases efficiently.
  • Learning with quantum memory — processing several copies of a state coherently — can be exponentially more sample-efficient for some tasks; Huang et al. (Science 2022) demonstrated this on Google hardware, as the fault-tolerant chapter explains.
  • Shadows power 'quantum-enhanced classical' surrogates: gather shadows once from hardware, then evaluate many losses classically — a central argument in the trainability-simulability debate.
  • PennyLane provides the qp.classical_shadow and qp.shadow_expval measurements plus a ClassicalShadow class for post-processing; derandomised shadows (Huang, Kueng & Preskill, PRL 2021) reduce snapshots for fixed observable sets.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using random Pauli shadows for global observables such as fidelity with an entangled state: variance grows exponentially; use random Clifford shadows instead.
  • Treating a shadow as the full state: it is an unbiased estimator of linear properties, not a compact exact description.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate several observables of a Bell state from one set of shadows
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp

dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=2)

@qp.set_shots(2000)
@qp.qnode(dev)
def bell_shadow():
    qp.Hadamard(wires=0)
    qp.CNOT(wires=[0, 1])
    return qp.shadow_expval([qp.Z(0) @ qp.Z(1), qp.X(0) @ qp.X(1), qp.Z(0)])

print(bell_shadow())     # ≈ [1, 1, 0] for the Bell state (|00> + |11>)/√2

docs.title: Chapter 6: Quantum Optimisation & Annealing for ML
docs.text: Many machine-learning problems hide a discrete optimisation inside — choosing features, clusters, weak learners or binary weights. This chapter shows how such tasks become QUBO and Ising models, how quantum annealers such as D-Wave's Advantage and Advantage2 attack them, and how gate-model algorithms like QAOA and its variants — and the VQE seen as a learning problem — do the same on today's processors. It ends with the habits that matter most: fair benchmarking against strong classical and quantum-inspired solvers, and realistic expectations based on published comparisons.

docs.title: 6.1 Optimisation in ML & Where Quantum Might Fit
docs.text:
Almost every machine-learning task is an optimisation problem: training minimises a loss, feature selection picks the best subset, clustering finds the best grouping, and tuning searches over settings. Most training is smooth (continuous) and handled superbly by gradient descent on GPUs. Quantum optimisers target the discrete, combinatorial parts — choosing subsets, assignments or binary weights — where problems can be NP-hard.

Two kinds of optimisation in ML

Continuous training Combinatorial ML tasks Examples network weights, regression feature selection, clustering, binary nets Landscape smooth, gradients available discrete, no gradients Best classical tools SGD, Adam, L-BFGS on GPUs MIP solvers, annealing, tabu search Complexity often tractable in practice NP-hard in general Quantum candidates few (see fault-tolerant chapter) annealing, QAOA, Grover-type search

Quantum optimisers aim at the right-hand column, not at training large networks.

Think of it like…

Training a neural network is like rolling a ball downhill on a smooth landscape — easy when you can feel the slope. Combinatorial problems are like finding the best setting of thousands of on/off switches, where there is no slope to follow.

Real-world example

The fictional insurer Harbourline wants a fraud model using the best 20 of 300 features. There are about 7.5 × 10³⁰ possible subsets, so trying them all is impossible. Its team can use greedy selection, L1 regularisation, a mixed-integer solver, or write the task as a QUBO for a quantum annealer or QAOA — and must benchmark every option fairly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the decision variables: continuous weights, or discrete choices such as bits, assignments and orderings.
  2. Classify the problem: convex or non-convex continuous, or combinatorial (NP-hard in general).
  3. Try strong classical tools first: gradient methods, mixed-integer solvers and metaheuristics.
  4. If the core is a binary quadratic problem, write it as a QUBO or Ising model for quantum or quantum-inspired solvers.
  5. Compare solution quality and time-to-solution against tuned classical baselines.

Who uses it

ML engineers, operations researchers, and quantum application scientists at banks, logistics firms, manufacturers and car makers who experiment with quantum optimisation.

Key takeaway

Remember: quantum computers are not expected to solve NP-hard problems efficiently in general; the hope is for better heuristics or polynomial speed-ups on specific problem families.

Going deeper

  • Training deep networks is non-convex continuous optimisation at a scale of 10⁹-10¹² parameters using first-order methods; no quantum optimiser comes anywhere near that scale.
  • Combinatorial ML sub-problems — feature selection, k-medoids clustering, L0-penalised sparse models, binary or quantised network training, graph partitioning, job scheduling — map naturally to binary variables.
  • NP-complete problems are not believed to lie in BQP, so quantum optimisers are heuristics or offer at most polynomial (often quadratic) speed-ups for generic search.
  • Approximation guarantees set the bar: Goemans-Williamson's 0.878 ratio for MaxCut (1995) is the best possible for efficient algorithms if the Unique Games Conjecture holds.
  • Useful metrics include gap to the optimum or best-known value, time-to-solution at a target success probability, and total cost including encoding, queueing and post-processing.
  • Abbas et al.'s 46-author perspective (Nature Reviews Physics, 2024) calls quantum optimisation promising but unproven, and urges rigorous benchmarks against state-of-the-art classical solvers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking quantum computers solve NP-complete problems in polynomial time; there is no evidence they can.
  • Turning continuous training into a QUBO by discretising weights and then claiming a speed-up; gradient methods are usually far better.
  • Benchmarking against brute force or untuned heuristics instead of modern solvers such as Gurobi or well-tuned simulated annealing.

docs.title: Key algorithms, circuits, techniques, tools & papers
docs.text: Name What it does Example Loss minimisationMachine-learning basics · Concept · Current · Beginner Training means finding parameters that minimise average error on data; usually smooth and solved with gradient methods. Fitting logistic regression to a million insurance claims with L-BFGS takes seconds on a laptop. Combinatorial optimisationOperations research · Concept · Current · Beginner Choosing the best option from a finite but astronomically large set of discrete choices — subsets, orderings or assignments. Assigning 50 vans to 2,000 orders has more combinations than atoms in the universe, yet good heuristics find near-optimal plans. NP-hardnessComplexity theory (Cook 1971; Karp 1972) · Concept · Current · Intermediate Problems at least as hard as every problem in NP; no efficient exact algorithm is known for them, classical or quantum. MaxCut, the travelling salesperson problem and general QUBO are NP-hard, so no solver is expected to crack every instance. Feature selection as subset optimisationMachine-learning practice · Technique · Current · Beginner Picking a small subset of input features that keeps predictive power while reducing noise, cost and overfitting. Choosing 20 of 300 fraud features with greedy forward selection, L1 regularisation, or a QUBO balancing relevance and redundancy. Clustering as optimisationMachine-learning practice · Technique · Current · Beginner Grouping points to minimise within-cluster distances; k-means is continuous-ish, while k-medoids and balanced clustering are discrete. Choosing 10 warehouse sites (medoids) among 500 candidate towns is a binary decision problem. A ±1-weight keyword spotter runs on a microcontroller; straight-through gradient estimators are the usual classical training trick. Hyperparameter optimisationBergstra & Bengio 2012; Optuna · Technique · Current · Beginner Searching learning rates, depths and other settings; done with random search or Bayesian optimisation, not quantum hardware. Optuna tries 100 configurations of a gradient-boosting model overnight on a small cluster. Approximation ratioApproximation algorithms · Metric · Current · Intermediate A heuristic's solution value divided by the optimum; the key quality metric for QAOA and other approximate optimisers. A cut of 87 edges when the maximum cut is 100 has approximation ratio 0.87. Time-to-solution (TTS)Rønnow et al. 2014 · Metric · Current · Intermediate Expected time to find the optimum (or a target quality) with given confidence, accounting for repeated runs. If one 20-μs anneal succeeds with probability 0.01, reaching 99% confidence needs 459 anneals — about 9 ms. Goemans-Williamson algorithmGoemans & Williamson 1995 · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Classical SDP-based MaxCut algorithm with a guaranteed 0.878 approximation ratio — the bar quantum optimisers must beat. Solving the SDP for a 1,000-node graph and rounding with a random hyperplane guarantees at least 87.8% of the maximum cut in expectation. 'Challenges and opportunities in quantum optimization'Abbas et al. 2024 (Nature Reviews Physics) · Paper · Current · Beginner Large community review of quantum optimisation algorithms, hardware results and benchmarking needs, stressing fair classical comparisons. A good first reading: it surveys QAOA, annealing and variational methods and lists open problems for students. Gradient-based optimisersRobbins & Monro 1951; Kingma & Ba 2015 (Adam) · Optimiser · Current · Beginner SGD, Adam and L-BFGS: first- or quasi-second-order methods that dominate continuous ML training. Adam trains a 100-million-parameter transformer on GPUs; no quantum optimiser competes at this scale.

docs.title: 6.2 QUBO & Ising Formulations
docs.text:
A QUBO (quadratic unconstrained binary optimisation) problem asks for binary variables xᵢ ∈ {0, 1} that minimise xᵀQx. The Ising model is the same thing written with spins sᵢ ∈ {−1, +1}, fields hᵢ and couplings Jᵢⱼ. These are the native language of quantum annealers and the usual input for QAOA, so a problem must be translated into this form first.

A QUBO is a weighted graph. Nodes carry linear weights; edges carry pairwise couplings the solver must balance.

Think of it like…

Picture a group of people each voting yes or no: each person has a personal preference (the linear term), and pairs of friends or rivals gain or lose points depending on whether they agree (the quadratic term).

Real-world example

Sofia at the fictional Verdant Logistics wants to split six depots into two balanced regions while minimising cross-region traffic. She gives each depot a binary variable, adds traffic between pairs as quadratic terms, and adds a penalty P·(Σxᵢ − 3)² to enforce three depots per region. The result is a 6×6 Q matrix ready for an annealer or QAOA.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose binary decision variables xᵢ (or spins sᵢ = 2xᵢ − 1).
  2. Write the objective as linear plus pairwise terms.
  3. Turn constraints into quadratic penalties, for example P·(Σxᵢ − k)².
  4. Collect coefficients into an upper-triangular Q matrix, or into fields h and couplings J.
  5. Choose the penalty weight P: large enough to enforce constraints, small enough not to swamp the objective.
  6. Hand the model to a solver — annealer, QAOA, simulated annealing or a MIP solver.

Who uses it

Quantum application developers, operations researchers, and anyone preparing problems for D-Wave, QAOA or Ising-machine hardware.

Key takeaway

Memorise the mapping x = (1 + s)/2: it converts a QUBO into an Ising model and back, shifting linear terms and adding a constant offset.

Going deeper

  • QUBO energy is E(x) = Σᵢ Qᵢᵢxᵢ + Σᵢ<ⱼ Qᵢⱼxᵢxⱼ and Ising energy E(s) = Σhᵢsᵢ + ΣJᵢⱼsᵢsⱼ; finding Ising ground states on general graphs is NP-hard (Barahona, 1982).
  • Lucas (Frontiers in Physics, 2014) gave Ising formulations of Karp's NP-complete problems and many more, and Glover, Kochenberger & Du (4OR, 2019) wrote a practical QUBO modelling tutorial.
  • Inequality constraints need slack variables, usually binary-encoded integers: a constraint Σwᵢxᵢ ≤ C adds about log₂C extra bits, increasing qubit count.
  • Integer variables can be encoded one-hot (k bits plus a penalty) or in binary (fewer bits but uneven coefficients), and the choice changes the precision demanded from hardware.
  • Higher-order terms such as xᵢxⱼxₖ are reduced to quadratic form with auxiliary variables and penalties (Rosenberg, 1975), again adding qubits.
  • On D-Wave Advantage systems, fields and couplings must fit ranges such as h ∈ [−4, 4] and J ∈ [−1, 1], so badly scaled QUBOs lose detail in hardware noise.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Picking penalty weights blindly: too small and constraints break; too large and the objective is flattened, hurting solution quality.
  • Forgetting that slack variables and one-hot encodings can multiply the number of qubits several times.
  • Mixing the QUBO {0, 1} and Ising {−1, +1} conventions in code, which silently flips signs and offsets.

docs.title: Try it: Build a QUBO, view it as an Ising model and solve it with D-Wave's open-source Ocean tools
docs.text:
# pip install dimod dwave-samplers
import dimod
from dwave.samplers import SimulatedAnnealingSampler
Q = {(0, 0): -1, (1, 1): -1, (2, 2): -1, (0, 1): 2, (1, 2): 2, (0, 2): 2}   # 'pick exactly one of three'
bqm = dimod.BinaryQuadraticModel.from_qubo(Q)
print(bqm.to_ising())                    # the same problem as (h, J, offset)
best = SimulatedAnnealingSampler().sample(bqm, num_reads=50).first
print(best.sample, best.energy)          # one variable set to 1, energy -1

docs.title: 6.3 Writing ML Tasks as QUBOs
docs.text:
Several machine-learning tasks can be written as QUBOs: choosing a subset of features, assigning points to clusters, picking which weak classifiers to combine (boosting), or training models with binary weights. Once in QUBO form they can run on annealers, QAOA or classical QUBO solvers — though the quantum step is usually one small piece of a bigger, mostly classical workflow.

From ML task to solver. The QUBO is a common interface: any solver below can attack any task above.

Think of it like…

Like translating a recipe into a universal cooking language: once it is written in 'QUBO', any compatible kitchen — quantum or classical — can cook it.

Real-world example

Ahmed at the fictional Meridian Health wants a compact, interpretable sepsis model. He builds a QUBO where each bit switches one of 40 simple decision stumps on or off; the objective rewards matching the labels and penalises using too many stumps. This is the QBoost idea first explored by Google and D-Wave researchers (Neven et al., 2008).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose the binary decision: feature on/off, point-to-cluster, weak classifier on/off, or a weight bit.
  2. Write the ML loss — squared error, correlation or distance — as a quadratic function of those bits.
  3. Add regularisation (such as a sparsity term) as linear terms and constraints as penalties.
  4. Solve the QUBO with an annealer, QAOA or a classical solver.
  5. Decode the bits into a model and validate it on held-out data as usual.

Who uses it

Applied quantum scientists at consultancies, research institutes and industrial labs, and ML researchers exploring alternative training methods.

Key takeaway

Squared-error losses become QUBOs naturally: expanding (Σ wᵢhᵢ(x) − y)² over binary wᵢ gives exactly linear plus pairwise terms.

Going deeper

  • QBoost (Neven, Denchev, Rose & Macready, 2008; extended 2012) selects a sparse combination of weak classifiers by minimising squared loss plus an L0-style penalty — a direct QUBO tested on early D-Wave hardware.
  • Mott, Job, Vlimant, Lidar & Spiropulu (Nature, 2017) used a QBoost-style annealing approach for Higgs-boson classification; it held up well with small training sets but did not beat boosted trees or neural networks with more data.
  • Willsch, Willsch, De Raedt & Michielsen (Computer Physics Communications, 2020) trained kernel SVMs on a D-Wave annealer by encoding dual coefficients with a few bits each and ensembling low-energy solutions.
  • Feature-selection QUBOs typically balance relevance (correlation or mutual information with the label) against redundancy between features, plus a cardinality penalty for choosing exactly k features.
  • Clustering formulations use one-hot bits x_{i,c} (point i in cluster c) with a penalty per point; N points and K clusters need N·K variables, quickly exceeding hardware capacity.
  • Most published studies use tens to a few hundred binary variables per QUBO — far below real ML sizes — so decomposition or hybrid solvers are needed for anything realistic.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Discretising continuous weights into many bits each: qubit counts explode and limited coefficient precision on annealers degrades results.
  • Reporting the lowest QUBO energy on training data instead of test accuracy; the ML goal is generalisation, not energy.
  • Skipping classical baselines such as L1-regularised regression or greedy selection, which often match QUBO-based selection.

docs.title: Try it: QUBO feature selection on a scikit-learn dataset (relevance minus redundancy, pick about 5)
docs.text:
# pip install dimod dwave-samplers scikit-learn
import numpy as np, dimod
from dwave.samplers import SimulatedAnnealingSampler
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
R = np.abs(np.corrcoef(np.c_[X, y].T))          # |correlation| matrix including the label
rel, red = R[-1, :-1], R[:-1, :-1]              # relevance to label, redundancy between features
k, alpha, P = 5, 0.5, 2.0                       # target size, redundancy weight, penalty weight
n = len(rel); bqm = dimod.BinaryQuadraticModel("BINARY")
for i in range(n):
    bqm.add_linear(i, -rel[i] + P * (1 - 2 * k))          # from P*(sum x - k)^2
    for j in range(i + 1, n):
        bqm.add_quadratic(i, j, alpha * red[i, j] + 2 * P)
best = SimulatedAnnealingSampler().sample(bqm, num_reads=100).first.sample
print("chosen features:", [i for i, v in best.items() if v])

docs.title: 6.4 Quantum Annealing: How It Works
docs.text:
Quantum annealing starts the qubits in the easy ground state of a 'transverse field' that puts every qubit in superposition, then slowly turns that field down while turning the problem's Ising energy up. If the change is slow enough (the adiabatic theorem), the system stays near its lowest-energy state and ends in a low-energy solution. Real devices are noisy and fast, so in practice they act as heuristic samplers.

One quantum anneal. Thousands of these short runs are sampled for every problem.

Think of it like…

Like slowly cooling molten glass in a mould: start with everything soft and spread out, then gradually 'freeze' into the shape the mould (the problem) favours — with quantum tunnelling letting it slip through thin walls instead of climbing over them.

Real-world example

Jun at the fictional Kestrel Robotics runs a 500-variable scheduling QUBO on a D-Wave annealer. Each anneal lasts 20 microseconds; she requests 1,000 reads, receives a histogram of solutions and keeps the lowest-energy valid schedule. QPU time is well under a second, though network and queueing time add more.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Encode the problem Hamiltonian H_P = Σhᵢσᶻᵢ + ΣJᵢⱼσᶻᵢσᶻⱼ on qubits and couplers.
  2. Start all qubits in the ground state of the driver H_D = −Σσˣᵢ, an equal superposition of all bitstrings.
  3. Sweep the schedule H(s) ∝ −A(s)·H_D + B(s)·H_P from s = 0 to 1, lowering A and raising B.
  4. At the end, measure every qubit to read out a spin configuration.
  5. Repeat hundreds or thousands of times and keep the best samples.

Who uses it

Users of annealing hardware in logistics, scheduling and finance, and physicists studying spin glasses and quantum phase transitions.

Key takeaway

Know the adiabatic condition: required run time grows roughly as 1/Δ², where Δ is the minimum energy gap — exponentially small gaps make annealing exponentially slow.

Going deeper

  • Kadowaki & Nishimori (Physical Review E, 1998) proposed quantum annealing in the transverse-field Ising model; Farhi, Goldstone, Gutmann & Sipser (2000) formulated adiabatic quantum computation.
  • Aharonov et al. (SIAM Journal on Computing, 2007) proved universal adiabatic computation equivalent to the circuit model, but that needs non-stoquastic Hamiltonians that today's commercial annealers do not provide.
  • D-Wave's schedule is H(s) = −A(s)/2·Σσˣ + B(s)/2·(Σhᵢσᶻ + ΣJᵢⱼσᶻσᶻ); A(s) starts at several gigahertz (times Planck's constant) and falls towards zero while B(s) rises.
  • The default anneal time on D-Wave systems is 20 μs and can be set from about a microsecond to milliseconds; a separate fast-anneal mode supports far shorter, nanosecond-scale anneals.
  • Real annealers are open systems at around ten to twenty millikelvin; thermal noise means outputs often resemble low-temperature Boltzmann samples rather than guaranteed ground states.
  • Stoquastic Hamiltonians, like the transverse-field Ising model, can often be simulated by quantum Monte Carlo — one reason experts doubt exponential speed-ups from today's annealers.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing annealers always return the optimum: they are heuristic samplers, so take many reads and check quality.
  • Equating quantum annealing with gate-model quantum computing: today's annealers cannot run Shor's algorithm or general circuits.
  • Assuming slower anneals are always better: noise and thermal effects mean longer anneals often help less than expected.

docs.title: Try it: Watch the energy gap change during a two-qubit anneal (NumPy)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Z = np.diag([1, -1]); I = np.eye(2)
k = np.kron
HD = -(k(X, I) + k(I, X))                     # transverse-field driver
HP = k(Z, Z) + 0.5 * k(Z, I) - 0.2 * k(I, Z)  # a tiny Ising problem
for s in np.linspace(0, 1, 6):
    e = np.linalg.eigvalsh((1 - s) * HD + s * HP)
    print(f"s={s:.1f}  ground={e[0]:+.3f}  gap={e[1] - e[0]:.3f}")

docs.text: Name What it does Example Quantum annealingKadowaki & Nishimori 1998 · Algorithm · Current · Beginner Heuristic that slowly lowers a transverse field while raising a problem Hamiltonian, so tunnelling helps reach low-energy solutions. D-Wave systems run thousands of 20-μs anneals per problem and return the lowest-energy samples. Adiabatic quantum computationFarhi, Goldstone, Gutmann & Sipser 2000 · Concept · Research · Intermediate Computation by slowly evolving a Hamiltonian's ground state; the universal version is equivalent to circuit-model quantum computing. Aharonov et al. proved equivalence using non-stoquastic Hamiltonians; commercial annealers implement only a restricted stoquastic version. Adiabatic theoremBorn & Fock 1928 · Theorem · Current · Intermediate A system stays in its instantaneous ground state if the Hamiltonian changes slowly compared with the inverse square of the gap. Shrinking the minimum gap from 1 to 0.01 can lengthen the required anneal by a factor of around ten thousand. Transverse-field driverKadowaki & Nishimori 1998 · Concept · Current · Beginner The Hamiltonian −Σσˣ whose ground state is an equal superposition; it enables tunnelling and is switched off during the anneal. At s = 0 every qubit is in |+⟩, so all 2ᴺ spin configurations have equal amplitude. Annealing schedule A(s), B(s)D-Wave documentation · Concept · Current · Intermediate Time-dependent strengths of the driver and problem terms; vendors publish the curves for each device. Changing the anneal time from 20 μs to 200 μs stretches the same schedule ten times longer. Minimum gap and avoided crossingsAdiabatic quantum computing theory · Concept · Current · Advanced The smallest separation between ground and first excited energies during the anneal; exponentially small gaps imply exponentially long runs. Some crafted instances show first-order transitions whose gaps shrink exponentially with problem size. Freeze-outAmin 2015 (PRA) · Concept · Current · Advanced Point late in the anneal where the driver becomes too weak to change the state; samples reflect conditions at that point. Studies model annealer output as a Boltzmann distribution at the freeze-out point rather than at the end of the anneal. Reverse annealingD-Wave (feature since 2017) · Technique · Current · Intermediate Starts from a chosen classical state, partly re-introduces the transverse field, then anneals forward — a quantum local search. Refining a good schedule from a greedy heuristic by reverse annealing to s = 0.6 and back. Anneal pauses and offsetsD-Wave · Technique · Current · Advanced Holding the schedule at a fixed point, or shifting individual qubits' timing, to improve sampling or balance chain dynamics. Pauses near the freeze-out region have raised ground-state probabilities in some published studies. Stoquastic HamiltonianBravyi, DiVincenzo, Oliveira & Terhal 2008 · Concept · Current · Advanced A Hamiltonian with non-positive off-diagonal elements; its ground states avoid the sign problem, so quantum Monte Carlo often simulates it. The transverse-field Ising model is stoquastic, making path-integral Monte Carlo a natural classical competitor for annealers. Quantum tunnellingQuantum mechanics · Concept · Current · Beginner Quantum systems passing through tall, thin energy barriers instead of climbing over them, which can help escape local minima. Denchev et al. (2016) built instances where tunnelling through narrow barriers gave the annealer a large edge over simulated annealing. Coherent vs open-system annealingKing et al. 2022 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Ideal annealing is coherent; real devices interact with their environment, so slow anneals thermalise while very fast anneals stay coherent. D-Wave fast-anneal experiments matched closed-system quantum predictions on chains and spin glasses — covered later in this chapter.

docs.title: 6.5 Running on a Real Annealer: Topology, Embedding & Tuning
docs.text:
Real annealers do not connect every qubit to every other. To run a QUBO you must 'embed' it: represent each logical variable by a chain of physical qubits tied together strongly so they act as one. You also tune chain strength, number of reads, anneal time and coefficient scaling — choices that strongly affect the answers you get.

D-Wave qubit topologies

Chimera Pegasus Zephyr System D-Wave 2000Q and earlier Advantage (2020) Advantage2 (2025) Qubits up to ~2,000 5,000+ 4,400+ Couplers per qubit 6 15 20 Role in 2026 legacy studies established workhorse newest generation

Richer connectivity means shorter chains and larger embeddable problems.

Think of it like…

Like seating guests at a long banquet table when some must talk to many others: you give a talkative guest several neighbouring seats (a chain) so they can reach everyone, and make sure those copies always agree.

Real-world example

Olga at the fictional Tessera Bank embeds a fully connected 120-variable portfolio QUBO on an Advantage system. The embedding tool finds chains of several qubits per variable, using over a thousand physical qubits. With weak chain strength many samples have broken chains; raising it fixes breaks but blurs the objective, so she settles on a value near the problem's coefficient scale.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inspect the hardware graph: Pegasus on Advantage, Zephyr on Advantage2.
  2. Find a minor embedding that maps each variable to a connected chain of qubits (minorminer or clique embedding).
  3. Set chain strength so chains rarely break without dwarfing the problem's coefficients.
  4. Scale coefficients into the allowed h and J ranges; choose anneal time and number of reads.
  5. Optionally apply spin-reversal transforms to average out hardware biases.
  6. Unembed: resolve broken chains, e.g. by majority vote, then polish with a quick classical local search.

Who uses it

Quantum application engineers and researchers who submit problems directly to D-Wave QPUs.

Key takeaway

Dense problems embed with long chains, so a fully connected problem uses many more physical qubits than variables — check the embedding before blaming the hardware.

Going deeper

  • Minor embedding (Choi, 2008 and 2011) maps a problem graph into the hardware graph as a graph minor; the heuristic of Cai, Macready & Roy (2014) underlies D-Wave's open-source minorminer.
  • Chimera (6 couplers per qubit) powered the D-Wave 2000Q; Pegasus (15 per qubit) powers Advantage with 5,000+ qubits; Zephyr (20 per qubit) powers Advantage2 with 4,400+ qubits, generally available since May 2025.
  • Ocean's EmbeddingComposite sets chain strength with a heuristic based on the problem's coefficients (uniform torque compensation) unless you override it, and reports a chain-break fraction for every sample.
  • Integrated control errors — small deviations of realised h and J from programmed values — limit effective precision, so problems relying on fine coefficient differences suffer.
  • Spin-reversal transforms (gauges) flip the encoding of random qubits to cancel systematic biases; splitting reads across several gauges usually gives more reliable statistics.
  • QPU access time per problem — programming plus sampling — is typically a fraction of a second; network latency and queueing come on top and matter for end-to-end comparisons.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Ignoring chain breaks: majority-vote repairs can silently produce poor or invalid solutions.
  • Comparing problem size with qubit count: a 5,000-qubit chip embeds only on the order of 100-200 fully connected variables.
  • Over-scaling coefficients so that most terms are squashed to tiny values comparable to hardware noise.

docs.title: Try it: Embed a fully connected 20-variable problem into a small Pegasus graph
docs.text:
# pip install minorminer dwave-networkx networkx
import networkx as nx, minorminer, dwave_networkx as dnx
source = nx.complete_graph(20)                 # fully connected 20-variable QUBO
target = dnx.pegasus_graph(6)                  # small Pegasus graph (Advantage family)
emb = minorminer.find_embedding(source.edges, target.edges, random_seed=1)
lengths = [len(chain) for chain in emb.values()]
print("physical qubits:", sum(lengths), " longest chain:", max(lengths))

Chain strengthD-Wave practice · Technique · Current · Intermediate Ferromagnetic coupling that ties a chain's qubits together; too weak breaks chains, too strong drowns the problem signal. A common starting point is somewhat above the largest problem coupling, then tuning while watching the chain-break fraction. Chain-break resolutionD-Wave (dwave-system) · Technique · Current · Intermediate Deciding a variable's value when its chain's qubits disagree, typically by majority vote or local energy minimisation. dwave-system reports chain_break_fraction per sample, with majority vote as the default repair method. Chimera topologyD-Wave · Hardware · Legacy · Intermediate Grid of 8-qubit bipartite unit cells with 6 couplers per qubit, used up to the 2,048-qubit D-Wave 2000Q. Many 2014-2018 benchmarking papers, such as Rønnow et al. and Denchev et al., ran on Chimera hardware. Pegasus topologyD-Wave · Hardware · Current · Intermediate Advantage's qubit graph with 15 couplers per qubit, giving shorter chains and larger embeddable problems than Chimera. Advantage processors offer 5,000+ qubits and around 35,000 couplers in the Pegasus layout. Zephyr topologyD-Wave · Hardware · Current · Intermediate Advantage2's qubit graph with 20 couplers per qubit, further shortening chains for dense problems. At Advantage2's May 2025 launch, D-Wave cited 20-way connectivity, doubled coherence and a 40% higher energy scale. Clique embeddingBoothby, King & Roy 2016; dwave-system · Technique · Current · Intermediate Pre-computed embeddings for fully connected graphs that give uniform chain lengths for dense problems. DWaveCliqueSampler embeds dense QUBOs up to the largest clique the chip supports, without a slow heuristic search. Integrated control errors (ICE)D-Wave documentation · Concept · Current · Advanced Small random and systematic deviations between programmed and realised h and J values, limiting effective precision. Two couplings programmed as 0.50 and 0.51 may be physically indistinguishable, so QUBOs relying on that difference fail. Spin-reversal transform (gauge)D-Wave practice · Technique · Current · Advanced Flips the encoding of chosen qubits and their coefficients, leaving the problem unchanged but averaging out hardware biases. Submitting 10 gauges of 100 reads each, instead of one batch of 1,000, typically yields more reliable statistics. Coefficient scalingD-Wave practice · Technique · Current · Intermediate Rescaling h and J to fit hardware ranges such as J ∈ [−1, 1]; extreme ratios push small terms into the noise. A penalty of 100 next to objective terms of 0.1 squeezes the objective to a thousandth of the range — below the noise floor. Classical post-processingdwave-samplers (SteepestDescentSolver) · Technique · Current · Beginner Quick classical steepest-descent or tabu search applied to annealer samples to remove small errors. Greedy single-bit flips on each returned sample often lower energies for a few milliseconds of CPU time. QPU access timeD-Wave Leap · Metric · Current · Beginner Billed time the QPU spends programming and sampling a problem, excluding network latency and queueing. 1,000 reads of 20-μs anneals, plus readout and delays, add up to roughly a few hundred milliseconds of QPU time.

docs.title: 6.6 D-Wave Advantage, Advantage2, Leap & Hybrid Solvers
docs.text:
D-Wave Quantum, founded in 1999 near Vancouver, Canada, is the main commercial maker of quantum annealers. Its Advantage (2020) and Advantage2 (generally available May 2025) systems are reached through the Leap cloud service and the open-source Ocean SDK. Most production users run 'hybrid solvers' that mix classical heuristics with QPU calls to handle problems far bigger than the chip itself.

D-Wave hardware and services. Qubit counts rose, then connectivity and coherence became the focus.

Think of it like…

The QPU is a specialist chef; the hybrid solver is the restaurant kitchen around it — prep cooks (classical heuristics) do most of the chopping and send only the trickiest steps to the specialist.

Real-world example

The fictional grocery chain FreshFold uses D-Wave's hybrid CQM solver to schedule 3,000 staff shifts under labour-law constraints. The solver returns feasible schedules within its time limit. FreshFold's team benchmarks it against its existing Gurobi model, finds similar quality, and chooses whichever is cheaper and easier to operate.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install Ocean (pip install dwave-ocean-sdk) and configure a Leap API token.
  2. Build a model: a BQM for the QPU or hybrid BQM solver, a CQM for constrained problems, or a nonlinear model for the Stride solver.
  3. Choose a sampler: DWaveSampler with EmbeddingComposite for direct QPU access, or a Leap hybrid sampler.
  4. Set time limits or numbers of reads, submit, and receive a SampleSet.
  5. Check feasibility and energy, and compare with classical solvers.

Who uses it

Operations-research and quantum teams at companies trialling D-Wave in manufacturing, logistics, telecoms and retail, and academic researchers with Leap access.

Key takeaway

Know the generations: D-Wave One (2011, 128 qubits) → D-Wave 2000Q (2017, 2,048) → Advantage (2020, 5,000+) → Advantage2 (2025, 4,400+ with richer connectivity).

Going deeper

  • Advantage (2020) has 5,000+ qubits in a Pegasus graph with 15 couplers per qubit; Advantage2 (generally available 20 May 2025) has 4,400+ qubits in Zephyr with 20 per qubit, plus claimed doubled coherence and 40% higher energy scale.
  • Leap hybrid solvers include hybrid BQM for unconstrained binary problems, hybrid CQM for explicit constraints with binary, integer and continuous variables, and a nonlinear solver renamed the Stride hybrid solver in January 2026.
  • Hybrid solvers run classical heuristics in the cloud and call the QPU for parts of the search; D-Wave does not publish how much each QPU call contributes, which complicates attributing results to quantum effects.
  • Ocean SDK components include dimod (models), dwave-system (QPU and Leap samplers), dwave-samplers (classical samplers), minorminer (embedding), dwave-networkx (topologies) and dwave-optimization (nonlinear models).
  • Solver limits depend on version and account; query them live, for example LeapHybridCQMSampler().properties['maximum_number_of_variables'], rather than trusting older white papers.
  • D-Wave's 2025 Science paper (King et al.) claimed beyond-classical quantum simulation of spin-glass dynamics on an annealer — a simulation result, not an optimisation or ML speed-up.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Attributing hybrid-solver results to quantum effects without ablation tests; the classical part may be doing most of the work.
  • Assuming more qubits always means bigger problems: Advantage2 has fewer qubits than Advantage but better connectivity and coherence.
  • Forgetting cost: Leap usage is billed by solver time, so compare cost per good solution, not just speed.

docs.title: Try it: A constrained model solved locally with Ocean (a Leap account adds hybrid and QPU solvers)
docs.text:
# pip install dimod dwave-samplers
import dimod
from dwave.samplers import SimulatedAnnealingSampler
cqm = dimod.ConstrainedQuadraticModel()
x = [dimod.Binary(f"x{i}") for i in range(5)]
cqm.set_objective(-3*x[0] - 2*x[1] - 4*x[2] - x[3] - 2*x[4] + 2*x[0]*x[2])
cqm.add_constraint(sum(x) == 2, label="pick_two")
bqm, invert = dimod.cqm_to_bqm(cqm, lagrange_multiplier=10)
best = SimulatedAnnealingSampler().sample(bqm, num_reads=100).first
print(invert(best.sample), best.energy)
# With Leap access: from dwave.system import LeapHybridCQMSampler
#                   LeapHybridCQMSampler().sample_cqm(cqm)

docs.title: 6.7 Coherent Annealing, Beyond-Classical Claims & Other Analogue Optimisers
docs.text:
Early critics doubted that annealers were 'quantum' at all. Since 2022, D-Wave experiments with very fast, coherent anneals have reproduced textbook quantum dynamics in chains and spin glasses of thousands of qubits, and a 2025 Science paper claimed simulations beyond classical reach. These are physics-simulation results; they have not yet translated into faster ML or optimisation. Other analogue machines — optical Ising machines and Rydberg-atom arrays — pursue similar goals.

The evidence trail for quantum annealing. Strong physics evidence accumulated; optimisation speed-ups stayed limited.

Think of it like…

Like proving a race car's engine really is turbocharged on a test bench: impressive engineering evidence, but not yet proof that it wins on the roads you actually drive.

Real-world example

Students in the fictional Northbridge University physics club read King et al. (2023): a 5,000-qubit spin glass was annealed quickly and its defects matched quantum predictions for a phase transition. They then ask whether this helps their feature-selection QUBO. The honest answer is 'not directly' — simulation advantage and optimisation advantage are different claims.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run very short anneals (nanoseconds) so the environment has little time to disturb the qubits.
  2. Compare measured correlations or defect densities with closed-system quantum predictions.
  3. Scale up the system and check where classical simulation methods stop keeping up.
  4. Separate simulation claims (physics) from optimisation claims (finding low energies faster).
  5. Ask whether the same coherence improves time-to-solution on useful optimisation instances.

Who uses it

Physicists studying quantum phase transitions, annealing-hardware engineers, and analysts judging quantum-advantage announcements.

Key takeaway

Distinguish three claims: coherence (is it quantum?), simulation advantage (can classical computers reproduce it?), and optimisation advantage (does it find better answers faster?).

Going deeper

  • Johnson et al. (Nature 473, 194, 2011) showed quantum annealing with eight 'manufactured spins' — early evidence of quantum behaviour in D-Wave's superconducting flux qubits.
  • King et al. (Nature Physics 2022) observed coherent dynamics in a 2,000-qubit Ising chain matching closed-system theory; King et al. (Nature 2023) extended this to a 5,000-qubit three-dimensional spin glass.
  • King et al. (Science 388, 199, 2025) claimed annealer samples of spin-glass quench dynamics that leading tensor-network and neural-network methods could not match; classical-simulation groups soon posted counter-simulations for parts of the problem.
  • King et al. (Nature Communications 2021) reported a scaling advantage over path-integral Monte Carlo for simulating frustrated magnets — again simulation, not optimisation.
  • Coherent Ising machines from NTT and Stanford encode spins in optical parametric oscillator pulses (Inagaki et al. and McMahon et al., Science 2016); Rydberg-atom arrays solve maximum independent set natively (Ebadi et al., Science 2022).
  • Gate-model teams also run digitised, annealing-like schedules such as counterdiabatic or linear-ramp QAOA, blurring the line between annealing and QAOA.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reading a simulation advantage as an optimisation advantage; they answer different questions.
  • Assuming coherence persists in default 20-μs anneals; the coherent results relied on very fast anneals.
  • Ignoring classical rebuttals: beyond-classical claims are often narrowed by improved classical algorithms within months.

docs.title: 6.8 QAOA: The Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm
docs.text:
QAOA (Farhi, Goldstone & Gutmann, 2014) is a gate-model algorithm for combinatorial problems. It alternates two operations p times — a 'cost' step that adds a phase to each bitstring according to its objective value, and a 'mixer' step that shuffles amplitude between bitstrings — with angles tuned by a classical optimiser. With many layers it can mimic annealing; with few layers it is a trainable heuristic.

The QAOA training loop. The quantum computer only evaluates; the classical optimiser decides.

Think of it like…

Like kneading dough: press it according to the recipe (cost layer), fold it to spread things around (mixer layer), and repeat a few rounds, adjusting how hard you press and fold until it is just right.

Real-world example

Lucía at the fictional Saltmarsh Telecom runs QAOA with p = 2 on a 12-node MaxCut problem in PennyLane. A classical optimiser tunes four angles; 1,000 shots give cuts averaging about 85% of the maximum, and the best sampled bitstring hits the optimum. Since Goemans-Williamson already guarantees 87.8% on average, she treats QAOA as a learning exercise, not a production tool.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write the problem as a cost Hamiltonian H_C — for MaxCut, Σ(1 − ZᵢZⱼ)/2 over the edges.
  2. Prepare |+⟩ on every qubit: an equal superposition of all bitstrings.
  3. Apply p layers of the cost unitary e^{−iγₖH_C} and the mixer e^{−iβₖΣXᵢ}.
  4. Measure many shots to estimate ⟨H_C⟩ for the current angles γ and β.
  5. Let a classical optimiser update the angles; repeat until converged.
  6. Return the best bitstring sampled.

Who uses it

Quantum algorithm researchers, quantum software engineers, and finance or logistics teams prototyping gate-model optimisation.

Key takeaway

Memorise the first result: for p = 1 on 3-regular graphs, QAOA's MaxCut approximation ratio is at least 0.6924 — below Goemans-Williamson's 0.878.

Going deeper

  • Farhi, Goldstone & Gutmann (arXiv:1411.4028, 2014) introduced QAOA and proved a p = 1 MaxCut ratio of at least 0.6924 on 3-regular graphs; each MaxCut cost layer needs one ZZ rotation per edge.
  • Hastings (2019) and Bravyi, Kliesch, Koenig & Tang (PRL 2020) showed local classical algorithms match or beat low-depth QAOA on bounded-degree MaxCut, and that symmetry limits low-depth performance.
  • Farhi, Gamarnik & Gutmann (2020) showed QAOA 'needs to see the whole graph': on sparse random graphs, depth must grow with problem size before QAOA can outperform classical algorithms.
  • Parameter concentration (Brandão et al., 2018): for typical instances of a given type, optimal angles are nearly instance-independent, so angles trained on small graphs transfer to larger ones.
  • At high depth, Basso et al. (2022) computed QAOA performance on large-girth regular graphs and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model in the infinite-size limit, showing steady improvement with p.
  • PennyLane's qaoa.maxcut defines its cost Hamiltonian so that lower expectation means more edges cut; its minimum equals minus the maximum cut, which is why the optimiser minimises.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing the expected cut (an average) with the best sampled cut; report both, together with the classical baseline.
  • Assuming more layers always help on hardware: deeper circuits collect more noise, which often cancels the gains of extra layers.
  • Treating QAOA as a guaranteed speed-up: it is a heuristic with no proven advantage on practical problems.

docs.title: Try it: QAOA for MaxCut on a 4-node graph with PennyLane
docs.text:
# pip install pennylane networkx
import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import qaoa
from pennylane import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
g = nx.Graph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 0), (2, 3)])
cost_h, mixer_h = qaoa.maxcut(g)
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=4)
def layer(gamma, alpha):
    qaoa.cost_layer(gamma, cost_h)
    qaoa.mixer_layer(alpha, mixer_h)
@qml.qnode(dev)
def cost(params):
    for w in range(4):
        qml.Hadamard(wires=w)
    qml.layer(layer, 2, params[0], params[1])
    return qml.expval(cost_h)
params = np.array([[0.5, 0.5], [0.5, 0.5]], requires_grad=True)
opt = qml.GradientDescentOptimizer(stepsize=0.1)
for _ in range(60):
    params = opt.step(cost, params)
print("expected cost:", round(float(cost(params)), 3), "(lower = more edges cut; max cut here = 3)")

docs.text: Name What it does Example QAOAFarhi, Goldstone & Gutmann 2014 · Algorithm · Research · Intermediate Alternates cost and mixer layers with p pairs of tuned angles to prepare states concentrated on good solutions. p = 1 MaxCut on an 8-node ring needs 8 ZZ rotations and 8 X rotations per layer. Cost HamiltonianFarhi, Goldstone & Gutmann 2014 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Diagonal operator whose eigenvalue on each bitstring equals its objective value; the cost layer applies e^{−iγH_C}. For MaxCut, H_C = Σ(1 − ZᵢZⱼ)/2 over edges counts how many edges a bitstring cuts. Mixer HamiltonianFarhi, Goldstone & Gutmann 2014 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Operator, usually ΣXᵢ, that does not commute with the cost and moves amplitude between bitstrings. The transverse-field mixer is just an RX(2β) rotation on every qubit — one layer of single-qubit gates. 0.6924 approximation guaranteeFarhi, Goldstone & Gutmann 2014 · Theorem · Current · Intermediate Proven worst-case ratio of p = 1 QAOA for MaxCut on 3-regular graphs. On a 3-regular graph whose maximum cut is 90 edges, p = 1 QAOA's expected cut is at least about 62 edges. Parameter concentrationBrandão et al. 2018 · Concept · Current · Intermediate For typical instances from the same family, optimal QAOA angles are nearly identical, enabling transfer from small to large problems. Angles optimised on 12-node 3-regular graphs work well on 100-node 3-regular graphs without re-optimisation. Locality limits of low-depth QAOAHastings 2019; Bravyi et al. 2020; Farhi, Gamarnik & Gutmann 2020 · Theorem · Current · Advanced Low-depth QAOA sees only local neighbourhoods, so local classical algorithms can match it, and depth must grow to win. At p = 1 on 3-regular graphs, a simple local classical algorithm matches or beats QAOA's guarantee. Expected value vs best sampleQAOA practice · Metric · Current · Beginner QAOA can be judged by its average energy ⟨H_C⟩ or by the best bitstring among many shots; the two tell different stories. An average ratio of 0.75 can still yield the optimal cut in one of 1,000 shots on a small graph. QAOA as Trotterised annealingFarhi, Goldstone & Gutmann 2014 · Concept · Current · Intermediate Many layers with small angles approximate a discretised annealing schedule; few layers explore non-adiabatic strategies. Initialising angles from a linear annealing ramp often beats random starting angles. Its all-to-all couplings make it hard to run on planar chips, where every pair of qubits must interact. High-depth QAOA analysisBasso et al. 2022 (TQC) · Paper · Research · Advanced Computes QAOA's performance at growing depth for large-girth regular graphs and the SK model in the infinite-size limit. Shows performance rising steadily with p — evidence that depth, not just tuning, drives QAOA quality. PennyLane qaoa moduleXanadu (PennyLane) · Library · Current · Beginner Ready-made QAOA cost and mixer Hamiltonians for problems such as MaxCut and maximum independent set, plus layer helpers. qaoa.maxcut(graph) returns cost and mixer Hamiltonians; qml.layer repeats the cost and mixer layers p times. Qiskit QAOA toolsIBM Qiskit; qiskit-community (Qiskit Optimization) · Library · Current · Intermediate Core Qiskit's QAOAAnsatz builds QAOA circuits, while the community-maintained Qiskit Optimization package converts models into QUBOs. A docplex model is converted to a QUBO, then run with QAOA on a simulator and with a classical solver for comparison.

docs.title: 6.9 QAOA Variants: Warm-Start, Recursive, Multi-Angle & More
docs.text:
Plain QAOA struggles at low depth, so researchers modify it: warm-starting from a classical solution, recursively shrinking the problem, giving each qubit or edge its own angle, building the circuit adaptively, or using mixers that respect constraints. These variants often perform better in small experiments, but none has a proven practical advantage over classical methods.

The QAOA family. Each variant fixes a different weakness of vanilla QAOA.

Think of it like…

Like upgrading a basic recipe: start from a store-bought base (warm start), cook in smaller batches (recursive), season each ingredient separately (multi-angle), or use a pan shaped for the dish (constraint-preserving mixers).

Real-world example

At the fictional Quill Securities, Hana compares QAOA variants on choosing exactly 8 of 16 assets. An XY mixer keeps every state at exactly 8 assets, so no penalty is needed; a warm start from the continuous relaxation provides a good initial state. Together they raise the probability of feasible, high-quality portfolios compared with vanilla QAOA in her simulations.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start from vanilla QAOA and identify its weakness: low depth, constraints, or a poor initial state.
  2. Warm start: solve a relaxation classically and encode its solution in the initial state and mixer.
  3. Recursive QAOA: use measured correlations to fix or merge variables, shrinking the problem until it is solvable classically.
  4. Multi-angle or adaptive: add parameters per layer, or grow the circuit operator by operator using gradient signals.
  5. Constraint-preserving: replace X mixers with XY or Grover mixers that stay inside the feasible set.

Who uses it

Quantum algorithm researchers and applied teams at banks, IBM, national laboratories and start-ups benchmarking QAOA.

Key takeaway

Mention Hadfield et al.'s 'Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz' (2019) — same acronym, generalising QAOA to arbitrary constraint-preserving mixers.

Going deeper

  • Warm-start QAOA (Egger, Mareček & Woerner, Quantum 2021) turns a continuous relaxation's solution into initial single-qubit rotations and adapts the mixer so that the warm-start state is its ground state.
  • Recursive QAOA (Bravyi, Kliesch, Koenig & Tang, PRL 2020) measures ⟨ZᵢZⱼ⟩ correlations, imposes the strongest as Zᵢ = ±Zⱼ, removes a variable and repeats; it beat standard QAOA on instances where symmetry hampers it.
  • Multi-angle QAOA (Herrman et al., Scientific Reports 2022) gives every edge and qubit its own angle, improving shallow-circuit results but making the classical optimisation harder; ADAPT-QAOA (Zhu et al., 2022) grows mixers from an operator pool.
  • The Quantum Alternating Operator Ansatz (Hadfield et al., Algorithms 2019) and Grover mixers (Bärtschi & Eidenbenz, 2020) keep the search inside feasible solutions such as fixed Hamming weight or permutations.
  • CVaR-QAOA (Barkoutsos et al., Quantum 2020) optimises the mean of the best α fraction of samples rather than the full average, aligning training with the goal that the best sample wins.
  • Shaydulin et al. (Science Advances 2024) found fixed-parameter QAOA scaled better than branch-and-bound solvers on low-autocorrelation binary sequences in simulations up to 40 qubits, and ran small instances on Quantinuum hardware with error detection.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing a heavily tuned variant against vanilla classical heuristics; tune both sides with equal effort.
  • Counting only quantum time: recursive QAOA and warm starts include substantial classical processing.
  • Assuming scaling advantages seen in noiseless simulation survive noise and compilation on real hardware.

docs.title: Try it: An XY mixer keeps the number of chosen assets fixed (NumPy and SciPy)
docs.text:
import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import expm
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]]); Y = np.array([[0, -1j], [1j, 0]]); I = np.eye(2)
def pair(P, i, j, n=3):                       # P on qubits i and j, identity elsewhere
    ops = [I] * n; ops[i] = ops[j] = P
    out = ops[0]
    for o in ops[1:]:
        out = np.kron(out, o)
    return out
H_xy = sum(pair(X, i, j) + pair(Y, i, j) for i, j in [(0, 1), (1, 2), (0, 2)])
U = expm(-1j * 0.7 * H_xy)                    # XY 'ring' mixer
state = np.zeros(8); state[0b100] = 1         # exactly one asset chosen (Hamming weight 1)
out = U @ state
print({format(k, "03b"): round(float(abs(a) ** 2), 3) for k, a in enumerate(out) if abs(a) > 1e-9})

docs.text: Name What it does Example Warm-start QAOAEgger, Mareček & Woerner 2021 (Quantum) · Algorithm · Research · Intermediate Initialises QAOA from a classical relaxation's solution and adapts the mixer accordingly, improving low-depth results. A portfolio QP relaxation gives weights such as 0.9 and 0.1, which become initial qubit rotation angles instead of uniform |+⟩ states. Recursive QAOA (RQAOA)Bravyi, Kliesch, Koenig & Tang 2020 (PRL) · Algorithm · Research · Advanced Repeatedly uses QAOA correlations to eliminate variables, shrinking the problem until it can be solved classically. A 100-node graph is reduced by fixing strongly correlated pairs until 10 nodes remain, which are brute-forced. Multi-angle QAOA (ma-QAOA)Herrman et al. 2022 (Scientific Reports) · Algorithm · Research · Intermediate Assigns a separate angle to every cost term and every mixer qubit, adding expressiveness to each layer. For a graph with 10 edges and 8 nodes at p = 1, ma-QAOA trains 18 angles instead of 2. ADAPT-QAOAZhu et al. 2022 (Physical Review Research) · Algorithm · Research · Advanced Grows the circuit layer by layer, choosing each mixer from an operator pool by the size of its energy gradient. In small MaxCut simulations it reached high approximation ratios with fewer layers than standard QAOA. Quantum Alternating Operator AnsatzHadfield et al. 2019 (Algorithms) · Algorithm · Research · Advanced Generalises QAOA with problem-specific mixers and initial states that preserve constraints, avoiding penalty terms. For graph colouring, mixers swap colours within each node's one-hot register, so invalid encodings never appear. XY mixerHadfield et al. 2019; Wang et al. 2020 · Ansatz · Research · Intermediate Mixer built from XX + YY interactions that preserves Hamming weight, keeping 'choose exactly k' constraints satisfied. To select exactly 8 of 16 assets, start in a weight-8 state and apply ring-shaped XY mixers. Grover mixerBärtschi & Eidenbenz 2020 (IEEE QCE) · Ansatz · Research · Advanced Mixer that reflects about the uniform superposition of feasible states, prepared by a state-preparation circuit. Works for any constraint set whose uniform superposition is easy to prepare, such as fixed-weight strings. Dicke-state preparationBärtschi & Eidenbenz 2019 · Technique · Research · Intermediate Prepares the equal superposition of all n-bit strings with exactly k ones — the natural start for fixed-cardinality problems. The Dicke state with n = 4 and k = 2 is an equal superposition of the six 4-bit strings with two ones. CVaR objectiveBarkoutsos et al. 2020 (Quantum) · Technique · Research · Intermediate Optimises the average of the best α fraction of measured energies instead of the overall mean, focusing on good samples. With α = 0.1 and 1,000 shots, only the 100 lowest-energy shots enter the cost function. Annealing-ramp initialisationSack & Serbyn 2021 (Quantum) · Technique · Research · Intermediate Sets initial QAOA angles from a discretised linear annealing schedule (TQA initialisation), avoiding poor local minima. For p = 10, γ rises and β falls linearly across the layers, then a local optimiser fine-tunes them. Digitised counterdiabatic QAOAChandarana et al. 2022 (Physical Review Research) · Algorithm · Research · Advanced Adds counterdiabatic-inspired terms to QAOA layers to suppress unwanted excitations and reduce the depth needed. Adding one extra single-qubit rotation term per layer sped up convergence for small Ising problems in simulation. LABS scaling studyShaydulin et al. 2024 (Science Advances) · Paper · Research · Advanced Found fixed-parameter QAOA's runtime scaling beat branch-and-bound solvers on LABS in simulations up to 40 qubits. Combined with quantum minimum finding it gave the best empirical scaling reported for LABS; small runs used Quantinuum trapped ions.

docs.title: 6.10 Gate-Model Optimisation on Real Hardware
docs.text:
Running QAOA-style optimisation on real quantum processors adds practical problems: qubits are connected only to neighbours, so extra SWAP gates are needed; every cost evaluation costs thousands of shots; and noise lowers the quality of samples. Experiments by Google, university trapped-ion labs, Quantinuum and IBM show what is possible today — and where noise still dominates.

Two-qubit gate layers per QAOA layer (rough). Routing a dense problem onto sparse hardware multiplies depth and therefore noise.

Think of it like…

Like cooking a gourmet recipe in a cramped camping kitchen: the recipe is the same, but every extra step of moving pans around (SWAP gates) costs time and risks spilling something (errors).

Real-world example

Dev, a quantum engineer at the fictional Ridgeway Energy, runs QAOA on a 100-qubit IBM processor for a grid problem whose graph matches the chip's heavy-hex layout. With no SWAPs needed, a p = 2 circuit is shallow enough to give useful samples. When he tries a fully connected version of the same problem, routing adds hundreds of SWAPs and results approach random guessing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map the problem graph to the chip; prefer hardware-native graphs or use swap networks.
  2. Transpile with error-aware layout and dynamical decoupling where available.
  3. Choose a shot budget and parameter strategy — transfer angles from simulation where possible.
  4. Apply readout mitigation; use error detection or post-selection on symmetries if the problem allows.
  5. Compare the sampled solutions with classical solvers on the same instances.

Who uses it

Quantum software engineers, hardware benchmarking teams, and application scientists running optimisation on IBM, Quantinuum, IonQ and Google-class devices.

Key takeaway

Hardware-native problem graphs avoid SWAP overhead; if your problem is fully connected, expect circuit depth to grow at least linearly with the number of qubits per QAOA layer.

Going deeper

  • Harrigan et al. (Nature Physics 2021) ran QAOA on Google's Sycamore with up to 23 qubits: hardware-native problems kept their quality as size grew, while non-native graphs degraded towards random results.
  • Pagano et al. (PNAS 2020) ran p = 1 QAOA on up to 40 trapped-ion qubits, exploiting the ions' native long-range interactions to avoid routing.
  • Swap networks (Kivlichan et al., PRL 2018; O'Gorman et al. 2019) let every qubit pair become adjacent once per layer, giving linear-depth all-to-all interactions on a line of qubits.
  • Estimating ⟨H_C⟩ to precision ε needs about Var(H_C)/ε² shots, so a full optimisation with hundreds of iterations can need hundreds of thousands to millions of shots.
  • Zero-noise extrapolation improves expectation values but not individual bitstrings; for optimisation, where the best sample matters, error detection and post-selection are often more useful.
  • IBM's Qiskit Functions catalogue lists third-party optimisation services — such as Q-CTRL's Optimization Solver and Kipu Quantum's Iskay optimizer — that wrap QAOA-like methods with error suppression.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running dense problems on sparse hardware without counting SWAP overhead; routing noise can erase any signal.
  • Mitigating expectation values and then reporting the best raw sample as if it had been mitigated too.
  • Spending the whole shot budget on parameter training, leaving too few shots for the final sampling.

Teams favour them for QAOA on dense problems because no SWAP routing is required. Researchers run QAOA on heavy-hex-native graphs with over 100 qubits and compare samples with classical solvers.
