docs.title: 6.11 The Variational Quantum Eigensolver as a Learning Problem
docs.text:
The variational quantum eigensolver (VQE; Peruzzo et al., 2014) finds the lowest energy of a molecule or material by training a parameterised circuit to minimise the measured energy — just like training a model to minimise a loss. Viewing VQE as machine learning highlights familiar issues: choosing the model (ansatz), noisy gradients, optimiser choice, local minima and trainability.

VQE seen as machine learning

Machine learning VQE Model neural network parameterised circuit (ansatz) Loss error on training data measured energy ⟨H⟩ Data labelled examples none — the Hamiltonian defines the loss Gradients backpropagation (cheap) parameter-shift: 2 circuits per parameter Noise minibatch sampling shot noise plus hardware noise Failure modes overfitting, vanishing gradients barren plateaus, local minima

Same training loop, different 'data' and different noise.

Think of it like…

VQE is like tuning a guitar by ear: twist the pegs (parameters), listen to how far off the note is (energy measurement), and keep adjusting until the sound can't get any better.

Real-world example

Dr. Kwame Mensah at the fictional Lattice Pharma uses VQE to estimate the ground-state energy of a small molecular fragment on 12 qubits. A chemistry-inspired ansatz reaches chemical accuracy in simulation, but on hardware each energy needs thousands of shots across hundreds of Pauli terms, so he groups commuting terms and applies error mitigation — and still checks the answer against classical CCSD(T).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Map the molecular Hamiltonian to qubits (Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev) as a sum of Pauli strings.
  2. Choose an ansatz: chemistry-inspired (UCCSD), hardware-efficient, or adaptive (ADAPT-VQE).
  3. Estimate ⟨H⟩ by measuring groups of commuting Pauli terms with many shots.
  4. Update the parameters with a classical optimiser, gradient-based or gradient-free.
  5. Stop when the energy converges and validate against classical methods such as CCSD(T) or DMRG.

Who uses it

Computational chemists, materials scientists, and quantum algorithm teams at pharmaceutical, chemical and quantum-hardware companies.

Key takeaway

State the variational principle: for any trial state, ⟨ψ(θ)|H|ψ(θ)⟩ ≥ E₀, so lower measured energies mean better approximations — apart from noise.

Going deeper

  • Peruzzo et al. (Nature Communications 2014) introduced VQE on a photonic chip for HeH⁺; Kandala et al. (Nature 2017) used a hardware-efficient ansatz on superconducting qubits for molecules up to BeH₂ on six qubits.
  • The number of Pauli terms in molecular Hamiltonians grows roughly as N⁴ in the number of spin-orbitals, so measurement cost dominates; grouping commuting terms and shadow-style estimators cut shot counts substantially.
  • ADAPT-VQE (Grimsley, Economou, Barnes & Mayhall, Nature Communications 2019) builds the ansatz operator by operator from a pool using energy gradients, giving shorter circuits than UCCSD.
  • Chemical accuracy is 1.6 millihartree (about 1 kcal/mol); reaching it requires statistical error well below that, which can mean millions of shots for realistic molecules.
  • Bittel & Kliesch (PRL 2021) proved that training variational quantum algorithms is NP-hard in general, so local minima — not only barren plateaus — are a fundamental obstacle.
  • Unlike ML, VQE has no training data: the Hamiltonian is the loss, so 'generalisation' becomes transferability, such as reusing optimised parameters along a bond-stretching curve.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming VQE gives a chemistry advantage today: classical methods such as CCSD(T) and DMRG handle the molecules VQE has run so far.
  • Ignoring measurement cost: thousands of Pauli terms times thousands of shots times hundreds of iterations quickly reaches billions of shots.
  • Celebrating energies below the true ground state: noise and mitigation can bias estimates below E₀, which signals an error, not success.

docs.title: Try it: A two-qubit VQE trained with Adam in PennyLane
docs.text:
# pip install pennylane
import pennylane as qml
from pennylane import numpy as np
H = qml.Hamiltonian([0.5, -0.8, 0.3], [qml.PauliZ(0) @ qml.PauliZ(1), qml.PauliX(0), qml.PauliX(1)])
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=2)
@qml.qnode(dev)
def energy(t):
    qml.RY(t[0], wires=0); qml.RY(t[1], wires=1)
    qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 1]); qml.RY(t[2], wires=1)
    return qml.expval(H)
t = np.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3], requires_grad=True)
opt = qml.AdamOptimizer(stepsize=0.1)
for _ in range(200):
    t = opt.step(energy, t)
print("VQE energy:", round(float(energy(t)), 4), "  exact:", round(float(min(np.linalg.eigvalsh(qml.matrix(H)))), 4))

docs.title: Key algorithms, circuits, techniques, tools & papers
docs.text: Name What it does Example Variational quantum eigensolver (VQE)Peruzzo et al. 2014 (Nature Communications) · Algorithm · Current · Beginner Hybrid algorithm that minimises a measured energy over parameterised circuits to approximate a Hamiltonian's ground state. Estimating hydrogen's bond-dissociation curve with a four-qubit, one-parameter ansatz is the classic first exercise. Variational principleRayleigh-Ritz method · Theorem · Current · Beginner The energy of any state is at least the true ground-state energy, so minimising it approaches E₀ from above. If H₂'s exact minimal-basis energy is about −1.137 Ha, every valid trial state measures at or above that value, apart from noise. UCCSD ansatzPeruzzo et al. 2014; Romero et al. 2018 · Ansatz · Current · Intermediate Unitary coupled cluster with single and double excitations — chemistry-inspired and accurate, but produces deep circuits. For a 12-qubit molecule, UCCSD can need thousands of CNOTs — too deep for today's hardware without heavy simplification. Hardware-efficient VQEKandala et al. 2017 (Nature) · Paper · Current · Intermediate VQE with shallow layers of native rotations and entangling gates, demonstrated on superconducting qubits for small molecules. The team estimated energies for H₂, LiH and BeH₂, the last on six qubits. Fermion-to-qubit mappingsJordan & Wigner 1928; Bravyi & Kitaev 2002 · Technique · Current · Intermediate Encode fermionic orbitals into qubits so a molecular Hamiltonian becomes a weighted sum of Pauli strings. Under Jordan-Wigner, an orbital's occupation is a qubit's |1⟩, with strings of Z operators tracking fermionic signs. Classical chemistry baselinesCCSD(T): Raghavachari et al. 1989; DMRG: White 1992 · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Gold-standard classical methods VQE results must be checked against: CCSD(T) for weakly correlated molecules, DMRG for strongly correlated ones. Kwame's 12-qubit VQE energy is compared with a CCSD(T) calculation that runs in seconds on a workstation. Chemical accuracyComputational chemistry · Metric · Current · Beginner An energy error within 1.6 millihartree (about 1 kcal/mol) — the usual target for useful chemistry predictions. A VQE energy 3 mHa above the exact value misses chemical accuracy, even though it looks close. Training VQAs is NP-hardBittel & Kliesch 2021 (PRL) · Theorem · Current · Advanced Proves that optimising the parameters of variational quantum algorithms is NP-hard in general, even in simple settings. It explains why optimisers stall in local minima, and why good initialisation and problem structure matter. Energy as a loss functionVQE as machine learning · Concept · Current · Beginner In VQE the loss is the measured energy and there are no labelled examples; the Hamiltonian plays the role of the dataset. Changing the molecule's bond length changes the 'dataset', so parameters from one geometry warm-start the next. Variational quantum deflationHiggott, Wang & Brierley 2019 (Quantum) · Algorithm · Research · Intermediate Finds excited states by adding overlap penalties with previously found states to the VQE cost. After finding the ground state, adding β·|⟨ψ₀|ψ(θ)⟩|² to the cost locates the first excited state. Sample-based quantum diagonalisation (SQD)Kanno et al. 2023; IBM and RIKEN · Algorithm · Emerging · Advanced Samples electronic configurations on a quantum computer, then diagonalises the Hamiltonian classically in that subspace — a noise-robust VQE alternative. IBM and RIKEN combined Heron processors with the Fugaku supercomputer to study iron-sulfur clusters using up to 77 qubits.

docs.title: 6.12 Benchmarking Against Classical Heuristics
docs.text:
Claims of quantum optimisation advantage only mean something against the best classical methods, run fairly: simulated annealing, parallel tempering, tabu search, mixed-integer solvers such as Gurobi and CPLEX, specialised heuristics, and tensor-network simulations. Good benchmarks fix a target quality, measure total time-to-solution including overheads, tune every solver, and study how runtime grows with problem size.

What makes a benchmark fair. A single missing ingredient can turn a 'speed-up' into an artefact.

Think of it like…

A fair race: same track, same distance, and every runner properly trained — not a sprinter against someone who has never run before.

Real-world example

The fictional Arcadia Rail benchmarks a train-timetabling QUBO with D-Wave's hybrid solver, QAOA in simulation, Gurobi and tuned simulated annealing. Gurobi proves optimality on small instances within seconds; simulated annealing finds near-optimal answers on large ones in minutes; the annealer is competitive on mid-size instances but not cheaper. The report includes scaling curves and every solver's settings.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose instances: realistic, varied in size, including some with known optima.
  2. Pick metrics: time-to-target, quality at fixed time, success probability — including all overheads.
  3. Tune every solver with comparable effort: hyperparameters, number of reads, time limits.
  4. Measure how runtime scales with problem size rather than reporting a single win.
  5. Report hardware, software versions, settings and both wall-clock and pure compute time; publish data and code.

Who uses it

Quantum benchmarking researchers, operations-research teams, and technical due-diligence analysts at investors and government agencies.

Key takeaway

Quote Rønnow et al. (Science 2014): defining quantum speed-up needs scaling comparisons against the best classical algorithm — and their tests on random spin glasses found none.

Going deeper

  • Rønnow et al. (Science 345, 420, 2014) distinguished 'limited' from genuine quantum speed-up and found none for random spin glasses on a 503-qubit D-Wave Two against optimised simulated annealing.
  • Denchev et al. (Physical Review X 2016) reported a D-Wave 2X up to 10⁸ times faster than single-core simulated annealing on crafted instances, but quantum Monte Carlo and other classical algorithms closed most of that gap.
  • Albash & Lidar (Physical Review X 2018) demonstrated a limited scaling advantage of a D-Wave 2000Q over simulated annealing on frustrated-loop instances, carefully not claiming advantage over all classical methods.
  • Strong baselines include parallel tempering with isoenergetic cluster moves (Zhu, Ochoa & Katzgraber, PRL 2015), tabu search, Gurobi or CPLEX, Burer-Monteiro heuristics for MaxCut, and GPU-accelerated Ising solvers.
  • The Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library (QOBLIB; Koch et al., 2025) offers ten hard problem classes — the 'intractable decathlon' — with instances and records of best-known solutions.
  • Time-to-solution, TTS = t_run × ln(1 − 0.99)/ln(1 − p_success), is standard for annealers; for QAOA, also count shots, parameter optimisation and compilation.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing quantum hardware against single-threaded, untuned classical code instead of the best parallel solvers.
  • Reporting only the instances where the quantum solver wins instead of full performance distributions.
  • Ignoring overheads such as embedding, queueing, network latency and repeated parameter optimisation.

docs.title: Try it: Exact brute force vs simulated annealing on an 18-spin random spin glass (Ocean, runs locally)
docs.text:
# pip install dimod dwave-samplers
import dimod, time
from dwave.samplers import SimulatedAnnealingSampler
bqm = dimod.generators.ran_r(1, 18, seed=7)      # random +/-1 couplings on 18 fully connected spins
t = time.time(); exact = dimod.ExactSolver().sample(bqm).first.energy; t_exact = time.time() - t
t = time.time(); sa = SimulatedAnnealingSampler().sample(bqm, num_reads=200).first.energy; t_sa = time.time() - t
print(f"exact {exact} in {t_exact:.2f}s | SA best {sa} in {t_sa:.2f}s")

docs.title: Key algorithms, circuits, techniques, tools & papers
docs.text: Name What it does Example Simulated annealingKirkpatrick, Gelatt & Vecchi 1983 (Science) · Algorithm · Current · Beginner Classical heuristic that randomly walks over solutions, accepting worse moves with a probability that shrinks as 'temperature' falls. dwave-samplers' SimulatedAnnealingSampler solves a 1,000-variable sparse QUBO to good quality in seconds on a laptop. Parallel temperingSwendsen & Wang 1986; Hukushima & Nemoto 1996 · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Runs replicas at several temperatures and swaps them, escaping local minima better than single-temperature annealing. With isoenergetic cluster moves it is among the strongest classical solvers for two- and three-dimensional spin glasses. Tabu searchGlover 1986 · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Local search that forbids recently changed variables for a while, preventing cycling and encouraging exploration. D-Wave includes tabu search in its classical samplers because it performs strongly on many QUBOs. GurobiGurobi Optimization · Tool · Current · Intermediate Leading commercial mixed-integer programming solver that can solve moderate QUBOs exactly and prove optimality gaps. Gurobi solves a 200-variable dense QUBO and reports a certified optimality gap — something heuristics and annealers cannot provide. IBM CPLEXIBM · Tool · Current · Intermediate Commercial solver for linear, quadratic and mixed-integer problems; a common baseline in quantum optimisation papers. Qiskit Optimization converts docplex models to QUBOs, so CPLEX and QAOA can be compared on exactly the same model. 'Defining and detecting quantum speedup'Rønnow et al. 2014 (Science) · Paper · Current · Intermediate Defined quantum speed-up for annealers carefully and found none for a D-Wave Two over simulated annealing on random spin glasses. Introduced the distinction between speed-up against one chosen algorithm and speed-up against the best classical algorithm. 'What is the computational value of finite-range tunneling?'Denchev et al. 2016 (PRX) · Paper · Current · Intermediate Showed a D-Wave 2X tunnelling edge on crafted instances, up to 10⁸ times faster than single-core simulated annealing. Quantum Monte Carlo scaled similarly to the annealer, so the edge was over simulated annealing specifically. Scaling advantage over simulated annealingAlbash & Lidar 2018 (PRX) · Paper · Current · Advanced Reported a limited scaling advantage of a D-Wave 2000Q over simulated annealing on frustrated-loop instances. A model of careful wording: the advantage was relative to simulated annealing, not to every classical solver. Time-to-target (TTT)Benchmarking practice · Metric · Current · Intermediate Time for a solver to reach a specified quality, such as within 1% of the best-known energy, with given confidence. Arcadia Rail reports TTT at 1% and 0.1% gaps, since one solver may win at one threshold and lose at another. QOBLIBKoch et al. 2025 (Quantum Optimization Benchmarking Library) · Benchmark · Emerging · Intermediate Library of ten hard optimisation problem classes with instances and track records, built for fair quantum-classical comparisons. Researchers submit new results for a problem class, recording solver, hardware, runtime and the best objective found. Selby's algorithmSelby 2014 · Algorithm · Legacy · Advanced Classical solver exploiting the low-treewidth structure of Chimera graphs; it matched or beat early D-Wave hardware on native instances. It showed that hardware-native instance families can be easier classically than they first appear. Tensor-network simulationMatrix product states (White 1992; Vidal 2003) · Technique · Current · Advanced Classical methods such as MPS and PEPS that simulate low-entanglement circuits or annealing dynamics, testing whether quantum results are reproducible. MPS simulations of low-depth QAOA on 100+ qubits can match hardware results when entanglement stays small. Burer-Monteiro MaxCut heuristicBurer, Monteiro & Zhang 2002 · Algorithm · Current · Advanced Low-rank SDP-based heuristic for MaxCut that is fast and very strong in practice on large graphs. It handles MaxCut on graphs with tens of thousands of nodes in seconds to minutes — a tough baseline for QAOA.

docs.title: 6.13 Quantum-Inspired Optimisation
docs.text:
Quantum-inspired optimisers borrow ideas from quantum annealing and physics but run on classical hardware — special digital chips, GPUs, FPGAs or supercomputer cards. They often solve QUBOs very quickly at large scale today, which makes them both useful tools and tough competitors for quantum hardware.

The quantum-inspired landscape. All of these run on classical hardware.

Think of it like…

Like a flight simulator inspired by real planes: it captures the useful dynamics without leaving the ground — and for many training tasks it is cheaper and good enough.

Real-world example

The fictional chemicals firm Corrin Materials schedules 5,000 batch jobs every night. A GPU-based simulated-bifurcation solver finds good QUBO solutions in under a minute. The team keeps a quantum annealing pilot running alongside, but uses the quantum-inspired result in production because it is cheaper, faster to obtain and more predictable.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Formulate the problem as a QUBO or Ising model, exactly as for an annealer.
  2. Choose a quantum-inspired engine: digital annealer, simulated bifurcation, GPU parallel tempering or a tensor-network optimiser.
  3. Tune engine parameters such as time limit, number of replicas and temperatures.
  4. Compare solutions against MIP solvers and quantum hardware on the same instances.
  5. Deploy whichever offers the best quality per unit cost for the use case.

Who uses it

Operations-research teams in manufacturing, finance and logistics, and vendors such as Fujitsu, Toshiba, NEC and Hitachi.

Key takeaway

When you hear 'quantum-inspired', ask what hardware it runs on — it is classical, available today, and it keeps raising the bar for quantum optimisation.

Going deeper

  • Toshiba's simulated bifurcation algorithm (Goto, Tatsumura & Dixon, Science Advances 2019) evolves classical nonlinear oscillators through a bifurcation; ballistic and discrete variants (Goto et al. 2021) improved speed and accuracy.
  • Toshiba says its SQBM+ product now supports problems with up to one billion variables and ten billion nonzero coefficients (June 2026 announcement) — a scale far beyond any quantum annealer.
  • Fujitsu's Digital Annealer is a dedicated CMOS design implementing parallel-trial Markov-chain Monte Carlo with fully connected couplings; later generations handle problems with on the order of 100,000 binary variables.
  • Microsoft's Azure Quantum optimisation (QIO) solvers, inspired by annealing and quantum Monte Carlo, were deprecated after 30 June 2023 and released as open source; Azure's Toshiba solvers were deprecated in February 2024.
  • Simulated quantum annealing (Santoro, Martoňák, Tosatti & Car, Science 2002) runs path-integral Monte Carlo of a transverse-field Ising model on classical computers and often tracks annealer scaling.
  • 'Quantum-inspired' also names Tang-style dequantised linear-algebra algorithms — a different idea, covered in the fault-tolerant chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Calling quantum-inspired solvers 'quantum computers': they run entirely on classical hardware, available today.
  • Dismissing them as toys: on many industrial QUBOs they currently beat available quantum hardware on scale and cost.
  • Confusing quantum-inspired optimisation (annealing-like heuristics) with quantum-inspired algorithms from dequantisation (sampling-based linear algebra).

docs.text:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 30
J = np.triu(rng.choice([-1.0, 1.0], size=(n, n)), 1); J = J + J.T   # random +/-1 couplings
def energy(s):
    return -0.5 * s @ J @ s                          # Ising energy to minimise
x = 0.01 * rng.normal(size=n); y = np.zeros(n)
dt, steps, c0 = 0.5, 2000, 0.5 / np.sqrt(n)
for k in range(steps):                               # ballistic simulated bifurcation
    a = k / steps                                    # pump ramps from 0 to 1
    y += dt * (-(1 - a) * x + c0 * J @ x)
    x += dt * y
    hit = np.abs(x) > 1
    x[hit] = np.sign(x[hit]); y[hit] = 0             # inelastic walls at +/-1
best_random = min(energy(rng.choice([-1, 1], size=n)) for _ in range(1000))
print("simulated bifurcation:", energy(np.sign(x)), "  best of 1,000 random guesses:", best_random)

Its updates are highly parallel, so it runs efficiently on GPUs and FPGAs for large, dense problems. Toshiba SQBM+Toshiba · Tool · Current · Intermediate Commercial quantum-inspired optimisation product based on simulated bifurcation, offered in the cloud and on-premises. Toshiba has showcased simulated bifurcation on financial tasks such as fast detection of arbitrage opportunities. Fujitsu Digital AnnealerFujitsu · Hardware · Current · Intermediate Dedicated digital circuit, offered as a service, that solves fully connected QUBOs with parallel-trial annealing. Fujitsu has trialled it with customers on logistics, production scheduling and drug-candidate search. Hitachi CMOS annealerHitachi (Yamaoka et al. 2016) · Hardware · Research · Intermediate CMOS chip implementing Ising spins in memory-like cells with local interactions, designed for low-power annealing. Hitachi presented it as a route to energy-efficient combinatorial optimisation at the edge. NEC Vector AnnealingNEC · Service · Current · Intermediate Annealing service running on NEC's SX-Aurora TSUBASA vector processor cards, marketed for large QUBO problems. NEC has also partnered with D-Wave, letting customers compare classical and quantum annealing on the same QUBO. Microsoft QIO (retired)Microsoft Azure Quantum · Tool · Legacy · Beginner Azure Quantum's quantum-inspired optimisation solvers, deprecated after June 2023 and later released as open source. Older Azure Quantum optimisation tutorials no longer run; the solver code lives on in an open-source release. Population annealingHukushima & Iba 2003; Machta 2010 · Algorithm · Current · Advanced Runs a large population of annealing replicas with resampling by Boltzmann weights, parallelising well on GPUs. Used in spin-glass physics and formerly among the solvers in Microsoft's QIO suite. Parallel-trial Monte CarloFujitsu Digital Annealer design · Technique · Current · Advanced Evaluates every possible single-bit flip at once and accepts one, avoiding long runs of rejected moves at low temperature. The Digital Annealer keeps making progress where serial simulated annealing would reject most proposals. GPU Ising solversAcademic and vendor codes · Tool · Current · Intermediate Massively parallel implementations of annealing, parallel tempering or simulated bifurcation on GPUs for very large QUBOs. A single data-centre GPU runs thousands of annealing replicas of a 10,000-variable QUBO in parallel. Simulated quantum annealing (SQA)Santoro, Martoňák, Tosatti & Car 2002 (Science) · Algorithm · Current · Advanced Classical path-integral Monte Carlo simulation of quantum annealing, used both as an optimiser and as an annealer benchmark. SQA's scaling often tracks D-Wave's on spin glasses, suggesting much of the hardware's behaviour is classically reproducible. Tensor-network optimisationResearch literature · Technique · Research · Advanced Uses tensor-network contraction or MPS-based sampling to find low-energy states of structured Ising problems. For QUBOs on graphs with low treewidth, exact tensor contraction finds ground states quickly. Quantum-inspired evolutionary algorithmsHan & Kim 2002 (IEEE TEVC) · Algorithm · Current · Intermediate Evolutionary algorithms that represent candidate solutions with 'Q-bit' probability amplitudes — quantum in name only. Common in engineering-design papers; treat the 'quantum' label here as a metaphor, not physics.

docs.title: 6.14 Realistic Expectations & Published Comparisons
docs.text:
After more than a decade of experiments, no quantum optimiser has shown a broad, practical advantage over the best classical methods for real-world ML or business problems. There are encouraging signs — scaling results on specific problems, coherent annealing at scale, better QAOA variants — and new claims keep appearing, but each must be checked for fair baselines, problem relevance and total cost.

The state of evidence (2026)

Shown so far Not yet shown Quantum annealing coherent dynamics at 5,000 qubits; simulation claims practical optimisation speed-up QAOA scaling edge in simulation (LABS) advantage on hardware for useful problems ML via QUBO competitive with small datasets better accuracy at realistic scale Hybrid solvers solve large industrial models proof the QPU drives the result Fault-tolerant future provable quadratic search speed-ups practical runtimes after overheads

Real progress on the left; the claims that matter for business remain on the right.

Think of it like…

Like an early electric-car prototype winning one carefully chosen hill climb: promising engineering, but not yet the car you would buy for your daily commute.

Real-world example

The board of the fictional Harlow Logistics asks whether to invest in quantum optimisation. Their analyst summarises: annealers and QAOA match classical solvers on small instances, show limited scaling edges on crafted problems, and hybrid solvers work but hide the quantum contribution. She recommends a small, well-benchmarked pilot plus strong classical tooling, revisited every year.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify the claim — speed, quality, scaling or cost — and the classical baseline it is measured against.
  2. Check instance relevance: crafted, random or real-world?
  3. Check end-to-end accounting: encoding, embedding, queueing, parameter training and post-processing.
  4. Look for independent replication or classical rebuttal papers.
  5. Decide between research, pilot and production — and set a date to re-evaluate.

Who uses it

Technology strategists, managers, journalists and students who need to evaluate quantum optimisation announcements.

Key takeaway

A balanced interview answer: 'No demonstrated practical advantage yet; promising scaling evidence on specific problems; fault-tolerant machines offer at most quadratic speed-ups for generic search, which overheads may cancel.'

Going deeper

  • Abbas et al. (Nature Reviews Physics 2024) conclude that quantum optimisation's value must be established by rigorous benchmarking on meaningful problems, pointing to finance and sustainability as sources of instances.
  • For QAOA, the strongest scaling evidence so far comes from noiseless simulations of specific problems such as LABS (Shaydulin et al. 2024); hardware runs remain small or noise-limited.
  • Industry 'runtime advantage' preprints in 2024-2025, for example counterdiabatic methods from Kipu Quantum run on IBM processors, should be treated as contested until replicated against tuned classical heuristics.
  • Generic unstructured search on fault-tolerant machines gains at most a quadratic speed-up; the beyond-quadratic argument of Babbush et al. (2021) suggests that alone won't give early practical advantage.
  • Montanaro's quantum-walk speed-up of backtracking (2018) and Campbell, Khurana & Montanaro's resource analysis (Quantum 2019) show fault-tolerant constraint solving might help, but only for large instances with long runtimes.
  • QOBLIB and the community working group behind the 2024 review aim to make claims comparable over time by tracking best-known results per instance.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting press releases over peer-reviewed comparisons; always look for the classical baseline and the instance details.
  • Dismissing the field entirely: honest negative results and narrow positive ones both guide where quantum optimisation may eventually help.
  • Ignoring cost: equal quality at higher price and latency is not an advantage for a business.

Every claim should state which kind it is — most published annealing results are limited speed-ups. A quantum application scientist at a bank models portfolio problems, benchmarks Gurobi against QAOA, and writes the comparison report.

docs.title: Ten Things Every QML Student Should Master
docs.text: Quantum machine learning rewards people who combine solid quantum and ML fundamentals with healthy scepticism. If you can explain and apply these ten ideas, you can read the literature critically, build honest experiments and hold your own in interviews.

docs.title: 1. Know the map and the honest status
docs.text: QML spans four quadrants of classical or quantum data and algorithms. As of 2026 there is no demonstrated practical advantage on classical data; the best-founded advantages involve learning from quantum data.

docs.title: 2. Data loading is the hidden bottleneck
docs.text: Basis, angle, amplitude and IQP encodings trade qubits for circuit depth. Amplitude encoding packs 2^n numbers into n qubits but usually costs about 2^n gates, and practical QRAM does not exist yet.

docs.title: 3. Variational circuits are trainable functions
docs.text: A parameterised circuit plus a measured observable gives a model trained in a hybrid loop. The parameter-shift rule yields exact gradients on hardware at two circuit runs per parameter.

docs.title: 4. Trainability and simulability are linked
docs.text: Barren plateaus make gradients vanish exponentially for expressive, global or noisy circuits. Local costs and structured ansätze help, but provably trainable models are often classically simulable.

docs.title: 5. Encodings define what a model can learn
docs.text: Quantum models behave like Fourier series and kernel machines whose frequencies and features are set by the encoding. Data re-uploading adds expressivity; entanglement alone guarantees nothing.

docs.title: 6. Quantum kernels need care
docs.text: Fidelity kernels compare encoded states, but their values can concentrate exponentially with qubit count. Bandwidth tuning, projected kernels and the power-of-data test decide when they are worth trying.

docs.title: 7. Read the fine print on speed-ups
docs.text: HHL-style and amplitude-estimation algorithms need fault tolerance, efficient state preparation and cheap readout. Dequantisation and resource estimates show many headline speed-ups shrink or vanish.

docs.title: 8. Simulate first, budget hardware carefully
docs.text: Prototype in PennyLane, Qiskit or CUDA-Q on exact, then finite-shot and noisy simulators. On real QPUs, count circuits × shots × price, mitigate errors and log every job.

docs.title: 9. Benchmark like a sceptic
docs.text: Use tuned classical baselines, equal hyperparameter budgets, multiple seeds, statistical tests, ablations and scaling studies. The 2024 'Better than classical?' study is the template.

docs.title: 10. Build evidence, not hype, for your career
docs.text: Employers value fundamentals, clean code, honest projects and open-source contributions. ML for quantum hardware, learning from quantum data and quantum software engineering are strong paths.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Tools, Simulators & Hands-On QML
docs.text: This chapter is the practical toolbox. It walks through the main QML frameworks — PennyLane, Qiskit Machine Learning, TensorFlow Quantum, Cirq, TorchQuantum and others — with their real maintenance status in late 2026, then GPU simulation with CUDA-Q and cuQuantum, cloud access through Amazon Braket, IBM Quantum Platform and Azure Quantum, and what running on noisy hardware really costs. It closes with datasets, error mitigation, fair experimental practice and a ladder of mini-projects with runnable code.

docs.title: 7.1 The QML Software Landscape at a Glance
docs.text:
Quantum machine learning code is written in ordinary Python. A QML framework lets you describe a small quantum circuit, run it on a simulator or a real quantum computer, and train its knobs with the same tools used for normal machine learning. Picking the right stack first saves weeks of frustration.

The QML software stack. You write code at the top; the same model can run on any layer below it.

Think of it like…

Choosing a QML stack is like choosing a kitchen: the recipe book (framework), the oven (simulator or quantum chip) and the delivery service (cloud platform) must all fit together before you can cook.

Real-world example

Amara, a master's student at the fictional Lakeside University, wants to compare a quantum classifier with a classical one. She installs PennyLane with PyTorch for training, prototypes on the free default.qubit simulator, moves to lightning.gpu when circuits reach 24 qubits, and finally sends a 6-qubit version to an IBM Heron processor through the PennyLane-Qiskit plugin.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a front-end framework that matches your ML habits: PennyLane (PyTorch/JAX), Qiskit Machine Learning (scikit-learn style) or CUDA-Q (C++/Python, GPU-first).
  2. Prototype with an exact (noise-free) simulator on your laptop; keep circuits small (4-12 qubits).
  3. Scale up with high-performance simulators (Lightning, Qiskit Aer, CUDA-Q on GPUs) when you need more qubits or speed.
  4. Add realistic noise models and shot counts before you believe any result.
  5. Only then run a reduced experiment on real hardware through a cloud service (IBM Quantum Platform, Amazon Braket, Azure Quantum).

Who uses it

Every QML student, researcher and quantum software developer makes these choices; job adverts usually name PennyLane, Qiskit or CUDA-Q explicitly.

Key takeaway

In interviews, show you know the maintenance status of each tool: PennyLane, Qiskit and CUDA-Q are actively developed, while TensorFlow Quantum and TorchQuantum are much quieter projects.

Going deeper

  • As of October 2026 PennyLane is on the 0.45 series (May 2026), Qiskit on 2.5, Qiskit Machine Learning on 0.9.1 (August 2026), CUDA-Q on 0.16 and Cirq on 1.7; check PyPI because all release several times a year.
  • PennyLane now recommends `import pennylane as qp` (announced March 2026) to signal it covers general quantum programming; older tutorials use `qml`, and both are just Python aliases for the same package.
  • TensorFlow is fading from QML: PennyLane deprecated its TensorFlow interface in v0.43 and dropped maintenance in v0.44, steering users to PyTorch or JAX, while TensorFlow Quantum still needs legacy Keras 2.
  • Most frameworks talk to each other through plugins or OpenQASM, so a PennyLane model can run on IBM, Braket, IonQ or Quantinuum back ends without rewriting the model code.
  • Exact state-vector simulation needs 16 bytes per amplitude in double precision, so memory doubles with every qubit: about 16 GiB at 30 qubits, which is why laptops stop around 26-30 qubits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Installing every framework into one environment: dependency pins clash (TensorFlow Quantum pins Cirq 1.5 and TF 2.18); use one virtual environment per stack.
  • Copying 2021-era tutorials: Qiskit 1.0/2.0 and the V2 primitives removed many older APIs (QuantumInstance, execute), so old notebooks often fail.
  • Assuming a bigger framework means better results: model design and fair baselines matter far more than which library you pick.

python -m venv qml-env
# Windows: qml-env\Scripts\activate   macOS/Linux: source qml-env/bin/activate
pip install pennylane qiskit qiskit-machine-learning scikit-learn torch
python -c "import pennylane as qp, qiskit; print('PennyLane', qp.__version__, '| Qiskit', qiskit.__version__)"

docs.title: 7.2 PennyLane Essentials: QNodes, Devices, Templates and Interfaces
docs.text:
PennyLane turns a quantum circuit into a Python function you can differentiate. You choose a device (where the circuit runs), decorate a function with @qnode, and PennyLane works out gradients so a normal optimiser can train the circuit's parameters.

What happens when a QNode is trained. PennyLane handles the quantum part; your ML library handles the loop.

Think of it like…

A QNode is like a smart vending machine: you put in numbers (data and weights), it runs a hidden quantum process and hands back a number, and it can also tell you which way to turn each knob to get a better result.

Real-world example

Diego, an analyst at the fictional Northwind Insurance, builds a 2-qubit classifier. He encodes two claim features with AngleEmbedding, adds two StronglyEntanglingLayers (12 weights), returns the expectation of Pauli-Z on qubit 0 and trains with qp.AdamOptimizer for 60 steps on a 200-row toy dataset.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create a device, for example qp.device('default.qubit', wires=4), which fixes the simulator and number of qubits.
  2. Write a quantum function that applies an embedding template, trainable layers and returns a measurement (expval, probs, sample).
  3. Decorate it with @qp.qnode(dev); choose diff_method ('backprop', 'parameter-shift', 'adjoint') or let PennyLane pick.
  4. Wrap a classical loss around the QNode and compute gradients with qp.grad, PyTorch autograd or jax.grad.
  5. Update parameters with an optimiser in a loop; inspect circuits with qp.draw and resource counts with qp.specs.

Who uses it

QML researchers, students doing coursework and quantum software engineers prototyping hybrid models use PennyLane daily; most QML papers since 2020 include PennyLane code.

Key takeaway

Remember the three moving parts — device, QNode, interface — and that 'backprop' only works on simulators while 'parameter-shift' also works on real hardware.

Going deeper

  • default.qubit simulates exactly and supports backpropagation through the simulator, which costs about the same as one forward pass; parameter-shift needs two extra circuit runs per parameter but works on hardware.
  • Shots are now set per QNode with the @qp.set_shots decorator (introduced in v0.43) rather than only on the device; without shots, expectation values are exact.
  • Templates such as AngleEmbedding, AmplitudeEmbedding, IQPEmbedding, BasicEntanglerLayers and StronglyEntanglingLayers provide tested building blocks with .shape() helpers for weight tensors.
  • PennyLane's TensorFlow interface was deprecated in v0.43 and its maintenance dropped from v0.44 (January 2026); the supported ML interfaces are autograd (NumPy), PyTorch and JAX.
  • qp.specs(circuit)(x, w) reports gate counts, depth and number of trainable parameters, useful for reporting resources honestly in papers and for estimating hardware cost.
  • Since v0.45 (May 2026) PennyLane requires NumPy 2 and Python 3.11+, so very old environments must be upgraded.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Forgetting requires_grad=False on input data with pennylane.numpy, so the optimiser tries to 'train' your dataset as well as the weights.
  • Using diff_method='backprop' and then expecting the same code to run on hardware; switch to parameter-shift or let PennyLane choose 'best'.
  • Mixing `qml.` examples from old tutorials with `qp.` code: both work, but keep one alias per file to avoid confusion.

docs.title: Try it: A 2-qubit variational circuit and its gradient in PennyLane
docs.text:
import pennylane as qp
from pennylane import numpy as np

dev = qp.device("default.qubit", wires=2)

@qp.qnode(dev)
def circuit(x, w):
    qp.AngleEmbedding(x, wires=[0, 1])
    qp.StronglyEntanglingLayers(w, wires=[0, 1])
    return qp.expval(qp.Z(0))

shape = qp.StronglyEntanglingLayers.shape(n_layers=2, n_wires=2)   # (2, 2, 3)
w = np.random.random(shape, requires_grad=True)
x = np.array([0.3, 1.2], requires_grad=False)
print(circuit(x, w))
print(qp.grad(circuit, argnums=1)(x, w).shape)
print(qp.draw(circuit)(x, w))

docs.text: Name What it does Example QNodePennyLane (qp.qnode / qp.QNode) · Concept · Current · Beginner A quantum function bound to a device that behaves like a differentiable Python function. @qp.qnode(dev) turns circuit(x, w) into something PyTorch can call inside a loss function. default.qubitPennyLane built-in device · Tool · Current · Beginner PennyLane's reference state-vector simulator; exact, supports backprop and shot sampling, ideal up to about 20 qubits. All of Diego's prototyping runs on default.qubit before he touches a GPU. default.mixedPennyLane built-in device · Tool · Current · Intermediate Density-matrix simulator that supports noise channels such as depolarising and amplitude damping. Adding qp.DepolarizingChannel(0.01) after each layer shows accuracy falling from 92% to 81%. Measurement functionsqp.expval, qp.probs, qp.sample, qp.counts, qp.state · Concept · Current · Beginner Define what a QNode returns: expectation values, probabilities, raw samples, counts or (simulator only) the full state. A 3-class classifier returns qp.probs(wires=[0, 1]) and reads three of the four probabilities. qp.set_shotsPennyLane (since v0.43) · Technique · Current · Intermediate Decorator that sets how many measurement repetitions a QNode uses, making results finite-sample like hardware. @qp.set_shots(1000) shows Diego his clean 0.71 expectation actually fluctuates by about ±0.02. JAX interfacePennyLane + Google JAX · Framework · Current · Intermediate Lets QNodes be differentiated with jax.grad and compiled with jax.jit for faster training loops. jax.jit(cost) speeds a 10-qubit training loop several-fold after the first compilation. qp.draw and qp.specsPennyLane · Tool · Current · Beginner Utilities that print a text diagram of a QNode and report its gate count, depth and parameters. qp.specs shows the model uses 24 rotations, 8 CNOTs and depth 10, which Diego reports in his write-up. TensorFlow interface (PennyLane)PennyLane · Framework · Legacy · Intermediate interface='tf' and KerasLayer: deprecated in v0.41-0.43, maintenance dropped since v0.44; use PyTorch or JAX instead. A 2022 Keras notebook is ported by swapping KerasLayer for TorchLayer and tf.GradientTape for loss.backward(). pennylane.numpyPennyLane (autograd-wrapped NumPy) · Tool · Current · Beginner NumPy wrapper whose arrays carry a requires_grad flag so the autograd interface knows what to differentiate. np.array([0.3, 1.2], requires_grad=False) marks Diego's input data as fixed. Templates libraryPennyLane (qp.templates) · Tool · Current · Beginner Ready-made, tested circuit blocks for embeddings, trainable layers and state preparation, each with a .shape() helper. Diego swaps one embedding template for another with a one-line change and reruns his comparison. Quantum operators (qp.RX, qp.CNOT, qp.Z)PennyLane operator classes · Concept · Current · Beginner Gates and observables written as Python objects applied to named wires inside a quantum function. qp.RX(0.5, wires=0); qp.CNOT(wires=[0, 1]); return qp.expval(qp.Z(1)).

docs.title: 7.3 PennyLane at Speed: Lightning Simulators, Catalyst and Plugins
docs.text:
Once circuits pass about 15-20 qubits or need thousands of training steps, the reference simulator becomes slow. PennyLane's Lightning devices are fast C++ (and GPU) simulators, Catalyst compiles the whole hybrid training loop, and plugins let the same code run on other companies' simulators and hardware.

One QNode, many back ends. Changing the device string is often the only edit needed to move a model.

Think of it like…

It is like moving from cycling to driving to taking the train: same destination (your QNode), but the Lightning engine, the Catalyst express line and the plugin tickets to other networks get you there faster.

Real-world example

Mei at the fictional Harbourview Lab trains a 22-qubit model. On default.qubit each epoch takes 9 minutes; on lightning.qubit with adjoint gradients it drops to under a minute, and on lightning.gpu on one NVIDIA A100 to a few seconds. Wrapping the loop in @qp.qjit removes the remaining Python overhead.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Swap the device name: 'lightning.qubit' (CPU), 'lightning.gpu' (NVIDIA, via cuStateVec), 'lightning.kokkos' (CPU/GPU via Kokkos) or 'lightning.tensor' (tensor networks).
  2. Use diff_method='adjoint' on Lightning devices: gradients for all parameters cost roughly one extra pass.
  3. Install pennylane-catalyst and add @qp.qjit to compile the quantum program and classical control together.
  4. Install a plugin (pennylane-qiskit, amazon-braket-pennylane-plugin, pennylane-cirq) to target external back ends.
  5. Benchmark: time one epoch on each device and keep the fastest that fits in memory.

Who uses it

Researchers running large simulation studies, HPC centres and teams preparing hardware runs use Lightning and Catalyst to keep simulation costs down.

Key takeaway

Memorise the trio: lightning.qubit for CPUs, lightning.gpu for NVIDIA GPUs, lightning.kokkos for portable HPC — and adjoint differentiation is the reason they train fast.

Going deeper

  • PennyLane 0.45 and Catalyst 0.15 shipped together in May 2026; Lightning-GPU supports Catalyst and needs CUDA 12 on Volta-generation (SM 7.0) or newer NVIDIA GPUs.
  • Adjoint differentiation stores the final state and walks the circuit backwards, giving all P gradients for about the memory of two state vectors and time comparable to a couple of forward passes — but it only works on simulators.
  • Lightning-GPU and Lightning-Kokkos can distribute a state vector over several GPUs with MPI, pushing exact simulation into the mid-30s of qubits on a multi-node cluster.
  • Catalyst lowers Python + quantum code to MLIR and LLVM so loops, conditionals and mid-circuit measurements run without returning to Python on every step; it integrates with JAX for jit and grad.
  • lightning.tensor uses NVIDIA cuTensorNet with matrix product states, trading exactness for the ability to simulate many more qubits when entanglement stays low.
  • Plugins translate operations into the target's gate set; check that a template's decomposition does not explode in depth on hardware with limited connectivity.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Timing only the first call of a qjit or jax.jit function: compilation dominates; time the second and later calls.
  • Using lightning.gpu for 10-qubit circuits: GPU launch overhead makes small circuits slower than lightning.qubit.
  • Expecting adjoint gradients with shots: adjoint is analytic only; with shots PennyLane must fall back to parameter-shift.

docs.title: Try it: Compile a QNode on the Lightning simulator with Catalyst
docs.text:
# pip install pennylane pennylane-catalyst   (lightning.qubit ships with PennyLane)
import pennylane as qp
from jax import numpy as jnp

dev = qp.device("lightning.qubit", wires=4)

@qp.qjit
@qp.qnode(dev)
def cost(params):
    for i in range(4):
        qp.RY(params[i], wires=i)
    for i in range(3):
        qp.CNOT(wires=[i, i + 1])
    return qp.expval(qp.Z(3))

print(cost(jnp.array([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4])))

docs.title: 7.4 Qiskit Machine Learning and the Qiskit Primitives
docs.text:
Qiskit Machine Learning is a Python library of ready-made quantum models — quantum kernels, quantum neural networks and variational classifiers — built on IBM's Qiskit. It runs circuits through two standard 'primitives': the Estimator (returns expectation values) and the Sampler (returns measured bit-string counts).

How Qiskit ML is layered. Models sit on QNNs or kernels, which call a primitive, which runs on a simulator or IBM hardware.

Think of it like…

The primitives are like two counters at a lab: the Estimator counter hands back an average reading, the Sampler counter hands back the raw tally sheet; Qiskit ML's models simply order from one counter or the other.

Real-world example

Kofi at the fictional Ridgeway Bank tests a quantum kernel on 120 labelled transactions. He builds a zz_feature_map on 4 qubits, wraps it in FidelityQuantumKernel, trains QSVC, and compares it with an RBF support vector machine using the same cross-validation folds. The classical model wins by 3 points, which he reports honestly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Build a feature map (data encoding) and an ansatz with the Qiskit circuit library, e.g. zz_feature_map and n_local.
  2. Choose a primitive: StatevectorEstimator/StatevectorSampler for exact local runs, Qiskit Aer for noisy simulation, or qiskit-ibm-runtime EstimatorV2/SamplerV2 for IBM hardware.
  3. Wrap circuits in a model: EstimatorQNN/SamplerQNN, VQC/VQR, or FidelityQuantumKernel with QSVC/QSVR.
  4. Train with fit(); optimisers such as COBYLA, SPSA and ADAM ship inside qiskit_machine_learning.optimizers.
  5. For hardware, transpile circuits to the backend's native gates (ISA circuits) with a preset pass manager before calling the primitive.

Who uses it

Developers in the IBM Quantum ecosystem, banks and labs in the IBM Quantum Network, and students taking IBM Quantum Learning courses use Qiskit ML.

Key takeaway

Know the maintenance story: Qiskit ML lives in the qiskit-community organisation and, since version 0.7, is co-maintained by IBM and the UK STFC Hartree Centre; 0.9.0 (December 2025) moved it to Qiskit 2.x and the V2 primitives.

Going deeper

  • Release history: 0.7 (2023-24) moved stewardship to IBM plus the Hartree Centre, 0.8 (November 2024) absorbed the optimisers and gradient classes previously in qiskit-algorithms, 0.9.0 (December 2025) required Qiskit 2.0 and Python 3.10+, and 0.9.1 followed in August 2026.
  • 0.9.1 added regression kernel losses (SVRLoss, MSRLoss), a phase-of-matter quantum dataset generator, fixes to SamplerQNN with transpiled layouts, and deprecated automatic qubit alignment.
  • The V2 primitives take 'PUBs' (primitive unified blocs): a circuit plus observables and parameter values, so one call can evaluate many parameter sets — important for batching kernel matrices and QNN gradients.
  • On IBM hardware the V2 primitives accept only ISA circuits (already mapped to the device's native gates and qubit layout), so transpilation with generate_preset_pass_manager is a required step.
  • A library overview paper (arXiv:2505.17756, 2025) describes the architecture; cite it when you use the library in published work.
  • EffectiveDimension and LocalEffectiveDimension compute the effective dimension of QNNs (Abbas et al. 2021), a capacity measure sometimes used to compare quantum and classical models.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Following tutorials that import QuantumInstance or qiskit.utils.algorithm_globals: those were removed; use primitives and qiskit_machine_learning.utils instead.
  • Sending untranspiled circuits to IBM hardware: V2 primitives reject non-ISA circuits.
  • Treating ad_hoc_data success as evidence of advantage: the dataset was constructed to suit the ZZ feature map.

docs.title: Try it: Train a variational quantum classifier with Qiskit ML 0.9 (from the project README)
docs.text:
# pip install qiskit-machine-learning   (pulls in qiskit>=2.0)
from qiskit.circuit.library import n_local, zz_feature_map
from qiskit_machine_learning.optimizers import COBYLA
from qiskit_machine_learning.utils import algorithm_globals
from qiskit_machine_learning.algorithms import VQC
from qiskit_machine_learning.datasets import ad_hoc_data

algorithm_globals.random_seed = 1376
X_tr, y_tr, X_te, y_te = ad_hoc_data(training_size=20, test_size=10, n=2, gap=0.3)
feature_map = zz_feature_map(feature_dimension=2, reps=2, entanglement="linear")
ansatz = n_local(feature_map.num_qubits, ["ry", "rz"], "cz", reps=3)
vqc = VQC(feature_map=feature_map, ansatz=ansatz, optimizer=COBYLA(maxiter=100))
vqc.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
print(f"Test accuracy: {vqc.score(X_te, y_te):0.2f}")

docs.title: 7.5 TensorFlow Quantum and Cirq
docs.text:
Cirq is Google's Python library for writing quantum circuits close to the hardware. TensorFlow Quantum (TFQ) puts Cirq circuits inside TensorFlow/Keras models as layers. TFQ was influential in 2020-2022 and still works, but it is maintained slowly and depends on the legacy Keras 2.

Data flow in a TFQ model. Data enters as circuits, not as numbers — TFQ's distinctive design choice.

Think of it like…

TFQ is like a well-built classic car: it still drives and many famous trips were made in it, but spare parts are specific and most new drivers choose a newer model.

Real-world example

Lucía, a PhD student at the fictional Costa Institute, must reproduce a 2021 quantum convolutional neural network paper written in TFQ. She creates a Python 3.11 environment, installs TensorFlow 2.18.1 with TFQ 0.7.6, sets TF_USE_LEGACY_KERAS=1, and the notebook runs. She then ports the model to PennyLane for her new experiments.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write circuits in Cirq with GridQubit or LineQubit, using sympy symbols for trainable angles.
  2. Convert batches of data circuits to tensors with tfq.convert_to_tensor.
  3. Add tfq.layers.PQC (or ControlledPQC, Expectation) to a Keras model, giving the model circuit and readout operators.
  4. Choose a differentiator (adjoint, parameter shift, finite difference) and compile with a Keras optimiser and loss.
  5. Simulate with the built-in qsim-based simulator; real Google hardware access is restricted to partners.

Who uses it

Researchers reproducing earlier QCNN and quantum-data papers, and teams already invested in Google's Cirq tooling, still use TFQ and Cirq.

Key takeaway

In interviews say: TFQ is usable but legacy-leaning — version 0.7.6 (February 2026) pins TensorFlow 2.18.1 and needs Keras 2 — so new projects usually pick PennyLane, Qiskit ML or CUDA-Q.

Going deeper

  • TFQ was announced in March 2020 (Broughton et al., arXiv:2003.02989) by Google with the University of Waterloo and others; it treats quantum data as circuits fed into Keras models.
  • After a quiet 2023-2024, maintenance releases resumed: 0.7.4 and 0.7.5 in December 2025 (Grid Dynamics joined the maintainers) and 0.7.6 in February 2026, supporting Python 3.10-3.12, NumPy 2 and Cirq 1.5.
  • The GitHub README states TFQ is 'not an officially supported Google product', so treat it as community-maintained research software rather than a product with service guarantees.
  • Differentiators include tfq.differentiators.Adjoint (fast, simulator-only), ParameterShift and finite-difference variants; SampledExpectation layers model finite shots, letting you test training under realistic measurement noise.
  • Cirq itself is healthy: version 1.7 (June 2026) is the circuit language for Google Quantum AI research, with qsim and qsimcirq providing fast C++ and GPU simulation.
  • tfq.datasets provides quantum datasets such as ground states of transverse-field Ising (tfi_chain) and XXZ spin chains, useful for learning-from-quantum-data experiments.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Installing the newest TensorFlow with TFQ: version pins are strict; mismatches produce cryptic import errors.
  • Forgetting TF_USE_LEGACY_KERAS=1 before importing TensorFlow, so Keras 3 loads and TFQ layers fail.
  • Assuming TFQ gives access to Google's Willow chip: Google's hardware is not offered as a public cloud service.

docs.title: Try it: A one-qubit PQC layer in TensorFlow Quantum
docs.text:
# Python 3.10-3.12:  pip install tensorflow==2.18.1 tensorflow-quantum==0.7.6
import os; os.environ["TF_USE_LEGACY_KERAS"] = "1"   # TFQ requires Keras 2
import cirq, sympy, tensorflow as tf, tensorflow_quantum as tfq

q = cirq.GridQubit(0, 0)
theta = sympy.Symbol("theta")
model_circuit = cirq.Circuit(cirq.ry(theta)(q))
inputs = tfq.convert_to_tensor([cirq.Circuit(cirq.X(q)), cirq.Circuit()])
pqc = tfq.layers.PQC(model_circuit, cirq.Z(q))
print(pqc(inputs))   # one <Z> value per input circuit

docs.title: 7.6 TorchQuantum, sQUlearn, Qadence, Classiq and Other QML Libraries
docs.text:
Beyond the big three, several smaller libraries target special needs: PyTorch-native GPU batching (TorchQuantum), a scikit-learn style interface (sQUlearn), neutral-atom digital-analog programs (Qadence), high-level circuit synthesis (Classiq) and more. Their maintenance levels vary, so check activity before you depend on one.

Three specialised QML libraries

TorchQuantum sQUlearn Qadence Maintainer MIT HAN Lab Fraunhofer IPA team Pasqal Style PyTorch modules scikit-learn estimators Digital-analog blocks Strength GPU batch simulation Kernels, QNNs, reservoirs Neutral-atom programs Latest PyPI 0.1.8 (Feb 2024) 0.11.2 (Jun 2026) 1.11.5 (Jun 2025) Health Slow releases Active Quieter since 2025

Different niches, different maintenance signals (status as of October 2026).

Think of it like…

These libraries are like specialist tools in a workshop — a precise engraving pen or a pipe bender — brilliant for one job, but you check they still have spare parts before building a business on them.

Real-world example

Tobias, a data scientist at the fictional Fernwood Energy, wants a quantum kernel that drops straight into his scikit-learn pipeline. He tries sQUlearn because its estimators follow sklearn's API, checks PyPI (release 0.11.2, June 2026) and GitHub activity, and pins the version in his requirements file.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define what you need: GPU batching, sklearn API, analog/pulse control, circuit synthesis or a specific hardware vendor.
  2. Check health signals: last PyPI release, recent commits, open issues, supported Python and Qiskit versions.
  3. Run the library's quick-start and one of your own small problems before committing.
  4. Pin exact versions and record them, because small libraries can change APIs between minor releases.
  5. Keep a port path to a mainstream framework in case the library goes quiet.

Who uses it

Researchers with specialised workflows, start-ups tied to a hardware vendor, and industrial R&D teams that standardise on scikit-learn or PyTorch use these libraries.

Key takeaway

Quote evidence, not reputation: for example, TorchQuantum's last PyPI release (0.1.8) dates from February 2024 and pins Qiskit below 1.0, although its main branch merged a Qiskit 2 upgrade in July 2026.

Going deeper

  • TorchQuantum (MIT HAN Lab) simulates batches of circuits as PyTorch tensors on GPUs and powered the QuantumNAS noise-adaptive architecture search (HPCA 2022); its README claims scaling to 30+ qubits with multiple GPUs.
  • sQUlearn, developed at Fraunhofer IPA, offers quantum kernel methods (FidelityKernel, ProjectedQuantumKernel), QNN regressors/classifiers and quantum reservoir computing behind fit/predict, with Qiskit and PennyLane execution back ends.
  • Qadence from Pasqal expresses programs as composable blocks mixing digital gates and analog Rydberg interactions, simulated by its PyQTorch back end; PyPI releases have slowed since mid-2025.
  • Classiq is a commercial platform that synthesises optimised circuits from high-level models; its Python SDK (release 1.31 in October 2026) includes QML features such as PyTorch integration — check the current docs for details.
  • Other names you may meet: Qibo and its QML add-ons (Technology Innovation Institute, Abu Dhabi), TensorCircuit-NG (community continuation of TensorCircuit), MindQuantum (Huawei MindSpore) and Paddle Quantum (Baidu, quiet since Baidu handed its quantum lab to a Beijing institute in 2024).
  • Before adopting any small library, count active maintainers: a single-maintainer project can stall overnight, which matters for a thesis or a product.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Judging a library by GitHub stars: stars measure past popularity, not current maintenance.
  • Installing TorchQuantum's PyPI release into a Qiskit 2 environment: it pins qiskit<1.0, so install from source or isolate it.
  • Assuming results from a niche simulator are correct without cross-checking a small case against PennyLane or Qiskit.

# Then look at recent commit dates, e.g.:

Tobias rejects a promising package after seeing no commits for 18 months and 60 unanswered issues.

docs.title: 7.7 GPU Simulation with NVIDIA CUDA-Q and cuQuantum
docs.text:
Simulating quantum circuits is mostly huge matrix-vector arithmetic, which graphics processors (GPUs) do extremely fast. NVIDIA's CUDA-Q is a programming model for hybrid quantum-classical programs, and its cuQuantum libraries accelerate simulators — including PennyLane Lightning-GPU, Qiskit Aer and qsim.

Memory for an exact state vector. Each extra qubit doubles memory (complex128, 16 bytes per amplitude) — GPUs help with speed, not with this wall.

Think of it like…

A CPU simulator is a skilled accountant adding columns by hand; a GPU is a stadium of accountants each adding one cell at the same time.

Real-world example

Priyanka at the fictional Meridian Pharma sweeps 300 hyperparameter settings of a 28-qubit variational model. On a 64-core CPU node one setting takes 40 minutes; with CUDA-Q's 'nvidia' target on an H100 it takes under 2 minutes, and the 'mqpu' option spreads settings across 8 GPUs.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Write a kernel with @cudaq.kernel using qubits, gates and parameters.
  2. Build a Hamiltonian or observable with cudaq.spin operators.
  3. Call cudaq.observe for expectation values or cudaq.sample for bit-strings.
  4. Choose a target: 'qpp-cpu' (CPU), 'nvidia' (single GPU; options for multi-GPU memory pooling), 'tensornet'/'tensornet-mps' (tensor networks), or a hardware provider.
  5. Feed results into a classical optimiser (SciPy, cudaq.optimizers) or a PyTorch model.

Who uses it

HPC centres, pharmaceutical and materials R&D teams, hardware makers emulating future devices and QML researchers needing large simulations use CUDA-Q and cuQuantum.

Key takeaway

Know the split: CUDA-Q is the programming model and compiler; cuQuantum (cuStateVec, cuTensorNet, cuDensityMat) is the set of GPU math libraries that many simulators — not just CUDA-Q — call underneath.

Going deeper

  • CUDA-Q (formerly CUDA Quantum) is open source; the Python package cudaq reached 0.16 in September 2026, and kernels can also be written in C++ and compiled with nvq++.
  • The 'nvidia' target uses cuStateVec; single precision (fp32) halves memory versus fp64, so an 80 GB GPU holds about 33 qubits in fp32 (8 bytes per amplitude) or 32 qubits in fp64.
  • The 'mqpu' option treats each GPU as a virtual QPU so independent circuits (parameter-shift terms, kernel entries, hyperparameter settings) run in parallel — ideal for QML's embarrassingly parallel workloads.
  • cuTensorNet contracts tensor networks for circuits with limited entanglement; cuDensityMat targets time evolution of open quantum systems (noisy dynamics).
  • Many other tools use cuQuantum under the hood: PennyLane lightning.gpu and lightning.tensor, Qiskit Aer GPU builds and qsim, so the same speed-ups reach non-CUDA-Q users.
  • NVIDIA also promotes tight GPU-QPU coupling (DGX Quantum, and the NVQLink interconnect announced in 2025) for real-time error correction and hybrid algorithms; QML benefits mainly through faster classical co-processing.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing GPUs remove the exponential wall: they speed each step, but 40 exact qubits still need about 16 TiB of memory.
  • Using fp32 for gradient-sensitive studies without checking: tiny gradients near barren plateaus can be lost to rounding.
  • Comparing CPU and GPU timings with different batch sizes or precision, which makes speed-up claims meaningless.

docs.title: Try it: Expectation value of a 2-qubit Hamiltonian in CUDA-Q (runs on CPU too)
docs.text:
# pip install cudaq
import cudaq
from cudaq import spin

@cudaq.kernel
def ansatz(theta: float):
    q = cudaq.qvector(2)
    x(q[0])
    ry(theta, q[1])
    x.ctrl(q[1], q[0])

H = (5.907 - 2.1433 * spin.x(0) * spin.x(1) - 2.1433 * spin.y(0) * spin.y(1)
     + 0.21829 * spin.z(0) - 6.125 * spin.z(1))
print(cudaq.observe(ansatz, H, 0.59).expectation())   # about -1.75
# cudaq.set_target("nvidia")   # switch to GPU state-vector simulation

docs.title: 7.8 Choosing a Simulator: State Vectors, Density Matrices, Tensor Networks and Shots
docs.text:
Different simulators make different trade-offs. A state-vector simulator is exact but needs memory that doubles with each qubit; a density-matrix simulator adds noise but squares the memory; tensor-network simulators handle many qubits if entanglement stays low. You also choose between exact answers and realistic 'shot' sampling.

Three ways to simulate a circuit

State vector Density matrix Tensor network / MPS Memory 2^n amplitudes 4^n entries grows with entanglement Laptop limit ~26-30 qubits ~13-15 qubits 50-100+ if shallow Noise via trajectories exact channels limited support Exactness exact exact approximate (bond dim.) Best for training, debugging noise studies wide shallow circuits

No single simulator wins; match it to qubit count, entanglement and noise needs.

Think of it like…

It is like choosing a map: a full satellite photo (state vector) shows everything but is enormous, a weather map (density matrix) adds the storms but is even bigger, and a subway map (tensor network) is tiny and practical as long as the city is not too tangled.

Real-world example

Hamid at the fictional Orchid Analytics tests a 12-qubit QNN. Exact state-vector training gives 94% accuracy. With 1,000 shots per expectation value, gradients become noisy and accuracy settles at 91%. Adding a depolarising noise model on a density-matrix simulator (4^12 entries, 256 MiB) drops it to 86% — the realistic number he reports.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start exact (state vector, no shots) to debug the model and check that it can learn at all.
  2. Add shots matching your hardware budget to see the effect of statistical noise on training.
  3. Add a noise model (gate, readout and decoherence errors) using a density-matrix or trajectory simulator.
  4. For many qubits with shallow circuits, switch to tensor-network or MPS simulation and monitor truncation error.
  5. Record the simulator, precision, shots and noise model in every result table.

Who uses it

Every QML researcher and student chooses simulators; reviewers increasingly ask for finite-shot and noisy results, not only exact ones.

Key takeaway

Memorise the scaling: state vector 2^n amplitudes, density matrix 4^n entries, and shot noise of an expectation value shrinks only as 1/sqrt(shots).

Going deeper

  • For an observable with outcomes ±1, the standard error of the estimated expectation is sqrt((1 - <O>^2) / N); near <O> = 0 that is 1/sqrt(N), so 10,000 shots give only about ±0.01 precision.
  • Matrix product state (MPS) simulators keep a 'bond dimension' chi; memory scales roughly as n·chi^2, and truncation discards small singular values — report chi and the truncation error.
  • Stabiliser simulators such as Stim simulate Clifford-only circuits with thousands of qubits in polynomial time (Gottesman-Knill theorem), useful for error-correction data but not for general QML circuits.
  • Pauli-propagation and other classical surrogate methods can estimate expectation values of some shallow or noisy circuits efficiently; recent papers use them to show certain QML models are classically simulable.
  • Quantum trajectory (Monte Carlo wave-function) simulation samples noisy state vectors instead of storing a density matrix, trading memory for repeated runs.
  • Parameter broadcasting in PennyLane and jax.vmap let one simulator call evaluate many inputs at once, often giving 10-100x speed-ups for kernel matrices and batches.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Reporting exact-simulation accuracy as if it were what hardware would achieve; always add finite-shot and noisy results.
  • Using an MPS simulator without checking truncation error, then mistaking truncation artefacts for model behaviour.
  • Forgetting to fix random seeds for shot sampling, making runs impossible to reproduce.

docs.title: Try it: Memory and shot-noise arithmetic every QML student should be able to do
docs.text:
import math
for n in (12, 20, 25, 30):
    sv = 2**n * 16 / 2**30          # complex128 state vector in GiB
    dm = 4**n * 16 / 2**30          # density matrix in GiB
    print(f"{n:2d} qubits: state vector {sv:.4g} GiB | density matrix {dm:.4g} GiB")
for shots in (100, 1_000, 10_000):
    print(f"{shots:>6} shots -> worst-case std of <Z> = {1/math.sqrt(shots):.3f}")

docs.title: 7.9 Cloud Access: Amazon Braket, IBM Quantum Platform and Azure Quantum
docs.text:
Real quantum computers are reached over the internet. Amazon Braket rents several vendors' machines with pay-per-shot pricing; IBM Quantum Platform offers IBM's own processors with a small free monthly allowance; Azure Quantum gives access to partner hardware from Microsoft's cloud. Each also offers managed simulators.

A Braket Hybrid Job training loop. The classical optimiser runs in a managed container next to the QPU queue, with priority access for the job's tasks.

Think of it like…

Cloud quantum access is like booking time on a famous telescope: you submit your observing request, wait in a queue, and pay per observation — or reserve the whole night if you have a big project.

Real-world example

Grace at the fictional Brightwater College runs a 4-qubit classifier's test set (40 circuits, 1,000 shots each) on IQM Garnet via Braket: 40 × ($0.30 + 1,000 × $0.00145) = $70. The same test on IBM's Open Plan would use only a small part of her free 10 minutes of QPU time for that month.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Create an account and set a budget alarm (AWS Budgets, IBM plan limits, Azure cost alerts).
  2. Develop against the provider's local or managed simulator first (Braket LocalSimulator/SV1, Qiskit Aer, Azure simulators).
  3. Check the device's qubit count, native gates, connectivity, calibration data and queue status.
  4. Submit work in batches: Braket Hybrid Jobs or Qiskit Runtime batch/session modes keep iterative jobs together.
  5. Download results, record device name, calibration date and job IDs for reproducibility.

Who uses it

Students on free tiers, researchers with grants, and enterprise R&D teams evaluating hardware vendors all use these cloud services.

Key takeaway

Know the cost model: Braket charges $0.30 per task plus a per-shot fee (e.g. $0.00145 on IQM Garnet, $0.08 on IonQ Forte, October 2026 list prices), while IBM bills by QPU time with a free 10 minutes per month on the Open Plan.

Going deeper

  • Braket's QPU list (October 2026 pricing page) includes AQT IBEX-Q1, IonQ Forte, IQM Emerald and Garnet, QuEra Aquila (analog neutral atoms) and Rigetti Cepheus; every task costs $0.30 plus $0.000425-$0.08 per shot depending on the device.
  • Braket managed simulators are billed per minute (SV1 $0.075 per minute, with a 3-second minimum); the free tier includes one hour of simulation per month for the first 12 months, but no free QPU time.
  • Hybrid Jobs run your classical code in a managed container (default ml.m5.xlarge at about $0.23 per hour) and give the job's quantum tasks priority in the QPU queue, which matters for iterative QML training.
  • IBM Quantum Platform (quantum.cloud.ibm.com) gives Open Plan users up to 10 minutes of QPU time per month on Heron-class processors such as the 156-qubit ibm_kingston; a 2026 promotion offered eligible researchers 180 minutes for 12 months.
  • IBM's 120-qubit Nighthawk processor (introduced November 2025) is offered as early access (ibm_miami) to Premium and Flex plan users rather than the free Open Plan.
  • Azure Quantum's documentation lists IonQ, Quantinuum, Pasqal and Rigetti targets; provider availability and pricing change, so check the live target list before planning a project.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Launching a full training loop on a QPU without a cost estimate: thousands of circuits at $0.30 per task add up to thousands of dollars quickly.
  • Ignoring queue times: a job can wait hours, during which device calibration changes and results drift.
  • Assuming every cloud offers every machine: Google's processors, for example, are not available as a public cloud service.

docs.title: Try it: Run a Bell circuit on Braket's free local simulator (no AWS account needed)
docs.text:
# pip install amazon-braket-sdk
from braket.circuits import Circuit
from braket.devices import LocalSimulator

bell = Circuit().h(0).cnot(0, 1)
result = LocalSimulator().run(bell, shots=1000).result()
print(result.measurement_counts)   # roughly half '00' and half '11'

docs.title: 7.10 Running QML on Real Hardware: Shots, Queues, Costs and Noise
docs.text:
Real quantum processors are noisy, slow to access and charged by use. A model that trains beautifully on a simulator may need tens of thousands of circuit runs on hardware. Successful hardware experiments are small, carefully budgeted and often train on a simulator and only test on the device.

From simulator model to hardware result. Most of the budget is spent on planning so the expensive step runs once.

Think of it like…

Training on hardware is like rehearsing an orchestra that is only available for ten expensive minutes a month: you practise with recordings at home and use the live session for the performance that matters.

Real-world example

Omar at the fictional Silverline Fintech estimates a full hardware training run: 20 parameters, 50 training points, parameter-shift gradients (41 circuits per point), 100 epochs, 1,000 shots on IQM Garnet. That is 205,000 circuits — about $359,000. He instead trains on a simulator and runs only the 200-point test set on hardware for $350.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Count circuits: points × (2 × parameters + 1) per epoch with parameter-shift, times epochs.
  2. Multiply by shots and the provider's per-task and per-shot prices, or by expected QPU seconds.
  3. Transpile to the device and check depth and two-qubit gate count after routing (SWAPs).
  4. Reduce cost: fewer parameters, local observables, SPSA gradients, batching, or train-on-simulator then test-on-hardware.
  5. Run, then log device name, calibration time, qubits used, shots and job IDs.

Who uses it

QML researchers publishing hardware results, industry proof-of-concept teams and anyone spending a hardware grant must do this planning.

Key takeaway

A strong interview answer: parameter-shift needs two circuit evaluations per parameter per data point, so gradient cost — not a single forward pass — dominates hardware QML budgets.

Going deeper

  • Typical 2025-2026 figures: superconducting two-qubit gate errors around 0.1-1%, readout errors around 0.5-3%, and coherence times (T1, T2) of roughly 100-300 microseconds on leading devices; trapped ions have slower gates but higher fidelities, e.g. Helios's reported 99.921% two-qubit fidelity.
  • Routing on limited connectivity inserts SWAP gates, each costing three CNOTs; an all-to-all entangling ansatz on a heavy-hex or square lattice can triple in depth after transpilation.
  • SPSA estimates a gradient from just two circuit evaluations regardless of parameter count, making it popular on hardware despite noisier updates.
  • Global-cost observables (measuring all qubits) suffer more from noise and barren plateaus than local ones; measuring one or two qubits also reduces readout error.
  • Calibration drifts over hours; long training runs spanning several calibrations can show jumps in loss unrelated to learning, so record timestamps and calibration data.
  • Train-on-simulator, infer-on-hardware is the most common credible design for small studies, but report that training never saw the real noise.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Quoting a simulator accuracy in the abstract and a hardware accuracy only in an appendix; report both prominently.
  • Using all qubits on a chip instead of selecting the best-calibrated connected subset.
  • Forgetting the per-task fee, which dominates cost for small shot counts on cheap devices.

docs.title: Try it: Estimate what full hardware training would cost before you press run
docs.text:
params, points, shots, epochs = 20, 50, 1000, 100
circuits_per_epoch = points * (2 * params + 1)   # parameter-shift + forward pass
per_circuit = 0.30 + shots * 0.00145             # Braket task fee + IQM Garnet per-shot (Oct 2026 list)
print(circuits_per_epoch, "circuits per epoch")
print(f"${circuits_per_epoch * per_circuit:,.0f} per epoch")
print(f"${epochs * circuits_per_epoch * per_circuit:,.0f} for full training")
